interfaces.name: Gradient
interfaces.doc: A gradient value, as `gradient`, `radialGradient` and `conicGradient` build it. Any `Fill` slot takes one, and a drawing can too. Write it through a constructor rather than by hand: the shape is published so a program can read one back.

interfaces.name: Stroke
interfaces.doc: A border, built by `stroke(width, color)`. It is drawn INSIDE the box, so a stroke never changes a view's size — there is no `borderWidth` to add to a layout.

interfaces.name: Outline
interfaces.doc: A stroke around the edges of the GLYPHS, built by `outline(width, color)` — the value `Text.outline` takes. It rides under the fill, so a filled letter shows a thin ring and an unfilled one reads hollow; it is not a box around the run.

interfaces.name: Shadow
interfaces.doc: A drop shadow, built by `shadow(dx, dy, blur, color)`. It is also a `Filter`, so it composes in a filter list; on `textShadow` it shadows the glyphs.

interfaces.name: Cursor
interfaces.doc: The data a `:path` reads against — a view's place in the bound data, its `datapath` plus its position under replication. You rarely name the type: a `:path` reads through it for you.

interfaces.name: IslandPost
interfaces.doc: One message across the island boundary — what `post` sends and `onPost` receives between an embedded app and its host.

interfaces.name: IslandNavigation
interfaces.doc: A navigation the embedded app asked for — what an island's `onNavigate` receives: `to`, the address made absolute; `program`, the Declare program it names ("" when none); `location`, the place after its `#`; `newWindow`, whether it asked for a window of its own (`openWindow`).

interfaces.name: TextStyle
members: fontFamily?: string | Font | readonly (string | Font)[] | null
interfaces.doc: The style of one run of text that has no view — a `style` bundle, or an inline record with the same fields. Each field is the `Text` attribute of that name; a field left out takes its plain default, never an inherited value.

interfaces.name: BlockGeometry
interfaces.doc: One block type's geometry in a rich-text flow: a measure to cap its width at (0 = the full track), a `[left, right]` margin, and how it sits in what is left. Every field is optional; what a block does not state it takes from the map's `default` entry, field by field.

interfaces.name: TextMeasure
interfaces.doc: What measureText reports — a Text's own fact names.

interfaces.name: DelayHandle
interfaces.doc: What `afterDelay(ms, fn)` returns: `cancel()` drops the wait if it has not run.

interfaces.name: DrawGradient
members: addColorStop(offset: number, color: string | Color): void
interfaces.doc: A gradient built INSIDE a drawing, by `d.createLinearGradient` and its kin — the Canvas2D shape, stops added by call. The declarative `Gradient` is the one a `fill` slot takes; this one exists only for the duration of a recording.

interfaces.name: DrawImageSource
interfaces.doc: What `d.drawImage` accepts: any `Image` view, by its loading facts. Structural, so a subclass of `Image` qualifies — you hand over the node, not a URL, because the node is what knows whether the bytes have arrived.

interfaces.doc: The canvas drawing context a `draw(d: Draw)` body receives — a Canvas2D- shaped recorder whose operations every renderer replays (runtime/src/draw.ts).

interfaces.name: Touch
interfaces.doc: One finger in a multi-finger gesture: a stable id for its lifetime, and a point. The id is what lets you follow the same finger across moves.

interfaces.name: ValueChange
interfaces.doc: One value that ended a settle different from where it started — its name, and what it was and is. The unit `onChange` reports.

interfaces.name: ChangeEvent
interfaces.doc: What `onChange` receives: every value this node named in `trackChanges` that ended the settle different, in list order, once per settle.

interfaces.name: PointerEvent
interfaces.doc: A pointer's position, in both frames. `x`/`y` are in this view's own coordinates (through its whole transform); `rootX`/`rootY` are in root space — the frame a drag reads, since it does not move with the dragged view (and the one `app.viewAt` takes). `deltaX`/`deltaY` are how far the pointer has moved, in root space, since the press (0 with no press; on a wheel, the scroll amount).

interfaces.name: PointerUpEvent
interfaces.doc: A release, plus the one fact a drag handler must not miss: `canceled` is true when the browser reclaimed the gesture — a touch that became a scroll. Commit on release only when it is false, or an interruption reads as a drop.

interfaces.name: TouchEvent
interfaces.doc: The multi-finger stream: every finger down (`touches`) and the ones this event moved (`changed`). Declaring a touch handler claims every finger, so the app then owes its own zoom.

interfaces.name: WheelEvent
interfaces.doc: A wheel or trackpad scroll, by axis: how far is `deltaX` and `deltaY` (from PointerEvent), in pixels. A trackpad PINCH arrives here too, with `pinch` true — the browser reports it as a wheel event with a modifier, and hiding that would make a zoom impossible to write.

interfaces.name: PinchEvent
interfaces.doc: A resolved two-finger zoom: the accumulated `scale` (1 at `onPinchStart`) and the point between the fingers it pivots about. `center` is that point in ROOT space (the same as `rootX`/`rootY`); `x`/`y` are the same point in this view's own coordinates — what zooming "about the fingers" on this view wants.

interfaces.name: KeyEvent
interfaces.doc: A key, both ways: `code` is the physical key regardless of layout (what a shortcut wants), `key` is the character it produced (what typing wants). Plus the four modifiers and whether the key is repeating.

interfaces.name: FocusGeometry
interfaces.doc: Where the focus indicator should be, and where it came from — the rect and radius to draw, the view and root it belongs to, the scroller it sits in, and the `home…` fields it is travelling from. What a custom focus ring reads to animate.

interfaces.name: TooltipEvent
interfaces.doc: A tooltip's request: the text, and the rect of the view asking, so a custom tip can place itself against the thing it describes.

interfaces.name: StreamMessage
interfaces.doc: One message from an `EventStream` or `Socket`: its payload, its type, and its id. `onMessage` receives it, and `last` holds the most recent.

interfaces.name: File
interfaces.doc: A file the person chose (`Files.pick`) or dropped (`onFilesDrop`): its name, size in bytes, MIME type, when it last changed (ms since 1970), its path within a chosen or dropped folder ("" for a file on its own), and a `url` that reads it — an `Image`'s `source`, a `DataSource`'s `url` — or, in a `DataSource` body, uploads it.

interfaces.name: FilesOver
interfaces.doc: Files dragged over a view: how many (0 when the browser does not say), and where, in the view's own coordinates.

interfaces.name: FilesDrop
interfaces.doc: Files dropped on a view: the files — a dropped folder's, every file in it, each with its path — and where, in the view's own coordinates.

interfaces.name: PickOptions
interfaces.doc: What `Files.pick` offers: the types (MIME types or extensions), more than one file, or a whole folder.

interfaces.name: TraceChange
interfaces.doc: One attribute the wake trace saw change: the view it lives on (`path`) and the attribute, its value before and after, and — for a change the settle made — the rule that wrote it (`by`; null for a plain write).

interfaces.name: TraceSettle
interfaces.doc: One settle, as the wake trace recorded it: its number; when it opened (`at`, ms since the trace started) and how long it ran (`ms`); the user code that ran before it (`origin`); how many rules the kernel ran (`runs`); the writes that opened it (`triggers`) and what it changed in response (`changes`); and `unnamed`, cells that moved but belong to no addressable attribute.

aliases.name: Percent
aliases.doc: A percentage literal — what `width = 50%` becomes. Resolved against the parent on each axis, reactively, so a percent is a live relationship and not a number computed once.

aliases.name: Length
aliases.doc: What a geometry slot takes: a number in the view's own units, or a percent of the parent on that axis. There is no unit vocabulary — no px, em or rem — because there is one coordinate space and the renderer owns the device pixels.

aliases.name: Radius
aliases.doc: A corner rounding: one number for all four corners, or `[topLeft, topRight, bottomRight, bottomLeft]` to round only some.

aliases.name: Inset
aliases.doc: A room-inside: one number insets all four sides, or `[top, right, bottom, left]` to inset only some. The same literal shape as a `Radius` and a different meaning — a radius rounds corners and counts from the top-LEFT, an inset holds edges away and counts from the TOP.

aliases.name: Color
aliases.doc: A color as `0xRRGGBB`, or with alpha as the runtime's own encoding (see `colorWithAlpha`). `null` means NO color — an unfilled view, an unstroked box — which is why it is part of the type rather than a sentinel. In a bare slot the CSS names and `#RRGGBB` are also legal; inside `{ }` a color is a number.

aliases.name: Shape
aliases.doc: A clip path, as the `clip` slot takes it: an SVG path string in the view's own coordinates, or `null` for the plain rectangle. `clip = true` is the box; a shape is for everything else.

aliases.name: Fill
aliases.doc: What a fill slot holds: a flat color, or a gradient. `null` is no fill at all.

aliases.name: BoxStroke
aliases.type: Stroke | readonly [Stroke | null, Stroke | null, Stroke | null, Stroke | null] | null
aliases.doc: What the `stroke` slot holds: ONE Stroke on all four sides, or four — `[top, right, bottom, left]`, clockwise from the top, `null` for a bare side. The one-or-four shape is the house pattern for anything said per side (see `Radius`), and the slot reads back what was written, so a body that reaches into a stroke asks which form it has first: `Array.isArray(v.stroke)`, or `v.stroke && "width" in v.stroke`. `null` is no border at all.

aliases.name: Filter
aliases.type: { fn: "blur"; radius: number } | { fn: "brightness" | "contrast" | "saturate" | "grayscale" | "invert" | "sepia"; amount: number } | { fn: "hueRotate"; degrees: number } | { fn: "colorize"; color: Color } | Shadow
aliases.doc: One entry in a filter list: a blur, one of the amount filters, a hue rotation, a colorize, or a shadow. `filter` applies the list to the view's own paint as a GROUP (so a subtree blurs together, not child by child); `backdrop` applies the same list to what lies beneath. There is no CSS `filter` string: the tokens are functions, so a misspelling is a compile error rather than a silent no-op.

aliases.name: Backdrop
aliases.doc: What lies BENEATH a view, filtered: the same list `filter` takes, applied to the backdrop instead of the view's own paint. `frost` is the common one.

aliases.name: Theme
aliases.doc: A token record — every color and metric an app names once. Provided down the tree (`provided("theme")`), spread to override a token, and declared at the top level with `theme Name [ … ]`. Its keys are open by design: a record whose keys the program chooses cannot be closed without firing on correct code. A read of `provided("theme")` is closed all the same, over every token some theme declares, so a misspelled token is a compile error.

aliases.name: TextStyles
aliases.doc: The palette a `<span class>` names: style name → that style's fields. The KEYS are open — content chooses them — and the VALUES are closed, so a misspelled field is caught in the record form exactly as it is in a `style` bundle. This is the one record slot that can be narrowed without firing on correct code: only the value side has a declared shape.

aliases.name: RichTextLayout
aliases.doc: Per-BLOCK-TYPE geometry for a rich-text flow: block name → that block's `BlockGeometry`. The keys are the block types a document has — `default` for all of them, then `code`, `p`, `h1`, `blockquote` and the rest by name — so a reading measure with full-bleed code is two entries: `richTextLayout = { { default: { maxWidth: 560 }, code: { maxWidth: 0 } } }`. A `pre` with no entry of its own follows `code`. Keys open, values closed: a misspelled field is caught, a block type you invent is not.

aliases.name: MotionCurve
aliases.doc: An easing curve, built by `cubicBezier`, `back`, `steps` or `laszlo` — what an `Animator`'s `motion` takes, alongside the named tokens. Opaque by design: a curve is a value you pass, not a shape you inspect.

functions.name: activeTone
functions.doc: The house ACTIVE TONE: `accent` laid 22% over the `surface` it sits on — what a theme's `controlSelected` holds. An app that overrides `accent` computes it so the selected tone follows, instead of keeping the preset's, which was derived from a different accent: `controlSelected: activeTone(pick, base.surface)`. Both arguments are colors; nothing is read from the tree, so it means the same wherever it is called.

functions.name: gradient
functions.signature: gradient(...args: (Color | string | { offset: number | null; color: Color })[]): Gradient
functions.doc: A linear gradient: `gradient(#F8F8F8, #D8D8D8)` top to bottom, or with an angle first — `gradient("90deg", …)`. Colors spread evenly; `stop(offset, color)` places one exactly. Legal in a bare slot, which is why it is a call and not a record.

functions.name: radialGradient
functions.signature: radialGradient(cx: number, cy: number, r: number, ...stops: (Color | { offset: number | null; color: Color })[]): Gradient
functions.doc: A radial gradient from a center and radius, in the view's own units — a glow, a vignette, a sphere's shading.

functions.name: conicGradient
functions.signature: conicGradient(cx: number, cy: number, angle: number, ...stops: (Color | { offset: number | null; color: Color })[]): Gradient
functions.doc: A gradient swept AROUND a center from a starting angle — a hue wheel, a pie, a progress sweep.

functions.name: stroke
functions.doc: Build a border: `stroke = stroke(1, #B0B0B0)`. Drawn inside the box, so it costs no layout.

functions.name: outline
functions.doc: Build a ring drawn outside the box — what a focus silhouette wears.

functions.name: stop
functions.signature: stop(offset: number, color: Color): { offset: number; color: Color }
functions.doc: Place one gradient stop at an exact offset (0 to 1) instead of letting the colors spread evenly.

functions.name: shadow
functions.signature: shadow(dx: number, dy: number, blur: number, color: Color): Shadow
functions.doc: Build a drop shadow — offset, blur, color. On `shadow` it falls from the box, on `textShadow` from the glyphs, and in a filter list it composes with the rest.

functions.name: frost
functions.doc: The frosted-glass backdrop: blur what lies beneath, and lift its saturation a little so color shows through rather than going grey. `backdrop = frost(26, 1.5)`.

functions.name: blur
functions.doc: Blur, by radius in the view's own units. `filter = blur(4)` blurs this view's paint; `backdrop = blur(20)` blurs what is behind it.

functions.name: brightness
functions.doc: Scale brightness — 1 is unchanged, 0 is black, above 1 lightens.

functions.name: contrast
functions.doc: Scale contrast — 1 is unchanged, 0 is flat grey, above 1 hardens.

functions.name: saturate
functions.doc: Scale saturation — 1 is unchanged, 0 is grey, above 1 intensifies.

functions.name: grayscale
functions.doc: Remove color, 0 to 1, where 1 is fully grey.

functions.name: invert
functions.doc: Invert, 0 to 1, where 1 is a full negative.

functions.name: sepia
functions.doc: Warm toward sepia, 0 to 1.

functions.name: hueRotate
functions.doc: Rotate every hue around the color wheel by an angle in degrees.

functions.name: colorize
functions.doc: Replace the paint's color while KEEPING its alpha — the one-mask-many-colors idiom: one bitmap or drawing, recolored per use. `Image.tint` is the shorthand for an image.

functions.name: colorWithAlpha
functions.doc: A translucent color in the runtime's own encoding: an `0xRRGGBB` and an alpha from 0 to 255 — the same byte an `0xRRGGBBAA` literal carries, which is what the compiler lowers that literal to. Returns an opaque `0xRRGGBB` at 255, so the common case stays a plain color.

functions.name: measureText
functions.signature: measureText(text: string, style: TextStyle, width?: number): TextMeasure
functions.doc: Measure a run of text in a style, with the measurer and wrapping a `Text` uses — one line, or wrapped at `width`. Called in a constraint or a drawing, it re-runs when anything it measured with changes, a font's faces included. The style says everything the measurement uses: a field left out takes its plain default, never the face around it. **To measure the way a `Text` here would render, pass `providedTextStyle(…)`** — the provided face, with your overrides: `measureText(words, providedTextStyle({ lineHeight: 1.3 }), 300).width`.

functions.name: hostProvided
functions.doc: A value this program's HOST provides — the program that embeds it lists the name in its island's `provides`; a page embedding it calls `app.provide`. The default stands in when nothing is provided (the program running on its own, or the host not listing the name) and states the type: a value of a different kind is refused at the read, with a warning. The name must be a literal. Reactive: when the host's value changes, everything that read it re-derives. `theme = { hostProvided("theme", app.dark ? SanFranciscoDark : SanFrancisco) }`.

functions.name: hostProvided
functions.doc: A value this program's HOST provides — the program that embeds it lists the name in its island's `provides`; a page embedding it calls `app.provide`. The default stands in when nothing is provided (the program running on its own, or the host not listing the name) and states the type: a value of a different kind is refused at the read, with a warning. The name must be a literal. Reactive: when the host's value changes, everything that read it re-derives. `theme = { hostProvided("theme", app.dark ? SanFranciscoDark : SanFrancisco) }`.

functions.name: afterDelay
functions.doc: Run `fn` once, `ms` milliseconds from now — never in the frame that asked, so `afterDelay(0, fn)` is the next frame. The wait belongs to the node whose handler asked: discarding that node cancels it, and the handle's `cancel()` drops it sooner. Handlers and methods only. Rarely the tool: a value that should change when something happens is a constraint on that something, a repeating call is a `Time` member (`tick = 5000`), and motion is a Spring or an Animator.

functions.name: providedTextStyle
functions.doc: The `TextStyle` in force where you write this — the provided text face (`textColor`, `fontSize`, `fontFamily`, `fontWeight`, `letterSpacing`), each falling to the same default a `Text` would, with `overrides` replacing any of them. Hand it to `measureText` or a drawing's `fillText`/`strokeText` to measure or paint a run the way a `Text` here would render it. It is a property of the node, so a value body and that same view's `draw()` get the same record; a drawing's own `font` state is unrelated to it.

functions.name: escapeHtml
functions.doc: Make a value safe to CONCATENATE into rich-text content: `&`, `<`, `>`, `"` and `'` become entities, and nothing else changes. **Escape every interpolated value, never the markup you wrote** — the markup is how content names an inline view, so an unescaped `<` or `'` arriving from data does not merely read wrong, it closes an attribute or opens an element of its own. Content assembled in a `{ }` is the only place this matters; a literal document has nothing to escape. `html = { "Assigned to <Person name='" + escapeHtml(app.me) + "'/>" }`

functions.name: cubicBezier
functions.signature: cubicBezier(x1: number, y1: number, x2: number, y2: number): MotionCurve
functions.doc: An easing curve from two control points, the CSS `cubic-bezier` form — so a curve copied from a design tool or a stylesheet transfers unchanged.

functions.name: back
functions.doc: An easing curve that overshoots its destination and settles back. The argument is how far past it goes.

functions.name: steps
functions.doc: A stepped curve: `n` discrete jumps rather than a continuous ease — a ticking counter, a sprite flip. `jump` chooses whether the first or last step is taken at the ends.

functions.name: laszlo
functions.doc: An easing curve in OpenLaszlo's pole form: a begin and end pole rather than two control points. The same family of shapes as `cubicBezier`, reached the way the animations it came from were written.

functions.name: afterSettle
functions.doc: Run `fn` exactly once, at the close of the current settle — your handler's writes applied, views real, placed, and sized, nothing painted yet. What it writes lands in the same frame as the change itself. Reach for a constraint first; afterSettle is for work that is irreducibly a READING of the new geometry (aiming a camera at a view your write just caused to exist), never for waiting.

namespaces.name: Files
namespaces.doc: The person's files: `pick` opens the file dialog — from a press, as a browser allows one only then — and resolves to the files chosen, none if it was dismissed.

namespaces.name: Accessibility
namespaces.doc: What a program says to assistive technology with no view to say it from — "Message sent", "3 results": `announce` speaks it without moving the focus, `polite` (the default) at the next pause, `assertive` at once. A view whose own changes should be heard sets `accessibilityLive` instead.

steps.description: Install the toolchain's dependencies (TypeScript, esbuild, and the Chrome driver the checking tools run on). The clone ships prebuilt — no build step before first run. pnpm works too — the repo pre-approves esbuild's install script.

Start the dev server. It prints its address — http://127.0.0.1:8200/ unless that port is taken, in which case it says so and names the next (`PORT=8201 npm start`). Browse to any .declare file's URL under it and the server compiles and returns the running app.
Write a program to my-apps/hello.declare and browse to it under the server's address — http://127.0.0.1:8200/my-apps/hello.declare on the default port. The program URL is the app's address.
Recompile the runtime and compiler (tsc) — needed only after editing the toolchain's own .ts sources, never for writing Declare programs.
Climb the ladder — structure → resolution → analysis → boot (add --assert / --states / --baselines for behavior and visual rungs). Stops at the first failure; every diagnostic names its fix.

Compile and report, emitting nothing — parse, resolve, check, and typecheck, for one file or many (a library file too). --json emits a machine record per diagnostic (file, code, severity, line, col). Exit 1 on any error; warnings never fail.
Rewrite to the one house style (canon). --check exits 1 on drift (the CI gate); no flag prints to stdout.
Everything that tests the SOURCES, and rungs 1–4 for every app and class in the corpus. Needs no `npm run derive` and is meaningful on any tree — no suite here reads a derived artifact.

steps.cmd: npm run derive && npm run test:derived
steps.description: The suites whose SUBJECT is a derived artifact — the assembled doc model, declare-help's knowledge base, the committed prewarm cache, the production builds. Only meaningful straight after a derive, which is why the command carries it: run alone on a stale tree it tests yesterday's artifact.

The SLOW rungs, pre-release: every app shipping a tests/ folder (tests/assert.mjs, tests/states.mjs, tests/baselines/) is climbed to R5 (real input) and R6 (pixels vs baselines) in headless Chromium. Discovery-based, so a new script is picked up by existing. `npm run test:all` runs both suites.

maintaining.title: Maintaining the system (after changing toolchain sources or docs)

steps.description: Regenerate every committed derived artifact — bundles, the doc model, the prewarm cache, the production builds, the baked pages, the build id. One rule graph owns the order (tools/internal/derive.mjs), and a rule whose inputs are unchanged is skipped, so a doc edit runs the doc rules and nothing else. This is what writes the artifacts: no hook derives, and a commit writes nothing (the one exception is that a suite booting the dev server rebuilds a stale platform bundle). Required before a push, and before `npm run test:derived`.
Every declare-docs: symbolic link in the corpus resolves against the generated registry.
The three spine projections (declare-model.json, the marker-injected doc tables, the skill inventory) match a fresh assembly of the live registries.

Every `## heading` in tools/internal/doc/prose/ binds to a real attribute, event, or method — prose that binds to nothing is silently dropped from the reference (13 documented events once rendered blank this way).
Precompile to a self-contained production bundle (~45KB gz + your program). --render=canvas selects the canvas renderer; --debug keeps positions.
Also bake the crawled document (every linked location's content) into the built page for crawlers.
Append ?extract to any program URL to see the document a crawler gets.

forms.answer:
App [ members ]
A program is one tree, and `App [ … ]` is its root — one per program. With `width` and `height` unset it fills its host, which is the common case: the page, the window, the island it is mounted in. Everything else nests inside its brackets, and `app` (lower case) names the running instance from any depth — which makes it the place for the few values the whole app shares, such as the current selection or a mode.
3 rules the compiler enforces · docs: language/app · declare.md §4 Composition

Type [ members ]
  name: Type [ members ]
Square brackets hold a node's members — attributes, declarations, methods, handlers, children — and the nesting of brackets *is* the tree. Naming a type with a bracketed body instantiates it: `Text [ text = "OK" ]` is a Text, `bg: View [ … ]` a View reachable as `bg`. Every member inside is one of the five shapes (set, declare, child, method, handler), separated by commas.
4 rules the compiler enforces · docs: language/instance · declare.md §2 Two delimiters

class Name [ members ]                    // a view
  class Name extends Base [ members ]       // any other base
This is the one way to define a class. Everything inside the brackets is a **member**: `name = value` sets an attribute the base already has, `name: Type = value` declares a new one, `name: Type [ … ]` is a named child, `name() { … }` a method, `onThing() { … }` a handler for an event the node fires. Instantiate the class by naming it with a `[ ]` body, as many times as you like; each instance may set any attribute and add members of its own.
6 rules the compiler enforces · docs: language/class · declare.md §4 Composition

class Name extends Base [ … ]
Single inheritance from another class — a library class or one of your own. The subclass sees every attribute, child, method, and event of the base. Re-stating an attribute with `name = value` **overrides** its default; re-stating a method replaces it; and a base's named child is reached by name, not redeclared. Omit `extends` altogether and the base is `Node` — a model class with no box.
3 rules the compiler enforces · docs: language/extends · declare.md §4 Composition

HTMLText [ html = "Filed under <Chip label='docs'/> today." ]
  Markdown [ text = "Fixed by <Issue id='142'/>." ]
  <Chip key='a' label='docs'/>                 // key: this view's identity across a content change
Inside rich-text content, a **self-closing tag whose name is a view class the program declares** is one real view of that class, placed in the flowing line as an atomic box the words wrap around. There is no whitelist to extend and no attribute to set: the class existing is what makes the tag mean it, matched by the name exactly as written, in both formats (`HTMLText`'s `html` and `Markdown`'s `text`). A tag naming no class of yours keeps the meaning it already had — the HTML whitelist, an autolink, a literal `<` — and a `<span class>` stays a style, never a view.
5 rules the compiler enforces · docs: language/inlineview · declare.md §9 Style

name = literal
  name = { expression }
  name = :path
Sets an attribute the class already has. The right-hand side is one of three things, and the spelling says which: a **bare literal** (a number, a percent, a color, a string, a keyword — set once), a **`{ }` constraint** (TypeScript that stays true), or a **`:path`** read from bound data. A bare `[ … ]` list fills an array-typed attribute.
4 rules the compiler enforces · docs: language/set · declare.md §3 Members and scope

name: Type = value
  name: Type                                 // no default: undefined until written
  rows: Row[] = []
  panel: Menu? = null                         // a class — the attribute holds an instance
Declares a new reactive attribute — the way state enters a program. The type is a TypeScript type, the same vocabulary a signature uses: TypeScript's built-ins (`number`, `string`, `Map<string, Row>`), Declare's own (`Color`, `Length`, `Radius`), a class, a declared schema, a literal union (`"open" | "closed"`), an array, a tuple, or a function type. The default is a bare literal or a `{ }` expression.
4 rules the compiler enforces · docs: language/declare · declare.md §3 Members and scope

name: Type [ members ]
  Type [ members ]                           // anonymous
A child is a member that is itself an instance. Named, it is reachable from its siblings and its class as `name`; anonymous, it is placed and painted but never addressed. Children paint in declaration order — later siblings on top; there is no z-index — and a parent with a `layout:` member arranges them, while one without positions them by their own `x`/`y`.
3 rules the compiler enforces · docs: language/child · declare.md §3 Members and scope

name(a: T) -> R { … }
  f: (id: string) -> void                   // a function type, in a parameter or a declaration
The return-type marker in a signature, and the arrow of a function type. `quant(v: number) -> number { … }` returns a number; omit it for a method that returns nothing. In a type position, `(a: T) -> R` is a function type — a parameter that takes a callback, or a declared attribute holding one.
1 rule the compiler enforces · docs: language/arrow · declare.md §3 Members and scope

text = :title                              // a read, relative to the nearest datapath
  View [ datapath = :rows[], … ]             // [] replicates: one instance per record
  text = { :on ? :title : "—" }              // a read inside a body
  input(v: boolean) { :done = v }            // a write, in a handler or method
  Text [ datapath = :tags[], text = :@ ]     // :@ — the record itself
  text = { "" + :@[(classroot.field)] }      // [( … )] — a key computed by TypeScript
A colon-prefixed path reads from bound data, relative to the nearest enclosing `datapath`. `datapath` selects a place in a dataset; descendants read fields relative to it; and a path ending in `[]` **replicates** its node — one instance per record, reconciled by the record's `id`. This is what replaces `items.map(…)`: a collection of children comes from data, never from code in the tree.
5 rules the compiler enforces · docs: language/datapath · declare.md §7 Data

View [ datapath = :people[], key = :email ]
Replication reuses an instance across sorts, filters and edits when it can tell which record is which. By convention that is the record's `id` field, with nothing declared. When a collection's identity lives under another name, `key = :field` on the replicated node names it — a single `:path`, read per record. It is replication metadata, so it is legal only beside a many-path `datapath`.
2 rules the compiler enforces · docs: language/key · declare.md §7 Data

TextInput [ text <-> :title ]
  TextInput [ text <-> { fieldName } ]       // a { } yielding a field name
Two-way binding, opt-in and for leaf editors only. The left side is an editor's value; the right names a **place in data** — a `:path`, or a `{ }` yielding a field name — resolved against the nearest enclosing `datapath`. Edits in the field write back through the cursor, and a change in the data shows in the field. It is the only arrow in the language that writes.
3 rules the compiler enforces · docs: language/twoway · declare.md §7 Data

fill = gradient(#F8F8F8, #D8D8D8)          // bare: colors in the bare vocabulary
  fill = { gradient("180deg", 0xF8F8F8, 0xD8D8D8) }
  stroke = stroke(1, #B0B0B0)                // drawn inside the box
  stroke = [ stroke(1, #B0B0B0), null, stroke(1, #B0B0B0), null ]   // per side, top first
  shadow = shadow(0, 4, 12, #00000033)       // dx, dy, blur, color
  backdrop = frost(26, 1.5)                  // blur, saturate
The value constructors build the composite values decoration attributes take: a gradient, a stroke, a shadow, a frosted backdrop, a gradient `stop`. They are the only call forms a bare value admits, and each has one shape — the message names it when the call is wrong. Inside a `{ }` the same names are ordinary functions, with colors written as numbers.
2 rules the compiler enforces · docs: language/constructors · declare.md §9 Style

width = 240                                // a number
  width = 100%                               // a percent, of the parent
  x = center                                 // a position literal, on x/y
  fill = navy                                // a named color
  fill = #336699                             // a hex color; #RRGGBBAA carries alpha
  text = "one line"                          // a string ends at its line
  text = """
      several lines
      """                                    // a block string
  axis = y                                   // an enum token
The bare-value vocabulary the compiler owns: numbers, percents, the position literals `center` and `end`, colors by name or hex, strings, booleans, `null`, and the enum tokens each attribute names. A bare literal is the value itself, set once. Inside `{ }` none of this exists — there you are in TypeScript, where a color is `0x336699` and a size is arithmetic on the parent.
3 rules the compiler enforces · docs: language/literals · declare.md §2 Two delimiters

this.width                                 // the node the code is written on
  parent.width                               // its parent
  classroot.label                            // the instance of the class being defined
  app.theme                                  // the running application
A bare name resolves outward through the enclosing brackets, innermost first — the brackets are the scope exactly as they are the tree — and the compiler rewrites the read to an explicit path at compile time. Four reserved words say it explicitly: **`this`**, the node the code is written on; **`parent`**; **`classroot`**, the instance of the class being defined, from any depth inside it; and **`app`**, the running application, from anywhere.
5 rules the compiler enforces · docs: language/scope · declare.md §3 Members and scope

include [ "path.declare" ]
  include [ "a.declare", "b.declare" ]
Merges another file's **top-level declarations** — its classes, scripts, styles, themes, schemas — into this program, once, however many times it is named. It is not a module system: there are no exports, no namespacing, and no root instance comes across. Everything merges into one program, and a class in an included file may extend one declared here.
2 rules the compiler enforces · docs: language/include · declare.md §4 Composition

use [ Name, Other ]
Keeps classes the production build would otherwise drop. The build tree-shakes anything no tag instantiates; a class your code constructs **by name** at runtime — `app.createView("Badge")`, an icon named by a string in a control's `iconLeft` — is mentioned nowhere in the tree, so it would be removed. `use` says it is still needed.
1 rule the compiler enforces · docs: language/use · declare.md §4 Composition

ship [ islands = ["name", "../../other/other"] ]
  ship [ files = ["../../docs/model.json", "app.declare"] ]
  ship [ compiler = true, inspector = true ]
States what a **self-contained package** of this program must carry beyond what its source names. A production build (`declarec`) reads the block; the dev server and the static site, which carry every source and a compiler, read none of it. Each member is a fact about the program, never a build option:
5 rules the compiler enforces · docs: language/ship · declare.md §4 Composition

defaultFlags [ render = canvas ]
  defaultFlags [ kernel = js, crawler = true ]
The program's own defaults for the platform's flags, the same ones a request names in its URL (`?render=canvas`) and `declarec` takes (`--render=canvas`), with the same values. A flag the request or the command names wins; one it leaves out, the program's block decides; one neither names takes the platform's default.
4 rules the compiler enforces · docs: language/defaultFlags · declare.md §4 Composition

script { … }                               // inline TypeScript
  script [ "file.ts" ]                       // the same, from a file
A top-level block of plain TypeScript, wholly outside the reactive system: pure functions of their arguments (date arithmetic, formatting, parsing), stateful helpers, whole libraries. A program may hold any number of blocks, inline and files mixed; they share one scope in source order. A file is written module-style (`export` allowed); an inline block refuses `export`, since its top-level names are already visible to every `{ }`. A block may `import` ES modules — a relative file, or an npm package by bare specifier — bundled at compile by a Node host (the dev server, `declarec`, `verify`); the in-browser compile refuses imports by name.
4 rules the compiler enforces · docs: language/script · declare.md §4 Composition

brand: Font [ FontFace [ src = "brand-400.woff2" ], FontFace [ src = "brand-700.woff2", weight = bold ] ]
  ui: Font [ family = "Helvetica Neue" ]
  fontFamily = { [app.brand, "sans-serif"] }
A typeface is an **object in the tree**, not a top-level declaration: a `Font` with `FontFace` children, usually on the App, or a `Font [ family = "…" ]` with no faces for a system font. A family attribute holds it — `fontFamily = { app.brand }`, or a list in a `{ }`, `{ [app.brand, "sans-serif"] }` — so switching fonts is an assignment. `loaded` and `failed` are the font's facts; `wait` and `late` say what loading is worth. A FontFace's `weight` is a keyword, a number 1–1000, or `range(lo, hi)` for a variable font file. See the `Font` and `FontFace` classes.
4 rules the compiler enforces · docs: language/font · declare.md §9 Style

style Keyword [ textColor = #C678DD, fontWeight = bold ] HTMLText [ html = "class" ] // a run wears the bundle by name d.fillText("class", 0, 20, Keyword) // so does a drawn run A named **record of text attributes** — the style of a run of text that has no view of its own. `` inside `HTMLText` or `Markdown` wears it, and a drawing's `d.fillText` / `d.strokeText` and `measureText` take it. Its name is a value in any `{ }`, typed by the fields it sets (`Keyword.textColor`). 4 rules the compiler enforces · docs: language/style · declare.md §9 Style

theme Brand [ accent = #CC3333, surface = #FFF7F5 ]     // a named token record
  App [ theme = Brand ]                                    // PROVIDE it — a plain set, no keyword
  fill = { provided("theme").surface }                     // READ a token anywhere below
  theme = { { ...provided("theme"), accent: 0xCC3333 } }   // a descendant provides a modified one
A theme is a **named record of tokens** — colours, sizes, decorations — declared at the top level like a class or a schema. Token names are free; values are plain literals, value constructors, or lists of them. The library ships presets in scope by name (`SanFrancisco`, `Cupertino`, `MountainView`, `Redmond`, each with a `…Dark` companion), and `theme Brand [ … ]` declares your own.
4 rules the compiler enforces · docs: language/theme · declare.md §9 Style

provided("name")                           // the nearest ancestor's value under name
  provided("name", default)                  // … or the default when no ancestor provides one
  density: number = 2                        // PROVIDE: declare a typed value on an ancestor
  fontSize = 13                              // a built-in provided name is set bare on any container
The one explicit **up-the-tree read**: `provided("name")` is the value the nearest ancestor makes available under that name — bare in `[ ]` like `gradient(…)`, or a call in `{ }`. *Providing* is just holding a value: declare a typed attribute on an ancestor (`density: number = 2`) and every descendant may read it; the built-in provided names — the text face, `theme`, `iconSize`, the rich-text attributes — need no declaration at all, so `fontSize = 13` on a container provides it to every `Text` beneath. A value set locally always outranks a provided one.
3 rules the compiler enforces · docs: language/provided · declare.md §9 Style

schema Task [ id: string, done: boolean, status: "open" | "closed", note?: string ]
  d: DataSource [ url = "tasks.json", schema = [ tasks[]: Task ] ]
  sel: Task? = null                           // the name in any type position
A named data shape, declared at the top level like a class, and a **type** in the one type system: use the name in any type position — a declared attribute, a parameter, a return, a field of another schema — and declare a dataset's document with it. The dataset's `.value` is then typed, so a misspelled field dies at compile time; the runtime enforces the same declaration at every boundary — arrival, the literal body, and the mutation verbs — so malformed data yields `.failed` rather than `undefined` three steps downstream.
3 rules the compiler enforces · docs: language/schema · declare.md §7 Data

negative.answer: No app-facing bitmap cache or preload call. Today each `Image` instance decodes its `source` itself — a photograph shown on one surface is decoded again on the next. A platform-managed bitmap store (decode table shared across instances + cached draw rasterizations) is planned — see docs/system-design/ (adaptive draw cache) and the 2026-08-06 assessment; until it lands, the idiom is to keep the SAME view alive across surfaces (one sprung scalar, many followers) rather than to rebuild it.

No hooks, no stores, no props plumbing — state is an attribute declared where it lives (`count: number = 0` on a view), derived state is a `{ }` constraint reading it, and "effects" are the constraint graph's own propagation. A descendant reads an ancestor's attribute by name (`app.count`, `parent.width`, `classroot.…`) — no context, no lifting. Handlers write; constraints react.

No refs — a named member IS its handle (`box: View [ … ]` → `app.box`); reach any node by its dotted path. Replicated rows take their identity from the record's `id` field on their own, and `key = :field` on the replicated node names it when it lives under another name — that is Declare's `key`, an identity attribute, not React's reconciliation prop.

No SVG element — a vector mark is a `draw(d: Draw)` member (paths, arcs, gradients — a recorded, reactive drawing), the house icons are `Icon` subclasses drawn exactly that way, and an actual `<svg>` you already have lives inside a `DOMIsland`.

No grid layout strategy — `WrappingLayout` flows and wraps; a fixed N-column grid is a small `Layout` subclass of your own (`place()` is ~15 lines of arithmetic over `this.laid()` and `this.view.width`); and tabular DATA wants `Table` or `DataGrid`, which are classes, not layouts.

No ZStack and no overlay wrapper — children stack by default: a view with no `layout` imposes no arrangement, and declaration order is z-order (later siblings paint above). Place the layers with x/y; `ignoreLayout = true` floats one child above an arranged set.

No dedicated class — the library is deliberately small, and these are compositions: a skeleton is a few rounded Views whose opacity a `Time` pulses; a badge is a small rounded `Text` riding its parent's corner; an avatar is an `Image` with `stretches = cover` and rounding. Compose it, then keep it as your own class.

No `requestAnimationFrame`, and no timers: a body that names `setTimeout` or `setInterval` is refused. Motion is declared: a `Spring` drives an attribute toward a live target (interruptible for free), an `Animator` is the clock-shaped sibling, and per-frame integration (physics you step yourself) is `Time [ tick = frame, onTick(dt) ]`, which rides the one shared frame clock; a value that is a function of the current time — a clock face, a countdown — derives from a `Time` member's facts (`now`, `minute`, …). One call on the next frame is `afterDelay(0, fn)`. See the guide's Motion and states chapter.

No polling — nothing waits. A program never checks whether something has happened yet: readiness is a value to constrain on, completion an event to take — a loop or timer that checks whether something has happened yet is a constraint or an event written by hand, and almost always the wrong path. Ask what it is waiting for: a fetch landing → `visible = { data.loaded }` or `onLoad`; a view existing or having a size → `onInit`, `onReady`, `afterSettle`, `onArrive`; a value changing → a constraint on it (the constraint IS the notification); geometry after your own write → `afterSettle(step)`, same frame. Time is only ever an input: `Animator` over a duration, `Spring` toward a target, a `Time` fact (`clock.minute`, `clock.now`) to derive from, `Time [ tick = frame, onTick(dt) ]` to integrate (a per-frame handler that ignores `dt` is polling), `afterDelay(ms, fn)` for a genuine timing rule — a debounce, a request timeout — never to let things settle. See the guide's Time and change events chapter.

No formatting functions of Declare's own: numbers, money and dates are formatted by the host's `Intl`, called from a `{ }` or a script function like any other global — `new Intl.NumberFormat("en-US", { style: "currency", currency: "USD" }).format(1234.5)` is "$1,234.50", `(1234.5).toLocaleString("en-US")` is "1,234.5", and `Intl.DateTimeFormat` writes weekdays and months in the language it is given. Name the locale, and a `timeZone` for a date. Guide: docs/guide/12-text.md § Text. `Intl` is one of the globals every `{ }` body and handler may name; which globals code may name, by where it is written: declare-help globals.

No `<select>` element: a pop-up choice is a `Button` with a `menu`. Declare a `Menu` whose rows carry `checked`, derived from your state, and set the state in its `picked(id)`:
  sorts: Menu [ items = { [ ({ id: "name", label: "Name", checked: app.sort == "name" }), ({ id: "date", label: "Date", checked: app.sort == "date" }) ] }, picked(id: string) { app.sort = id } ],
  Button [ label = { "Sort by " + app.sort }, menu = { app.sorts } ]
The button draws the chevron and opens the menu under itself, and the menu checks the current row (declare-help Control.menu). Other ways to choose one of many: two to five short choices shown at once, `Segmented`; a few that need a sentence each, `RadioGroup`; a long list filtered by typing, `Combobox`; a day, `DatePicker`; your own content in a bubble, `Popover`. Guide: docs/guide/08-controls.md § Choosing one of many.

No host globals beyond a fixed set: what code may name depends on where it is written.
  Everywhere, `{ }` bodies and handlers included: the ECMAScript built-ins (`Math`, `JSON`, `Date`, `Intl`, `Number`, `String`, `Array`, `Object`, `Map`, `Set`, `RegExp`, `Promise`, …), and `URL`, `URLSearchParams`, `console`, `structuredClone`, `encodeURIComponent`, `decodeURIComponent`.
  Refused in a `{ }` body or handler, with the Declare way named: `fetch` (a `DataSource`), the timers `setTimeout`, `setInterval`, `queueMicrotask`, `requestAnimationFrame` (`afterDelay(ms, fn)`, a `Time`), `performance` (a `Time`), `globalThis`.
  In a `script { }` block: all of the above, `fetch`, the timers and `performance` included.
  In a `script [ host = browser ] { }` block: `window`, `document` and the rest of the browser as well. An unmarked script runs on every host, so the compiler refuses them there.
What a page reads from `window` is an App attribute here: the size is `app.width` / `app.height`, and a view is reached by its name (`app.sidebar.list`), not by a query. docs/declare.md § 5.

No lookup function: a member is a property of its view, reached as JavaScript reaches any property — `toolbar.share`, or by a name computed at run time, `toolbar[name]`. The two forms are the same access and chain freely: `app.prefs[section][field]`, `app.prefs[section].advanced`. Each bracket steps one level; its string names one member, not a dotted path. The result is the member by that name, or `undefined` when there is none. A string literal (`toolbar["share"]`) is checked like a path; a name known only at run time cannot be, so a path stays the form for names known as you write. Data can name a view: `anchorTo = { app.toolbar[:target] }`. Guide: docs/guide/04-structure.md § A member by a name known at run time.

View.x.name: x
View.x.doc:
The horizontal offset within the parent's content box, in pixels — `center` and `end`
place the view centered or flush against the far edge. **What a parent's `layout` places,
the child does not declare**: under a row (which places `x`), setting `x` in any spelling is
a compile error naming what to use instead, and a handler writing it while the layout
arranges the child is refused. Use `x` for free-form placement, a `layout` for arrangement,
and `ignoreLayout = true` for a child that must stand apart from its parent's layout.

View.y.name: y
View.y.doc:
The vertical offset within the parent's content box — the twin of `x`, with the same
ownership rule: a layout that places `y` (a stack, or a row with `align`) owns it.

View.width.name: width
View.width.doc:
The box's width, in **pixels** (`Length`). Left unset, a view is as wide as its content —
the run a `Text` lays out, the bitmap an `Image` shows, and the boxes of its visible
children (padding included); a view with nothing in it is `0`. Otherwise set a constant,
`100%` (the parent's content box), or a `{ }` constraint. Set it live and children
constrained to it reflow in the same frame; there is no re-layout call. To size to content
with a limit, constrain it: `width = { Math.min(contentWidth, 480) }`.

View.height.name: height
View.height.doc:
The box's height in pixels (`Length`), mirroring `width`: left unset, a view is as tall as
its content. A `Text` left unsized takes its natural measured height, so you usually set
`height` only to fix a size, to clip, or to limit growth.

View.fill.name: fill
View.fill.doc:
What paints the box: a solid `Color` or a `gradient(…)` — the one attribute, subsuming a
plain background color. `null` (the default) paints **nothing** — an unfilled box is
invisible but still lays out and still catches clicks. In a `[ ]` literal a color is
`#RRGGBB`; inside a `{ }` body it is `0xRRGGBB` (the one place the spelling differs).

```declare
App [
    View [ x = 20, y = 20, width = 260, height = 80, cornerRadius = 8, fill = { gradient("90deg", 0x1E2A36, 0x0B141B) } ]
    ]
```

View.padding.name: padding
View.padding.doc:
**The view's content box** — the inset between this box and the room its children live in.
One number insets all four sides; four are `[top, right, bottom, left]`, clockwise from the
top, the one-or-four house pattern `cornerRadius` and `stroke` share. A negative number is
clamped to 0. This is the attribute a fixed inset wants — not a wrapper view, and not the
layout.

**A padded view has an *inside*, and `x = 0` / `y = 0` mean that inside's origin — for
every child.** One a layout arranged, one that placed itself at `x = center`, one with
`ignoreLayout = true`: they all start at the content origin, because a position in this
view is *by definition* measured from the content box. There is no CSS-style split where
an absolutely-positioned child escapes the inset. A layout is not involved — it simply
arranges within the room it is given (`Layout.contentExtent`), so a view with no `layout:`
at all is padded just the same, a `place()` you write yourself honors the inset without
naming it, and **replacing a `layout:` member does not replace the padding** (`padding = 0`
is what takes it away).

**`100%` means the content box; `{ parent.width }` still means the parent's box.** A
percent — and `x = center` and `x = end` with it — resolves against the room you are given,
so `width = 100%` in a `padding = 16` card is the card's width less 32, and a centered child
is centered between the insets. `{ parent.width }` is the deliberate escape hatch — the
parent's literal width, padding and all — and an edge-to-edge child inside a padded box is
that paired with a negative `x`: `x = -16, width = { parent.width }`, the divider that runs
wall to wall across a card. The asymmetry is the point: "the space I am given" and "the
parent's own width" are different questions, and the spelling says which one you asked.

**Paint does not move.** `fill`, `stroke`, `cornerRadius` and `draw()` are all this view's
own box, so a card's background still covers its padding and a border still runs around the
outside of it — nothing about the inset changes what the view looks like, only where its
children begin. The inset lives in this view's own coordinate space, so it scales and
rotates with the box like any other geometry. Hit-testing walks the same content box a
layout places into, so a press finds a child exactly where it is drawn.

**Both insets count toward size.** A view with an unset width or height grows by the pair on
that axis, so a padded panel sizing to `contentHeight` reserves the room under its last
child as well as above its first. A *scrolling* view's extent includes them on all four
sides too: a padded scroller stops a full inset past its last child rather than flush
against it.

```declare
App [ fill = white, textColor = black,
    card: View [ x = 20, y = 20, width = 260, fill = whitesmoke, cornerRadius = 10,
        padding = 16,
        layout: SimpleLayout [ axis = y, spacing = 8 ],
        Text [ fontWeight = semibold, text = "Storage" ],
        Text [ textColor = slategray, text = "39.2 GB of 128 GB used" ]
        ]
    ]
```

View.cornerRadius.name: cornerRadius
View.cornerRadius.doc:
Rounds the **painted** box (default `0`, square). One number rounds all four corners;
four — `[topLeft, topRight, bottomRight, bottomLeft]`, clockwise from the top-left as
CSS orders them — round each on its own, and a corner given `0` stays square:
`cornerRadius = [0, 8, 0, 8]` rounds only the top-right and bottom-left, `[8, 8, 0, 0]`
is a tab that joins the pane below it. **One value, or four clockwise, is the house
pattern** for anything said per corner or per side: `stroke` and `padding`
read exactly the same way, each list starting at its own first edge — the top for those
two, the top-left corner for this one, because corners are what it names. A list of any
other length is a mistake, never a shorthand. Radii that would overlap along an edge shrink
together, so a radius past half the box is a pill, never a fold. It shapes fill, border,
and shadow — but not hit-testing or clipping: the box stays a rectangle for layout and
clicks. To clip children to the rounded shape, set `clip = true` as well. A `Spring` on
this attribute animates the number form.

View.hovered.name: hovered
View.hovered.doc:
True while the pointer is over this view — read-only, maintained by the same hit walk that
routes presses, so it agrees with what a click would reach. Read it in a constraint rather
than tracking enter/leave by hand: `fill = { hovered ? provided("theme").control : null }`. On a touch
device there is no hovering, so gate mouse-only affordances on `app.touchDevice`.

View.focused.name: focused
View.focused.doc:
True while this view holds keyboard focus — read-only, kept by the focus service, so a
constraint reading it re-derives when focus arrives or leaves:
`stroke = { focused ? stroke(2, provided("theme").accent) : null }`. It is the same on a
control, a text field and any `focusable` view. Move focus with `Focus.focus(v)`; ask which
view has it with `Focus.getFocus()`, also a tracked read. For the keyboard ring you need
neither — the app's `FocusRing` shows focus for you.

View.pressed.name: pressed
View.pressed.doc:
True while the pointer is down *and* this view was on the chain captured at pointer-down —
read-only. It stays true if the finger slides off and comes back, which is what makes a
button feel like a button; `hovered` alone flickers. The pair is the whole of press
styling: `fill = { pressed ? provided("theme").line : hovered ? provided("theme").control : null }`.

View.onScreen.name: onScreen
View.onScreen.doc:
Is this view **on screen** — inside the viewport, not scrolled away, not in a hidden
subtree? A coarse reactive fact that flips at threshold crossings, so a constraint
re-derives only when the answer changes: the gate for ambient work
(`running = { classroot.onScreen && app.pageVisible }`) and for load culling. Fed
lazily at the first read — a program that never reads it pays nothing. On the DOM the
feed sees the whole page, so an embedded app's box scrolled off its **host** page
reads `false` too. Read-only.

View.visibleRect.name: visibleRect
View.visibleRect.doc:
What of this view is visible, **in its own coordinates** — `{x, y, width, height}`,
all zeros when nothing shows. Updates **at rest** (when motion settles and scrolling
quiets), never per frame of a glide — a tile or rung decision wants the flight's end.
Cull margins are your arithmetic on the truth, not a platform knob. Read-only.

View.apparentScale.name: apparentScale
View.apparentScale.doc:
The composed scale from this view's units to **device pixels** — ancestor scales ×
devicePixelRatio. The raster-rung fact: an image pyramid picks its tier from it, a
drawn view its backing density, with no reimplemented transform math and no host
globals. Exact under Declare's own transforms (rotation does not participate); under
a non-similar host transform it is the largest axis ratio — the rasterization
convention. Same at-rest delivery as `visibleRect`. Read-only.

**The phase these facts have — and the one they don't.** All three answer *what is*,
at arrival: a camera flight lands, then a fact-bound tier re-derives, once. They never
answer *what will be* — the platform cannot know where a spring is headed, but **your
app can**, because the camera's target is your own attribute. A prefetch keyed on the
destination (`tierFor(cardH * app.camTarget)`) fires at departure and overlaps the
glide; a tier keyed on `apparentScale` asks on arrival and may land soft, then
sharpen. Those are opposite ends of the same flight, both legitimate: departure-phase
policy is written against your target state, arrival-phase truth against these facts,
and the two compose.

View.stroke.name: stroke
View.stroke.doc:
A border drawn **inside** the box (`stroke(width, color)`), so it never enlarges the
layout rectangle — the box stays the one geometry fact. `null` by default. Unlike
CSS's `border`, a bordered view and an unbordered one occupy the same space.

One `stroke(…)` borders all four sides; **four border them one at a time** — `[top,
right, bottom, left]`, clockwise from the top, the same one-or-four shape as

under a row is `[ null, null, stroke(1, #DBE1E9), null ]`; a pair of rails is the top
and bottom entries filled and the sides `null`. Widths may differ per side. Where the
box is rounded a side's band **follows the corner arc and tapers into it** rather than
mitring against its neighbour, so adjacent sides overlap along the curve instead of
meeting on a diagonal seam — the reason the form is written for rules and rails rather
than for a decorative frame.

```declare
        stroke = [ stroke(1, #DBE1E9), null, stroke(1, #DBE1E9), null ] ]

```

View.shadow.doc:

minus spread. `null` by default. The same value shadows glyphs as `Text.textShadow`,
and the painted **alpha** of any subtree inside a `filter` list — one `shadow(…)`, three
sites, one look (its `blur` is the box-shadow radius everywhere).

View.visible.name: visible
View.visible.doc:
Whether the view renders and participates in layout-that-skips-invisibles (default
`true`). A `false` view is fully inert — no paint, no hit-testing — but still
constructed, so toggling it is cheap and keeps its state.

View.ignoreLayout.name: ignoreLayout
View.ignoreLayout.doc:
Opt this child out of its parent's `layout` — the arrangement skips it and it owns
its own position on both axes (the decoration/overlay case: a badge floating over
a laid list). Its size still counts toward the parent's auto-extent.

View.flexes.name: flexes
View.flexes.doc:
Take an equal share of the room the parent's layout leaves along its axis. In a
column the layout sets this child's height to that share, in a row its width; the
children that do not flex keep their own sizes, and the flexing ones divide what is
left. It is how a page frame is written: a header, a toolbar, a body with
`flexes = true` that takes the rest, a footer. Across the flow it is aligned like any
other child — a search field that takes a toolbar's spare width still centres on the
row. A `Spacer` is an empty view that flexes.
`SimpleLayout` and `ResponsiveLayout` honour it, and in a `WrappingLayout` a flexing
child takes the rest of the row it lands on; a layout that does not divide a run
ignores it.

View.ignoreClip.name: ignoreClip
View.ignoreClip.doc:
Opt this child out of its parent's `clip`: outside the parent's frame it still
paints *and* still hits — frame chrome that straddles the frame (a window's
resize halo; a badge poking out of a clipped card). Parent-scoped — an ancestor's
clip above still applies — and the child is exempt from the parent's auto-extent
(frame geometry derives *from* the bounds, so it cannot also define them).

View.ignoreScroll.name: ignoreScroll
View.ignoreScroll.doc:
The third member of the opt-out family (`ignoreLayout` — the parent arranges everyone
but me; `ignoreClip` — the parent clips everyone but me): **the scroll carries everyone
but me — I ride the frame.** The child stands still against its parent's scroll frame —
the window when the parent is the App, the pane's frame when the parent `scrolls` — and
contributes nothing to the scroll range. It opts out of its **own parent's** scroll: a
view nested deeper, under a parent that does not scroll, moves with that parent (the boot
check names it — make it a child of the App, shown with its screen's condition). The
fixed header, the pinned toolbar, and the overlay layer that stages parked furniture are
all this one attribute.

View.opacity.name: opacity
View.opacity.doc:
Whole-view alpha, `0`…`1` (default `1`). Applies to the view **and its subtree** as a
group, so a fading panel fades its contents with it. It is not inherited by descendants —
its effect already composes down the render tree, so a per-descendant copy would apply it twice.

View.scale.name: scale
View.scale.doc:
A uniform transform — the view's subtree renders scaled about its pivot, and **every
reader agrees on the one geometry**: paint, hit-testing, `rootOrigin`, the parent's
auto-size, and layouts all compose the same transform, so a `scale = 0.5` child really
occupies half its space (the fractal idiom) — where CSS makes transform paint-only and
lets layout disagree with what you see. The view's **own** `width`/`height` stay local
(its interior world is untouched — that is what makes scale mean "the same world,
smaller"); the parent packs the transformed **footprint** (`bounds()`). Pair with
`pivotX`/`pivotY` to choose the center; `1` is unscaled; spring it for zoom effects.

View.pivotX.name: pivotX
View.pivotX.doc:
The horizontal center of `scale` and `rotation`, in the view's own coordinates. Defaults
to the origin; set both `pivotX`/`pivotY` to transform about the middle rather than the
top-left.

View.pivotY.name: pivotY
View.pivotY.doc: The vertical pivot — the twin of `pivotX`.

View.rotation.name: rotation
View.rotation.doc:
Rotation in **degrees**, clockwise, about the same (`pivotX`, `pivotY`) pivot `scale`
uses — and the same one-geometry rule: hit-testing follows the *visible* geometry
through the inverse transform (`hovered`, `pressed`, and `viewAt` all agree with what
you see), and layout and auto-size reserve the rotated frame's bounding box
(`bounds()`), so a rotated card takes the room it visibly covers. Composes with `scale`
in one documented order — scale, then rotate, about the shared pivot. `0` (the default)
is unrotated; spring it for turn effects.

View.scaleX.name: scaleX
View.scaleX.doc:
Per-axis scale, multiplied with the uniform `scale` — `scaleY = 0.2` squashes a card to a
sliver without changing its width (the frame of a flip). Same pivot, same one-geometry
rule: paint, the hit walk's inverse, `rootTransform()` and the footprint share one matrix.
`1` is unscaled.

View.skewX.doc:
A shear in **degrees**: `skewX = 20` slants the view's vertical edges by 20°, about the
pivot, composing with scale and rotation in one matrix. `0` is unsheared.

View.rotateX.name: rotateX
View.rotateX.doc:
A rotation about the view's **horizontal axis**, in degrees, about the pivot — the third
dimension, seen through the parent's `perspective`. A card tipped
away foreshortens; past 90° its back shows (`backface`). Hit-testing unprojects, so
`hovered`, `pressed` and `viewAt` name the view where it is drawn. `0` is flat.

View.translateZ.name: translateZ
View.translateZ.doc:
A push along the view's own depth axis, in px — toward the viewer while the view is
unrotated, and turned with it by `rotateX`/`rotateY`, so a face of a cube moves out along
its own normal (CSS's `rotateY(…) translateZ(…)`). Under the parent's `perspective` the
view grows as it comes closer. `0` is in the plane.

View.perspective.name: perspective
View.perspective.doc:
Sets this view as the **eye** for its children's `rotateX`/`rotateY`/`translateZ`: the
distance, in px, from the viewer to the plane, with the vanishing point at this box's
centre — CSS's model (`perspective: 700px`). `0` (the default) projects orthographically,
so a rotated child simply foreshortens.

`visible` (the default) or `hidden`: whether a view turned past 90° about X or Y still
shows (and hits) from behind.

View.blend.name: blend
View.blend.doc:
The **compositing operator** this view lands with against what has already painted
beneath it — `normal` (the default), or one of the W3C blend modes in camelCase
(`multiply`, `screen`, `overlay`, `darken`, `lighten`, `colorDodge`, `colorBurn`,
`hardLight`, `softLight`, `difference`, `exclusion`, `hue`, `saturation`, `color`,
`luminosity`, `plusLighter`). Declaration order — the z-order you already have — is
the blending order, and blending reaches down to the nearest **isolating** ancestor:
the `App` root, an `opacity < 1` group, a scrolling view's content, an island
boundary. A plain container is transparent to blending, so a `multiply` chip inside
nested layout Views blends against the card under them — which is what you meant.
A blending view blends **as a unit**, children included; compositing is paint, never
input — hit-testing and focus are unchanged. A token string in a `{ }` body, like
`scrolls` — so a blend can be state: `blend = { active ? "multiply" : "normal" }`.

View.scaling.name: scaling
View.scaling.doc:
How what is painted inside this view — its **images and drawings**, and everything inside
it — looks when it is shown larger or smaller. `smooth` (the default) blends neighbouring
pixels: right for photographs and for an ordinary interface under a zoom. `pixelated`
shows **every pixel as a solid block**, so pixel art stays sharp: a bitmap's pixels, and a
drawing's at one pixel to each unit of the view. Set it once on the view that holds the
scene; its whole subtree follows, as it follows that view's `scale`.

```declare
App [ width = 300, height = 140, fill = black,
    screen: View [ x = 20, y = 20, scale = 4, scaling = pixelated,
        // a ten-pixel mark, drawn at one pixel per unit and shown in sharp 4×4 blocks
        mark: View [ width = 10, height = 6,
            draw(d: Draw) { d.fillStyle = "#ffcc00"; d.fillRect(0, 0, 10, 1); d.fillRect(4, 1, 2, 5) } ]
        ]
    ]
```

When the scale — together with the display's own pixel ratio — comes to a whole number of
screen pixels, as at 2× or 3×, the blocks are all the same size. Otherwise they alternate
between the two nearest sizes (at 2.5× on an ordinary display, two pixels and three in
turn): uneven, but still sharp, never blurred — choose a whole-number scale for even
blocks. A smooth curve drawn inside a pixelated view comes out in blocks too; that is the
point. Paint only: hit testing, layout and focus are unchanged.

View.backdrop.name: backdrop
View.backdrop.doc:
The **frost** — `frost(radius)` or `frost(radius, saturation)`; `null` (the default) =
none. What has already painted beneath this view is sampled within the view's **own
painted shape** (its box, rounded by `cornerRadius`, or its `clip` shape), blurred by
`radius`, saturation-scaled, and the view's own `fill` then paints **over** the frosted
sample — a translucent wash over a blurred backdrop, which is how every platform's
material works. Content moving beneath re-frosts; that is the point. Samples reach the
same isolating ancestor `blend` does, and like `blend` it is paint only — input never
changes. `saturation` defaults to `1`; frosted materials read best around `1.4`–`1.8`.

```declare
App [ fill = #F6F8FA,
    art: View [ x = 10, y = 10, width = 220, height = 120, cornerRadius = 8, fill = { gradient("90deg", 0xC93B47, 0x2E6FE0) } ],
    panel: View [ x = 70, y = 40, width = 240, height = 70, backdrop = frost(20), fill = #F9F9FBDB, cornerRadius = 12,
        Text [ x = 14, y = 24, text = "frosted over the art behind it" ]
        ]
    ]
```

View.filter.name: filter
View.filter.doc:
The view's own painted subtree, filtered as a **group** — children included — before
`opacity` and `blend` land. One function or a bare list:
`filter = blur(3)`, `filter = [blur(2), brightness(0.8)]`, `filter = { [blur(k), saturate(1.4)] }`.
The functions are `blur(radius)`, `brightness(k)`, `contrast(k)`, `saturate(k)`,
`grayscale(k)`, `invert(k)`, `sepia(k)`, `hueRotate(deg)`, `colorize(color)` — the group's
alpha in one colour, what `Image.tint` is sugar for — and `shadow(dx, dy, blur, color)`, which
here shadows the painted **alpha** (a badge with a transparent background casts its own
outline) where the box `shadow` attribute casts the rectangle. Lengths are **view units** and
scale with the view's transform; the output may bleed past the box (a blur's 3σ, a shadow's
reach) and layout ignores the bleed. A filtered view isolates blending and backdrops inside
it. Paint only, never input — a blurred button is still its box. `null` (the default) is none.
The same vocabulary, sampled **beneath** the view, is `backdrop`.

View.mask.name: mask
View.mask.doc:
A soft alpha mask over the view's painted (clipped) subtree, applied before `opacity`:
a gradient's **alpha** over the box — `mask = gradient("180deg",
#00000000, #000000FF)` fades the top out; `radialGradient(…)` vignettes — or a **stencil**,
another view whose painted alpha, placed by its own `x`/`y` inside this box, is the mask:
`mask = { stencil }` with `stencil: Image [ visible = false, … ]` as a child is the idiom.
A masked view isolates. Paint only. `null` (the default) is none. On the DOM renderer a
stencil must be an `Image` or a view with `draw()` (its alpha is what CSS `mask-image`
can take); the canvas and Mac renderers take any view.

View.clip.name: clip
View.clip.doc:
Clips the subtree to a shape. `clip = true` clips to the view's **own box**
(reactively on width/height) — the common case; a `Shape` value clips to an arbitrary
path. `null`/unset (default) draws children unclipped, even outside the box. Kept
explicit (not implied by `cornerRadius`) so clipping is pay-per-use.

View.scrolls.name: scrolls
View.scrolls.doc:
Which **axes** of interior overflow this view scrolls — `none` (the default), `y`, `x`,
or `both`. One class overrides that default: an **`App` scrolls `y` by default**, and its
scroller is the page itself (see `App`). A scrolling view clips to its box; overflow along a declared axis becomes its
scroll range (live `scrollY`/`scrollX`), and overflow along any other axis is simply out
of frame. The value is a token **string** in a `{ }` body — compare explicitly
(`scrolls == "y"`), never truthily: `"none"` is a truthy string. Fixed chrome comes free — make it a **sibling** of the scroller, or a child that declares `ignoreScroll`.
**A scroller takes the pointer.** Declaring an axis says this view answers drags and wheels
over its box, so it is an input participant whether or not it declares a handler, and content
declared *behind* it is not reachable through it — a press on its empty area does not fall
through to whatever sits underneath. Something that must stay clickable belongs in front of
the scroller (later in the body), or outside it.

Both backends present the same model; only the overscroll *feel* differs, where the
platform can do better. On DOM the OS owns the scroll — overlay scrollbar, momentum, and
rubber-band overscroll *contained* to this pane, so it bounces on its own edges and never
chains to the page, and sibling panes overscroll independently. On canvas the runtime
manages the offset (clip+translate+wheel), as a single element must.

docSegs.md:
Which **axes** of interior overflow this view scrolls — `none` (the default), `y`, `x`,
or `both`. One class overrides that default: an **`App` scrolls `y` by default**, and its
scroller is the page itself (see `App`). A scrolling view clips to its box; overflow along a declared axis becomes its
scroll range (live `scrollY`/`scrollX`), and overflow along any other axis is simply out
of frame. The value is a token **string** in a `{ }` body — compare explicitly
(`scrolls == "y"`), never truthily: `"none"` is a truthy string. Fixed chrome comes free — make it a **sibling** of the scroller, or a child that declares `ignoreScroll`.
**A scroller takes the pointer.** Declaring an axis says this view answers drags and wheels
over its box, so it is an input participant whether or not it declares a handler, and content
declared *behind* it is not reachable through it — a press on its empty area does not fall
through to whatever sits underneath. Something that must stay clickable belongs in front of
the scroller (later in the body), or outside it.

Both backends present the same model; only the overscroll *feel* differs, where the
platform can do better. On DOM the OS owns the scroll — overlay scrollbar, momentum, and
rubber-band overscroll *contained* to this pane, so it bounces on its own edges and never
chains to the page, and sibling panes overscroll independently. On canvas the runtime
manages the offset (clip+translate+wheel), as a single element must.

View.hideScrollbars.name: hideScrollbars
View.hideScrollbars.doc:
A scrolling view that draws no scrollbars, across or down (default `false`). It scrolls as before, by
finger, wheel and trackpad; only the bars are gone. For a sideways strip people swipe through,
such as a row of filter chips or cards, which phone apps show without a bar:

```declare-fragment
chips: View [ width = 100%, height = 44, scrolls = x, hideScrollbars = true,
    layout: SimpleLayout [ axis = x, spacing = 8 ] ]
```

Leave the bars on a pane people read down through: it tells them how long it is and where they
are. (The page itself keeps the browser's own bar; a Mac host keeps its own bars too.)

View.claim.name: claim
View.claim.doc:
The axis a declared drag claims (`claim = x | y | both`, default `both`): `x` keeps
vertical pan with the enclosing scroll regime while the drag owns horizontal — a grid
column's header drag or edge-resize on touch. Scopes an existing drag declaration
(`onPointerMove`); it never creates one. The guide's Gestures chapter has the arbitration.

View.tooltipLabel.name: tooltipLabel
View.tooltipLabel.doc:
The tooltip text — the layer system's floor (one attribute at the use site): a non-empty
`tooltipLabel` makes this view hover-interactive, and after the theme's delay the auto-provided
`Tooltip` singleton shows the text beside it. Placement, delay, and size are theme data
(`tooltipPlacement` below | above | pointer, `tooltipDelay`, `tooltipFontSize`) — so Cupertino
tips appear near the cursor after ~1s at 11px (the Cupertino help tag), Redmond's above the
control (WinUI), Mountain View's below at ~500ms (M3) — always flipped and clamped inside
the app. Moving between tip-carrying controls while a tip is up retargets instantly; a
press dismisses. Look comes from `tooltipFill` / `tooltipTextColor` / `tooltipStrokeColor`. `""` (the
default) = no tip.

View.defaultplacement.name: defaultplacement
View.defaultplacement.doc:
Written on a **class**: names one of the class's own children (at any depth), and the children
its subclasses and use sites write go **into** that child, after the child's own, instead of
beside it. `class Sheet [ defaultplacement = body, body: View [ … ] ]` — a `DetailSheet`
extending it, and a `Sheet [ … ]` use site, fill `body`. The class's own children are never
placed. A placed child's `parent` is the child it went into; it is still reachable by name
from the class or use site that wrote it.

View.scrollY.name: scrollY
View.scrollY.doc:
**A fact, not a settable attribute.** The current vertical scroll offset in pixels of a `scrolls` view —
the **platform writes it** as the user scrolls (and as a glide moves); **read it** for
scroll-driven effects (a fading header, reveals, parallax): `opacity = { 1 - app.scrollY / 200 }`.
Nothing may set it: an assignment and an `Animator [ attribute = scrollY ]` are both
compile errors, each naming the verb. To move the pane, **call `scrollTo(y)`** — a
request the platform clamps to the real range and holds for a pane that cannot take it
yet; add a glide (`scrollTo(y, { duration, motion })`) for the platform's own motion. A
starting offset is declared with `scrollStartY`. The offset is sampled once per settle,
like the pointer: your view of it may trail the pixels by a frame, and the pixels never
wait on you. To reveal a particular view, `scrollIntoView()` on the target already does
the walk.

View.scrollX.name: scrollX
View.scrollX.doc:
**A fact, not a settable attribute.** The live horizontal offset of a `scrolls = x` (or `both`) view,
mirrored from the platform's scroll — `scrollY`'s twin, with the same enforcement: the
platform owns it, and an assignment or an Animator aimed at it is a compile error.
**`scrollToX(x)` is the verb** — a clamped, held request, with an optional glide
(`scrollToX(x, { duration: 260, motion: "cubicOut" })` is how the desktop's Files strip
slides a fresh column into view). `scrollStartX` declares a starting offset. Read it for
a paging strip's position or scroll-driven effects.

View.scrollStartY.name: scrollStartY
View.scrollStartY.doc:
The vertical offset a `scrolls` view **starts at** — applied once, at first layout, the
declared twin of a `scrollTo(y)` on arrival (`scrollStartX` for the other axis). The
`scrollY` fact then reports where the platform actually put it. A test fixture that must
be shot mid-scroll declares this rather than gesturing.
