attributes.name: iconLeft
attributes.doc:
A decorative icon for the leading slot, **named by class** (`iconLeft = "TrashIcon"`),
not nested as a child — a control is a leaf, and a name is the one form where authored
and data-bound are the same mechanism (`iconLeft = { "" + :icon }` in a replicated
toolbar). Control only declares the attribute; the concrete control lays it out. A
**computed** name needs `use [ Name ]` to survive the build, since no static reference
reaches it. The name is read once, when the control is built: a name read from data gives
each row its own icon, but changing the name later does not swap the icon (see `IconHost`).
Any icon class may be named, your own included — a library icon set another way is a
subclass: `class BackChevron extends ChevronIcon [ dir = "left" ]`, then
`iconLeft = "BackChevron"`.

tree.name: Checkbox
tree.doc:
A boolean control. Its value is the
`checked` attribute; **`input` owns the value's destination** — by default the
destination is the checkbox itself, so it works standalone with zero wiring:

    mute: Checkbox [ label = "Mute" ]          … visible = { mute.checked }

Hand the value to its real owner by overriding `input` and constraining down:

    Checkbox [ label = "Mute", checked = { app.muted }, input(v: boolean) { app.muted = v } ]

`press()` never writes `checked` directly — it only delivers — so a constrained
checkbox never fights its constraint.

```declare
row: View [ x = 20, y = 20,
    layout: SimpleLayout [ axis = y, spacing = 8 ],
    mute: Checkbox [ label = "Mute" ],
    Text [ text = { mute.checked ? "muted" : "audible" } ]
    ]
```

tree.name: Button
tree.doc:
A labeled action control. The action is its `onClick` — write it at the use site
exactly as on any View; `Button` adds the interaction states, the themed look, and
keyboard activation (Space/Enter drives the same `onClick`). `primary = true` fills
with the accent; the default is the quiet control look.

```declare-fragment
Button [ label = "Save", primary = true ]
Button [ label = "Add", iconLeft = "PlusIcon" ]
Button [ label = "Options", menu = { app.optionsMenu } ]      // chevron implied
Button [ iconLeft = "CloseIcon" ]                             // icon only
```

Three slots in a row — `iconLeft`, the label, `iconRight` — laid out by
`SimpleLayout` and sized from `contentWidth`, so an absent label or icon costs
nothing and needs no special case: an invisible child is skipped and its space
reclaimed. A `menu` supplies the right icon on its own (`control.declare`).

The fill walks the four-rung ladder — `control` at rest, `controlHovered`,
`controlPressed`, and `controlSelected` while its menu is open — so hovering a
button never looks like pressing it.

coordinates. A `SimpleLayout` or `WrappingLayout` with `align = baseline` sits the

```declare-fragment
    Text [ fontSize = 18, text = "Ready?" ],
    Button [ label = "Save", primary = true ]      // its label sits on the text's line
    ]
```

holds the selected tint, so the button stays lit while its menu is up; pressed beats
hovered; at rest, the quiet `control`. A primary button climbs the same ladder in

`accentHovered`, at rest `accent`. Every rung is a theme token, so a theme restyles
every button's states at once; a platform whose controls do not answer a passing
pointer states its hover tones equal to its rest tones (Cupertino does).

example.name: Button.2-icons
example.title: Icons, and the padding
example.lead: `iconLeft` and `iconRight` name an icon class; an absent slot costs nothing, so an icon-only button is just a button with no label. `padH` gives a short word room; `gap` spaces the icon from it.
example.source:
use [ PlusIcon, ChevronIcon, CloseIcon, CheckIcon ]   // named by string, so kept by name

App [
    row: View [ x = 20, y = 20, height = 40, width = { this.contentWidth },
        layout: SimpleLayout [ axis = x, spacing = 10 ],
        Button [ label = "Add", iconLeft = "PlusIcon" ],
        Button [ label = "Next", iconRight = "ChevronIcon" ],
        Button [ iconLeft = "CloseIcon" ],                       // icon only: no label, no gap
        Button [ label = "Wide", padH = 32, gap = 14, iconLeft = "CheckIcon" ]
        ]
    ]

example.name: Button.3-menu
example.title: An attached menu
example.lead: `menu` takes an instance, declared once. The chevron is implied, the menu opens on press, and the button holds the selected tint while it shows — `menuOpen` is a fact the menu keeps, never a flag you set.
example.source:
App [ chose: string = "",
    edit: Menu [ items = { [ ({ id: "cut", label: "Cut", key: "⌘X" }),
                            ({ id: "copy", label: "Copy", key: "⌘C" }),
                            ({ divider: true }),
                            ({ id: "paste", label: "Paste", enabled: false }) ] },
        picked(id: string) { app.chose = id }
        ],
    Button [ x = 20, y = 20, label = "Edit", menu = { app.edit } ],   // the chevron is implied
    Text [ x = 20, y = 78, textColor = slategray,
        text = { app.chose == "" ? "nothing picked" : "picked: " + app.chose } ]
    ]

example.name: Button.4-baseline
example.title: In a row of text
example.lead: A button claims its baseline, so a layout with `align = baseline` sits the label on its neighbours' line. A taller or shorter button still lines up — the row aligns by the text, not the box.

tree.name: TextLabel
tree.doc:
A `Text` that centers its ink in its parent's height — the vertical placement a
*label* wants, as opposed to a paragraph. Use it for the text inside a control
or any centered caption; use plain `Text` for flowing copy.

Why it exists. `y = center` on a plain `Text` centers the geometric box (the
ordinary meaning, matching every other view). But a label sitting in a box wants
its **letterforms** optically centered, not the font's box with its asymmetric
ascent/descent leading — otherwise the text reads a hair low. `TextLabel`
supplies a `y` that centers the cap band (cap-top to baseline), the optical
centre for a label:

    y = { parent.height / 2 - this.baseline + this.capHeight / 2 }

That expression cap-centres the label: the ink sits centred by its cap band rather
than by its box, which is what reads as centred for a label. It is written out here,
once, instead of at every use site. It is a plain constraint over the Text's own live
metric facts
(`baseline`, `capHeight`, measured from the effective font), so it re-centers
when the font, the size, or the parent's height changes. Override `y` on an
instance to opt out.

The centre is the cap band because that is what the platform control themes
(Cupertino, Mountain View, Redmond) are matched against.

tree.name: Switch
tree.doc:
A boolean control with a sliding thumb — same value contract as Checkbox (`checked`,
`input` owns the destination), different body language: the thumb **springs**
between its two rest points, so toggling moves rather than jumps.

tree.name: Slider
tree.doc:
A bounded number by drag. Same value contract as every control — `value` is the
attribute, **`input` owns the destination** (default: itself) — and the delivery
is continuous during a drag. Pressing the track jumps to that position (local
coordinates); the drag then follows the pointer by root-space delta
(`app.pointerX`), so it survives the pointer leaving the control. Arrow keys
nudge by `step`.

```declare
col: View [ x = 20, y = 20,
    layout: SimpleLayout [ axis = y, spacing = 10 ],
    vol: Slider [ value = 40 ],
    Text [ text = { `volume ${Math.round(vol.value)}` } ]
    ]
```

docSegs.md:
A bounded number by drag. Same value contract as every control — `value` is the
attribute, **`input` owns the destination** (default: itself) — and the delivery
is continuous during a drag. Pressing the track jumps to that position (local
coordinates); the drag then follows the pointer by root-space delta
(`app.pointerX`), so it survives the pointer leaving the control. Arrow keys
nudge by `step`.

code.source:
App [
    col: View [ x = 20, y = 20,
        layout: SimpleLayout [ axis = y, spacing = 10 ],
        vol: Slider [ value = 40 ],
        Text [ text = { `volume ${Math.round(vol.value)}` } ]
        ]
]

tree.name: RadioGroup
tree.doc:
One-of-N. Radios are written as the group's **direct children** — the group's
layout arranges them, and each radio reaches its group as `parent`:

    RadioGroup [ value = "m", input(v: string) { app.size = v },
        Radio [ choice = "s", label = "Small" ],
        Radio [ choice = "m", label = "Medium" ],
        Radio [ choice = "l", label = "Large" ],
        ]

```declare
size: RadioGroup [ x = 20, y = 20, value = "m",
    Radio [ choice = "s", label = "Small" ],
    Radio [ choice = "m", label = "Medium" ],
    Radio [ choice = "l", label = "Large" ]
    ]
```

tree.doc:
One choice in a `RadioGroup`: a direct child of the group, naming itself with
`choice`. A radio stores nothing — it derives `on` from the group's `value` and
delivers its `choice` to the group when pressed, so turning one on can never leave
another stale.

```declare
    size: string = "m",
    RadioGroup [ x = 20, y = 20, value = { app.size }, input(v: string) { app.size = v },
        Radio [ choice = "s", label = "Small" ],
        Radio [ choice = "m", label = "Medium" ]
        ],
    Text [ x = 160, y = 20, text = { "size: " + app.size } ]
    ]
```

tree.name: FocusRing
tree.doc:
The travelling focus indicator: a **shape-hugging** rounded outline that flies to
the focused control and reshapes to its own silhouette on arrival. The ring springs
position, size **and** `cornerRadius` together, which is why a Radio's row ring, a
pill Switch's ring and a text field's ring each differ — the targets do.

The model:

- **The fact** — the ring listens to Focus (a `Focus [ onFocusChange(v: View) { … } ]` member) and
  tracks the target's root-space geometry on every change, pointer or
  keyboard. A pointer focus **parks** the ring there silently (snap, no show) —
  so the next Tab's flight departs from the control the user just clicked,
  never from a stale perch.
- **Roles, theme-elected** — `provided("theme").focusRingStyle`: `"both"` (or `true`, the
  default) · `"travel"` (flight, then an idle fade) · `"rest"` (no flight —
  the ring appears in place and stays) · `false` (no ring; the theme's
  classes carry the at-rest indication — the invariant lives with the
  theme-and-classes pair). While keyboard modality holds and the role
  includes rest, the ring rests — no idle fade; a pointer press clears
  modality and the ring hides (web :focus-visible semantics).
- **The flight is the flourish** — `provided("theme").focusAnimate = false` snaps every
  move; the underdamped travel is default-on.

It arrives automatically with any Control-descended class; declare your
own `FocusRing [ ]` (or subclass) to replace it. Pure chrome: never focusable,
never a pointer target. The silhouette is the target's `focusShape()` when it
declares one, else its bounds at its `cornerRadius`.

**You do not instantiate this, and you do not position it.** Tab between the controls
below and watch it fly; the members exist for a subclass that replaces the rendition,
and for the theme tokens that elect its behaviour.

```declare
row: View [ x = 20, y = 20,
    layout: SimpleLayout [ axis = x, spacing = 12 ],
    Button [ label = "One" ],
    Button [ label = "Two" ],
    Checkbox [ label = "Three" ]
    ]
```

tree.name: Accordion
tree.doc:
Stacked pane headers with one pane open at a time, each pane sliding open and
closed on a spring over its height.

The load-bearing mechanic: a pane's content is **present through the whole open
and close**, revealed and concealed by the pane's own clip as its height
animates. That is what makes the motion read as a pane opening rather than as
content appearing — never an instant pop, never a blank gap.

The open pane is **one attribute on the group** — `value`, the open pane's name
— which is exactly `RadioGroup`'s shape. Panes are
the group's direct children; each names itself (`name`, defaulting to its
`label`) and derives `open` from the group. Content is authored as the Pane's
ordinary children — the Pane stacks its header then the content, and clips.

The pane stacks them **flush**, header against content, because the header is
edge-to-edge and an inset that reached it would break that. So the breathing
room around a pane's content is the content's own `padding`:

```declare
Accordion [ x = 20, y = 20, width = 260,
    Pane [ label = "Account", initial = true,
        View [ width = 100%, padding = 12,
            Text [ width = 100%, wrap = true,
                text = "Panes slide on a spring; the content rides the whole way." ]
            ]
        ],
    Pane [ label = "Privacy",
        View [ width = 100%, padding = 12,
            Text [ width = 100%, text = "One pane open at a time." ]
            ]
        ]
    ]
```

tree.name: Pane
tree.doc:
One pane of an `Accordion`: a header you press and the content you write as its
ordinary children. A pane derives `open` from the group's `value` — it never stores

whole way and revealed by the pane's own clip.

```declare
App [ width = 300, height = 180, fill = white, textColor = black,
    Accordion [ x = 20, y = 20, width = 260,
        Pane [ label = "Details", initial = true,
            Text [ width = 100%, padding = 12, text = { "open: " + parent.open } ]
            ],
        Pane [ label = "More", Text [ padding = 12, text = "Press a header." ] ]
        ]
    ]
```

tree.name: Carousel
tree.doc:
Pages side by side, one in view at a time. A finger drags the row of pages and it
follows 1:1; on release it settles on a page on a spring — the next one when the drag
went past a third of the width or was a quick flick, otherwise back where it started.
Assigning `page` from anywhere springs the row there the same way.

A carousel's children are its pages: each is laid out as wide and as tall as the
carousel's content box, in order. A drag that goes up or down rather than sideways is
left to the page around it (`claim = x`), and a press that never travels still reaches
the page's own controls.

```declare
Carousel [ width = 100%, height = 160,
    View [ fill = #F6D7C3, Text [ x = center, y = center, text = "One" ] ],
    View [ fill = #CFE5D2, Text [ x = center, y = center, text = "Two" ] ],
    View [ fill = #CFDCF2, Text [ x = center, y = center, text = "Three" ] ]
    ]
```

tree.name: CarouselLayout
tree.doc:
Pages side by side, one in view at a time. A finger drags the row of pages and it
follows 1:1; on release it settles on a page on a spring — the next one when the drag
went past a third of the width or was a quick flick, otherwise back where it started.
Assigning `page` from anywhere springs the row there the same way.

A carousel's children are its pages: each is laid out as wide and as tall as the
carousel's content box, in order. A drag that goes up or down rather than sideways is
left to the page around it (`claim = x`), and a press that never travels still reaches
the page's own controls.

```declare
Carousel [ width = 100%, height = 160,
    View [ fill = #F6D7C3, Text [ x = center, y = center, text = "One" ] ],
    View [ fill = #CFE5D2, Text [ x = center, y = center, text = "Two" ] ],
    View [ fill = #CFDCF2, Text [ x = center, y = center, text = "Three" ] ]
    ]
```

tree.name: Tooltip
tree.doc:
The layer system's floor: any view sets `tooltipLabel = "…"` and this singleton renders
it — hover delay, placement, flip, and theming are nobody's problem at the use
site. It arrives automatically when any view in the program carries a tip, as
`FocusRing` does; declare your own `Tooltip [ ]` (or subclass) to replace the
rendition.

It listens to the Tooltips service (a `Tooltips [ onTooltip(e: TooltipEvent) { … } ]` member), which owns the platform
conventions (the show delay — `tooltipDelay`, ~1s in the Cupertino and Redmond
conventions, ~500ms MountainView — instant retarget while showing, hide on
press). **Placement is theme data too** (`tooltipPlacement`): "below" (the
default — under the target, centered, flipping above at the edge), "above"
(flipping below), or "pointer" (the Cupertino help tag —
offset below-right of where the cursor rests). Always clamped inside the
app. Pure chrome — never focusable, never a pointer target, always above
content (the auto-splice puts it last in the App, and source order stacks).

Theming (the four cities carry the tokens): `tooltipFill` / `tooltipTextColor` /
`tooltipStrokeColor` (null = no border) / `tooltipFontSize` (11 in Cupertino, 12
elsewhere). Cupertino and Redmond wear bordered surface chips; San
Francisco and Mountain View the inverse chip.

**You do not instantiate this.** Set `tooltipLabel` on any view and the singleton appears; the
members below exist for a subclass that replaces the rendition.

```declare
View [ x = 20, y = 20, width = 130, height = 38, cornerRadius = 8, fill = steelblue,
    tooltipLabel = "Saves your changes",
    Text [ x = center, y = center, textColor = white, text = "Save" ]
    ]
```

tree.name: Menu
tree.doc:
The record-driven menu: **items are data** — the class arranges; the
author never composes rows. The standard record covers real OS menus:

    { id, label, key?, icon?, enabled?, checked?, divider?, submenu?, kind?, props?, minWidth? }

- `key` renders right-aligned — display only; the menu registers no shortcut.
- `icon: "ClassName"` names an icon class for the leading column, and the label
  shifts right to make room — the same vocabulary `Segmented`'s choices use.
  One field covers every mark, including the ones no font gives you; a computed
  name needs its class kept with `use [ Name ]`, since no static reference
  reaches it.
- `enabled: false` dims the row (provided("theme").disabledOpacity) and refuses pick.
- `{ divider: true }` is a separator line.
- `submenu: [ …records… ]` marks a cascade (the ▸ arrow).
- `kind: "ClassName"` renders the row's content with a named author class
  (app.createView — keep data-only classes with `use [ Name ]`), passed
  `props` as its datapath context. Behavior stays the row's: highlight,
  pick, keyboard are the menu's, always.
- `minWidth` is the room a row needs when it has no label to measure — a
  `kind:` row's own content. The panel is at least this wide; a longer label
  elsewhere still wins. Only a custom row needs it.

Declared once, opened by many: rows carry
`onContextMenu(e) { app.rowMenu.openAt(this, e) }`; the menu's `items`
constraint derives from `opener` — per-row variation with zero per-row
instances, live while open. `openAt` point-positions (the context-menu
rule); `openFor` drops below a control (the attached-menu rule); both
place it in the overlay layer of its context — above everything opened before it — and clamp
it inside the app. A menu is a `Floating` (floating.declare).

Dismissal: a press outside closes the whole chain **and** is swallowed, the Mac rule (a
submenu lets a press on its parent menu through); Escape closes the chain; pick closes
after delivery.

```declare
App [ width = 320, height = 130,
    chose: string = "",
    edit: Menu [ items = { [ ({ id: "cut", label: "Cut", key: "⌘X" }),
                            ({ id: "copy", label: "Copy", key: "⌘C", checked: true }),
                            ({ divider: true }),
                            ({ id: "paste", label: "Paste", enabled: false }) ] },
        picked(id: string) { app.chose = id }
        ],
    Button [ x = 20, y = 20, label = "Edit", menu = { app.edit } ],
    Text [ x = 20, y = 74, text = { app.chose == "" ? "nothing picked" : "picked: " + app.chose } ]
    ]
```

attributes.name: items
attributes.doc:
The rows, as **records — never children**. A menu arranges its own rows, so handing it
views is not merely discouraged, there is nowhere to put them. The record is
`{ id, label, key?, icon?, enabled?, checked?, selected?, divider?, submenu?, kind?, props?, minWidth? }`
(`selected` is read only in a list of choices: see `asList`);
a plain array is fine (no `Dataset` required). Because it is an ordinary attribute it
can be a constraint — **derive it from `opener` and one menu serves every row of a
table**, live while it is open.

commands leads its text 17 in; one with a checkable row, 24.

air — the metrics of a real macOS menu, measured (the longest label trails the edge by

floors it.

tree.name: MenuBar
tree.doc:
The record-driven menu bar: **whole menus are data** —

    menus = { [ ({ id, label, bold?, items: [ …menu records… ] }), … ] }

— and the class arranges. One internal Menu serves every title; its
`items` constraint derives from the open title's record, so item state
(enabled, checked, labels) stays live while the menu is up. An item's
`key:` is a keyboard shortcut for the whole program (`Shortcuts`): the menu
bar is the program's shortcut table, and nothing is declared twice.

Tracking is the classic desktop behavior: titles do not highlight on mere hover;
a click opens (and highlights) a title; while any menu is open, moving
across another title switches to it; clicking the open title closes.

Delivery is the one seam: `picked(id)` — override at the use site.

A dropped menu paints over the bar's later siblings: the bar raises itself when a menu
opens (stacking is source order, and `raise()` is the runtime verb for it). A bar nested
inside a container that sits under other content wants that container declared last,
or a menu hosted at the app layer as `Combobox` does.

```declare
App [ width = 380, height = 190, chose: string = "",
    bar: MenuBar [ x = 12, y = 8,
        menus = { [ ({ id: "file", label: "File", items: [ ({ id: "new", label: "New", key: "⌘N" }),
                                                          ({ id: "open", label: "Open…" }) ] }),
                    ({ id: "edit", label: "Edit", items: [ ({ id: "undo", label: "Undo" }),
                                                           ({ divider: true }),
                                                           ({ id: "cut", label: "Cut" }) ] }) ] },
        picked(id: string) { app.chose = id }
        ],
    Text [ x = 20, y = 70, text = { app.chose == "" ? "nothing picked" : "picked: " + app.chose } ]
    ]
```

tree.name: Dialog
tree.doc:
A modal over its context: everything behind it is held back — presses aimed past it go
nowhere and do not close it — and Tab stays inside it. It closes by its buttons, or Esc.
Its content is yours (its children), and an alert is the most common use, so it carries
the alert verbs too: a title, a message, and buttons as **records** (the records door):
`{ id, label, default?, cancel? }`, rendered as themed library Buttons in the platform
arrangement. Open it with a verb — `show()` for a dialog of your own content, `ask`, `notice`,
`error` or `open` for an alert. Focus is saved on open and restored on close, one turn late,
deliberately: an immediate restore would hand the in-flight keystroke back to the opener. It
fades in and out.

Keyboard: Return picks the default button — unless the focused view takes Return
itself: a focused button or control presses itself (Return on Cancel is Cancel), and a
multi-line field types a line break. Escape picks the cancel record when one exists,
else just closes. Every control inside keeps its own keys (Space, the arrows).

The idioms — one verb each, an optional callback receiving the picked id
(the `picked(id)` override remains the declarative seam):

    dlg.notice("Saved", "Your changes were saved.")
    dlg.ask("Save changes?", "Unsaved changes will be lost.", (id) => …)
    dlg.error("Could not connect", "The server refused the connection.")

`ask` is Cancel / No / Yes-default; `error` renders the title in the
theme's error.

**Platform structure is data**: `dialogWidth`, `dialogButtonLayout` = `"end"` (a
right-aligned row — San Francisco, Material) | `"stack"` (the stacked alert —
full-width buttons stacked, default on top) | `"fill"` (WinUI ContentDialog —
equal-width buttons filling the row), `dialogTextAlign` = `"left"` | `"center"`
(the Cupertino centered title), `dialogTitleFontSize` / `dialogBodyFontSize`. Plus
`scrimFill` + `scrimOpacity` (Cupertino barely dims — alerts separate by
shadow; Material's scrim is 32%; Fluent's smoke 30%), the `menuShadow` family,
`error`.

**Declare one and call it.** A `Dialog` is not a view you show and hide around your
content — it is a standing member you open with a verb, so the same instance serves
every prompt in the program.

```declare
App [ width = 520, height = 260, said: string = "",
    dlg: Dialog [ ],
    Button [ x = 20, y = 20, label = "Delete…",
        onClick() { app.dlg.ask("Delete this file?", "This cannot be undone.",
                                (id) => { app.said = id }) }
        ],
    Text [ x = 20, y = 80, text = { app.said == "" ? "—" : "you chose: " + app.said } ]
    ]
```

A dialog of your own:

```declare
App [ width = 520, height = 300,
    rename: Dialog [ title = "Rename", buttons = { [ { id: "cancel", label: "Cancel", cancel: true }, { id: "ok", label: "Rename", default: true } ] },
        TextInput [ width = 100%, accessibilityLabel = "New name" ]
        ],
    Button [ x = 20, y = 20, label = "Rename…", onClick() { app.rename.show() } ]
    ]
```

tree.name: AppIsland
tree.doc:
`AppIsland` embeds a live Declare application: give it a `program` and it mounts
that program as its own child app — its own reactive graph, input router, and
stage — sized to this view's box. There is no coordinate sync: the tenant fills
the box, so your width/height constraints size it like any view.

It composes `DOMIsland` (the sanctioned foreign-content leaf) and builds the
host's mount key from structured inputs, so callers never hand-splice the
`run:…` wire. The page host (`browser/host-client.js`) sees the key on the box,
resolves the program on its boot ladder — prewarm → cache → in-browser compile,
identical on the dev server and a static host — and renders the child.

`childName` (inherited from `DOMIsland`) is the reverse channel: the running child's
`appName` reflected back up, so a host can title itself by what it shows.

### The boundary

What crosses an island says its direction (the guide's Embedding chapter). DOWN: list names in
`provides = ["dark", "base"]`, and the tenant reads each with
`hostProvided("dark", false)` — a value resolves at the island as `provided()`
does, the island's own attribute first, then its ancestors' provisions. UP: the
tenant lists names in its App's `exposes = ["docH"]`, and the host reads them
with `island.exposed("docH", 0)`. Both are reactive, per settle, with no

attributes.name: program
attributes.doc:
What to run: the program's path without its `.declare`, relative to the program that
names it like any address in a program (`"player"` is `player.declare` beside it, and
`"../calendar/calendar"` reaches the real app — **no copy of the source, ever**), or the reserved `"__raw__"` live-edit
channel, where the running program is the host app's `liveSource` and recompiles as it
changes. **`""` detaches the island** and nothing mounts, which is how a closed panel
stops paying for its tenant — and what bounds the recursion when a program embeds a
view of itself.

attributes.name: containOverlays
attributes.doc:
Keeps the program's overlays — its menus, popovers, dialogs — inside the island's box, where
they would otherwise open in the nearest overlay layer above it (its window's) and hang past
the box. For a host that shows programs as self-contained tiles. `false` by default.

The tenant runs in the host page's runtime, as its own app. Where its compiled program
comes from is the host's arrangement: on the distro, a prewarmed artifact or
a compile; in a **production build**, an artifact `declarec` made ahead of time — for
every island whose `program` is a literal, and for every name the program declares in its
`ship [ islands = [ "name", … ] ]` when the value is computed. A build carries no compiler
unless the program declares `ship [ compiler = true ]`, so an island naming a program the
build did not produce reports that, with the fix, rather than mounting nothing.

attributes.name: location
attributes.doc:
Where the program is: its own `location`, carried both ways. Set it before the program
mounts and the program starts there, as a page starts at its URL's fragment; set it
later and the program follows it (its `onFollow` applies). The program's own
navigation is reflected back here, so a host can show where it is, keep it, or walk
it back — Back and Forward across an island are the host's to give. Assign it from a
handler or `onInit`: a constraint here would own a value the program also writes.

attributes.name: place
attributes.doc:
Set it, together with `location`, to return the program to a place it left: once
the move has settled and the content can hold it, each pane and the island's box
scroll back to where `departedPlace` said they were. The user's first scroll
cancels a landing still in progress. Read back, it is `""` again once taken.

window) stores it with the location being left, and hands it back as `place`.
Written by the platform; nothing to set.

tree.name: SimpleLayout
tree.doc:
The stacking idiom: siblings placed one after another along
`axis`, in child order, `spacing` apart (negative overlaps). The cross axis
and all sizes stay the children's own — a child centers itself across a row
with the ordinary `y = center`. Invisible children are skipped and their
space reclaimed; a skipped child still gets the place it would occupy, so
re-showing it needs no special case. A child with `flexes = true` takes an
equal share of the run's slack along the axis: a list that fills the room
between a header and a footer, or an empty `Spacer` (between two groups it
pushes them apart; one on each side centers the run).

Written in Declare over the Layout kernel: the whole strategy is this one
pure place() — one box per laid child, aligned by index.

**Padding is the view's** (`View.padding`), and this stack obeys it without
knowing it exists: it arranges inside the room the view gives it, so a run
placed at `0` starts at the content origin, the cross-axis band `align` works
in is the room *between* the insets, and a view that sizes itself from the
stack grows by both. The inset reaches **every** child, on both axes,
`align = none` included — a child placing its own `x = 0` sits on the content
edge, not the view's, because the content box is the parent's and not this
arrangement's.

```declare
col: View [ x = 20, y = 20,
    layout: SimpleLayout [ axis = y, spacing = 8 ],
    View [ width = 160, height = 24, cornerRadius = 6, fill = steelblue ],
    View [ width = 120, height = 24, cornerRadius = 6, fill = cadetblue ],
    View [ width = 190, height = 24, cornerRadius = 6, fill = slategray ]
    ]
```

attributes.name: axis
attributes.doc:
Which way children stack: `y` (the default) or `x`. **A bare literal, not a string** —
`axis = x`, and note that `x` here is the axis token, not the position attribute.

`axis = x`, and note that `x` here is the axis token, not the position attribute.

attributes.name: spacing
attributes.doc:
The gap between adjacent children. **Negative overlaps them**, which is how a stack of
cards or avatars is built.

docSegs.md:
The gap between adjacent children. **Negative overlaps them**, which is how a stack of

attributes.name: align
attributes.doc:
The **cross axis** — `y` on a row, `x` on a stack. `none` (the default) leaves it to the
children, who place themselves with the ordinary `y = center`. `start | center | end`
aligns every child within the **band**: the view's own cross **content** extent — so a
column `width = 260` centres a `width = { parent.width - 32 }` child at 16, with the slack
split evenly — falling back to the **line**, the tallest (widest) laid child's extent, on a view
that derives its own cross size from these very children (reading an extent this
arrangement feeds would be a cycle, and on such a view the line *is* that extent). A
child wider than the band keeps the line, so it never hangs out both sides.
`baseline` — a row only — sits every child on one
baseline: a `Text` reports its own, and a composite **declares** which part carries it
(`baseline: number = { cap.y + cap.baseline }`); a laid child that declares none is
refused by name, at the child, and the checker says so before anything runs. A
flexing child is aligned like any other (a `Spacer` declares a baseline of 0, so a
baseline row takes it as it is). A row of figures and words that must wrap when the view
is narrow — "4 sessions · 3h 40m" on a phone — is a `WrappingLayout [ align = baseline ]`,
which keeps each line on its own baseline. A bare literal.

methods.name: place
methods.doc:
The whole strategy: one box per laid child, positioned along the axis in child order.
**Every size stays the children's own, and so does the cross axis unless `align` says
otherwise** — then the boxes carry that attribute too, and own it. Override it in a subclass
for custom geometry; a `Layout`'s `place()` **may** aggregate over children, which is the
one place that is allowed.

tree.name: WrappingLayout
tree.doc:
A horizontal flow that **wraps**: children run left to right `spacing` apart,
and when the next one would overflow the view's width it drops to a new row,
`rowSpacing` down. With room for
one row it is a plain row; as the view narrows it stacks — cards that reflow
on a phone with no media query. It owns both axes of each child (a flow is
2-D); sizes stay the children's own. `justify`
sets each finished row along the flow — `start`, `center`, `end`, or `fill`,
which spreads a row's slack into its gaps the way justified text does;
`indent` and `hangingIndent` inset the first row and every row after it, the
two shapes a paragraph takes. A child with `flexes = true` takes the rest of the
row it lands on: it wraps by its content width, then grows into what the row
has left, or gives up what the row is short — a strip of filters that fills
the room its row's other children leave, and scrolls when that is too little.

Division of labor: this is the tool for uniform, replicated collections
that reflow by fitting. Managing named regions per width tier is
ResponsiveLayout's.

Written in Declare over the Layout kernel — the whole strategy is place().

**Padding is the view's** (`View.padding`), and a flow answers to it on
both axes: rows **wrap at the content width** — the room between the left and
right insets, never the view's own width — and a view that sizes itself from
the flow grows by the vertical pair, so no row runs under the inset.

```declare
box: View [ x = 20, y = 20, width = 260,
    layout: WrappingLayout [ spacing = 8, rowSpacing = 8 ],
    View [ width = 70, height = 26, cornerRadius = 6, fill = steelblue ],
    View [ width = 110, height = 26, cornerRadius = 6, fill = cadetblue ],
    View [ width = 90, height = 26, cornerRadius = 6, fill = slategray ],
    View [ width = 120, height = 26, cornerRadius = 6, fill = darkslateblue ]
    ]
```

attributes.name: spacing
attributes.doc: The horizontal gap between children in a row.

docSegs.md: The horizontal gap between children in a row.

attributes.name: rowSpacing
attributes.doc:
The vertical gap between rows. The two gaps are independent: a uniform grid writes
the same number for both, and a negative `rowSpacing` pulls rows into each other,
which is what a large display face wants when it wraps — the row height a big face
reports is looser than the line wants to sit.

the same number for both, and a negative `rowSpacing` pulls rows into each other,
which is what a large display face wants when it wraps — the row height a big face
reports is looser than the line wants to sit.

attributes.name: justify
attributes.doc:
How a finished row sits along the flow: `start` (the default, left), `center`, `end`
(right), or `fill` — the row's slack is spread evenly into the gaps between its
children, so every full row ends flush at the right edge, as justified text does. As
in text, the last row is left at `start` under `fill` (a ragged last line), and a row
of one child has no gap to widen and stays put. A bare literal.

children, so every full row ends flush at the right edge, as justified text does. As
in text, the last row is left at `start` under `fill` (a ragged last line), and a row
of one child has no gap to widen and stays put. A bare literal.

attributes.name: align
attributes.doc:
Where each child sits **within its row**: `start` (the default — the row's top),
`center`, `end`, or `baseline`, which sits every child in the row on one baseline — a
`Text` reports its own, a composite **declares** which part carries it
(`baseline: number = { cap.y + cap.baseline }`), and a child that declares none is
refused by name and placed at the row's top. A row's height grows to hold the
baseline-shifted children. When the flow **never wrapped** — one row, which is the whole
content — `center` and `end` align it in the view's own height instead, so a single row
in a `height = 90` bar really sits in the middle of it; a view that derives its height
from this flow keeps the row as the band. A bare literal.

attributes.name: indent
attributes.doc:
The first row's inset from the left, in pixels — a paragraph's first-line indent. The
first row's usable width shrinks by it; later rows are unaffected (see `hangingIndent`).

docSegs.md:

first row's usable width shrinks by it; later rows are unaffected (see `hangingIndent`).

attributes.name: hangingIndent
attributes.doc:
The inset of every row after the first — a hanging indent, the shape of a bibliography
entry or a wrapped signature whose continuation lines step in under the name. The two
compose: `indent` sets where the first row starts, `hangingIndent` where the rest do.

compose: `indent` sets where the first row starts, `hangingIndent` where the rest do.

attributes.name: columns
attributes.doc:
A grid of equal cells (default `0`, off): every row holds this many children, each in a
cell of the row's room shared out — the content width less `spacing` between them, and the
row's indent. A child with `flexes = true` takes its cell's width; any other keeps its own
and sits at its cell's left. With `columns = { narrow ? 5 : 10 }`, ten options are one row
at a desk and two of five on a phone, every cell the same width.

```declare
scale: View [ width = 100%,
    layout: WrappingLayout [ columns = { app.width < 600 ? 5 : 10 }, spacing = 6, rowSpacing = 6 ],
    View [ datapath = { app.levels[] }, flexes = true, height = 44, cornerRadius = 6, fill = gainsboro ]
    ]
```

methods.name: place
methods.doc:
Runs the flow, wrapping when the next child would overflow the view's width. **It owns
both axes of each child** — a flow is 2-D — while sizes stay the children's own. A child
never wraps when it is first in its row, so one over-wide child overflows rather than
looping forever. Each finished row starts at its indent, is justified along the flow, and
has its children aligned across it, in one pass over the row.

tree.name: ResponsiveLayout
tree.doc:
A view's children often want one arrangement when there is room and another
when there isn't: three panels side by side on a wide screen, the same panels
stacked on a phone; an optional control that appears only when space allows.
ResponsiveLayout states those alternatives directly. You give it a list of
**plans** — each one says *"from this width up, arrange the children like
this"* — and it keeps the right plan applied as the view's width changes.
Hiding, showing, and dividing the width are all part of a plan, not separate
wiring.

    bar: View [
        layout: ResponsiveLayout [ plan = { [
            { from: 900, flow: "row",  share: { logo: 15, nav: 55, actions: 30 } },
            { from: 600, flow: "row",  share: { logo: 20, nav: 80, actions: 0 } },
            { from: 0,   flow: "stack" },
        ] } ],
        logo:    Logo    [ ],
        nav:     Nav     [ ],
        actions: Actions [ ],
    ]

Each entry's `from` means *use this plan when the view is at least this wide*
— the entry with the largest `from` that fits wins, wherever it sits in the
list, and an entry with `from: 0` is the fallback for anything narrower.
`flow` is the arrangement: `"row"` places children left to right; `"stack"`
places them top to bottom. **`share` divides width in either flow** — in a
row it apportions the run; in a stack it sets how wide each band is, as a
plain percentage of the view. The names are the view's own child names,
checked when the layout first arranges (a name with no child is a loud
error). `logo: 15` gives logo 15% of it; **a share of `0` drops that child
while the plan is active** — so "the actions disappear on small screens" is
just a number in the narrow plan, and they reappear by themselves when the
view widens. `gap` sets the space between children (an entry may carry its
own `gap` to override the layout's). Heights are never touched: children keep
their own heights, and the view's height falls out of its content, as always.

So the example reads as a storyboard: at 900 and up, a three-across row split
15/55/30; between 600 and 900, the actions drop and the nav takes their room;
below 600, everything stacks.

**A plan need not name every child, and 20% means 20% of what is left.** A
child the plan leaves out keeps its natural width and the flow just places
it — and the run a row's shares divide is what remains **after the gaps and
after those naturals**. So a fixed-width logo beside two proportional regions
composes without the author computing a percentage for the logo:

    layout: ResponsiveLayout [ gap = 10, plan = { [
        { from: 0, flow: "row", share: { nav: 60, actions: 40 } },
    ] } ],
    logo:    View [ width = 200 ],          // not named: keeps its 200
    nav:     Nav  [ ],                      // 60% of what is left
    actions: Actions [ ],                   // 40% of what is left

In an 880-wide bar that is 200 for the logo and 396 / 264 for the two
regions — the row fills, exactly. Change the logo's width and the regions
answer; they were never told about it.

**`share: { logo: "auto" }` says that out loud.** The word means precisely
what leaving the child out means — keep its natural size, divide the rest —
so it buys no new geometry, only legibility: the plan reads as a complete
statement of the row, and a name in a plan is checked against the tree, where
an omission is mentioned nowhere. It is **not** `share: 0`, which is the
opposite: `0` drops the child and reclaims its space, `"auto"` keeps the
child at the size it chose for itself. In a stack `"auto"` is accepted and
changes nothing — the flow axis there is height, which a share never touches.

**Two shares are refused, where the plan is read** — both of them mistakes
with no arrangement they could mean. A row's shares
divide one run, so a row whose shares add to more than 100 is an error naming
the plan and the total, rather than a row that runs its children off the end.
And a share that is neither a number from 0 to 100 nor the word `"auto"` is
an error naming the child, rather than a `NaN` width on it and a `NaN`
position on its neighbours.

**The two things authors miss.** `share` is not row-only: a `"stack"` entry
may carry shares too, and they set each band's width — the narrow plan above
could say `{ from: 0, flow: "stack", share: { logo: 100, nav: 100 } }` to make
both bands full-bleed. (A stack's shares are independent percentages of the
view, not slices of one run, which is why two hundreds are fine there and a
row's total is held to 100.) And `share: 0` is the whole of "hide it when
it's tight": a child dropped this way leaves the flow entirely and its space
is reclaimed, so there is no reason to branch a tree on a width
(`narrow ? … : …`) — appearing and disappearing is one number in one plan,
and the plan is the only place the breakpoint is written down.

**Slack and alignment.** When a row's children keep natural widths, the run
may not fill the view — and where the run sits is said with structure, not a
knob: a `Spacer [ ]` child absorbs the slack. Between two groups it pushes
them apart; one on each side centers the run; one first right-aligns it.
Shares are cut from what the naturals leave, so shares adding to 100 leave no
slack at all and a `Spacer` beside them collapses — *shares fill; naturals
align.*

**Across the flow, the layout places every child** — `y` in a row, `x` in a
stack, in every plan. Where each one sits there is the layout's `align`:
`start` unless it says otherwise, and a plan entry may say otherwise for its
own tier. A plan entry's `offset` shifts one named child from where `align`
put it — a nudge that belongs to that arrangement, so it goes away with the
tier, which is exactly when it stops meaning anything:

    actions: View [ width = 100%,
        layout: ResponsiveLayout [ plan = { [
            { from: 420, flow: "row",   gap: 18, align: "center", offset: { source: 1 } },
            { from: 0,   flow: "stack", gap: 14 },
        ] } ],
        run:    Button [ width = 240, height = 46 ],   // the row centres the pair on it
        source: Text   [ text = "View & edit source →" ],
    ]

So a child under a ResponsiveLayout declares neither `x` nor `y` — the
checker says so at the line, and says which of these to use instead. A child
that needs a finer arrangement of its own contents is the next case down:
give it a layout of its own.

**Nesting — who decides what.** A ResponsiveLayout watches its own view's
width — not the window's. The parent's plan decides how much room each child
gets; each child decides what to do with the room it got — if the child has
its own ResponsiveLayout, its plans answer to its own width, automatically.
Room flows down; each level responds locally. (A plan can only name direct
children — managing a grandchild is the child's own plan's business.)

This is the answer to most things a plan cannot say by itself, and it wants no
class: an **ordinary inline child** carries its own `layout:` like any other
view. A class nested this way answers to **its allocation, not the
window** — the same child reads correctly in a sidebar, a dialog, or a
full-bleed row, and picks its own flow in each. One thing to get right: the
parent's plan must actually **give** the child a width in every tier. A tier
that allocates it nothing leaves it at its content width, and a child sized by
its content is measuring what it is trying to arrange — so name it in the
stack tier's shares (`share: { acts: 100 }`) or give it `width = 100%`.

**Division of labor.** ResponsiveLayout manages **named regions**. A collection
of uniform, replicated cards that should reflow to fit is the other tool:
`WrappingLayout` (it wraps by fitting, no plan needed) with a width
constraint on the card.

**Padding, and what `from` then means.** The inset is the view's
(`View.padding`), and a plan is selected against the **content** width, with
the shares dividing it — so a padded bar's tiers answer to the room its
children actually get, and `from: 600` means 600 of usable room, not 600 of
outer width.

**When the rules aren't enough.** A plan speaks width, flow, share, and gap.
Reach for **nesting** first, and most of the time last: give the part that
needs its own mind a `layout:` of its own and let it arrange itself inside the
room this plan hands it (above). A child that decides for itself is almost
always the answer to "this plan cannot say what I need", and it composes — the
same child then reads correctly wherever it is put.

Past that: whole alternate configurations beyond geometry are a `State`
applied on a width condition; fully custom geometry is a subclass overriding
`place()` — the same seam every layout in the library is built on.

attributes.name: plan
attributes.doc:
The storyboard: a list of `{ from, flow, share?, gap?, align?, offset? }` entries. **`from` means "use
this plan when the view is at least this wide"** — the largest `from` that fits wins,
wherever it sits in the list, and `from: 0` is the fallback. `flow` is `"row"` or
`"stack"`. **`share` divides width in either flow** — not row-only: a `"stack"` entry may
carry shares, and they set each band's width. It names the children by their **own child
names**, checked when the layout first arranges — a name with no child is a loud error.
**A share of `0` drops that child while the plan is active** — out of the flow, its space
reclaimed — so "the actions disappear on small screens" is one number rather than a
`narrow ? … : …` branch, and they return by themselves when the view widens.

**A child a plan does not name keeps its natural width, and a row's shares divide what
is left after it** — the gaps and the naturals both come out before the percentages are
cut, so `60` means 60% of the remainder and a fixed-width logo composes beside two
proportional regions with no arithmetic by hand. `"auto"` is the word for that said out
loud (`share: { logo: "auto", nav: 60, actions: 40 }`): identical geometry to leaving the
child out, and the opposite of `0` — `0` drops the child, `"auto"` keeps it at the size
it chose for itself. In a stack `"auto"` is accepted and changes nothing, since a stack's
shares are widths and its flow axis is height.

**`align` and `offset` are per tier.** A plan entry's `align` — a string, `"start"`,
`"center"`, `"end"` or `"baseline"` — overrides the layout's own for that tier, as
its `gap` does. Its `offset` names children the way `share` does and shifts each one
**across the flow** — down in a row, right in a stack — by a signed number of pixels
from where `align` placed it. A name with no child, or an offset that is not a number,
is an error naming it.

**Two values are refused where the plan is read.** A row whose shares add to more than
100 is an error naming the plan and the total — a row's shares divide one run and cannot
claim more of it than there is. (A stack's do not compete: each is an independent percent
of the view, so `{ logo: 100, nav: 100 }` is the full-bleed idiom, not an overflow — but a
single share above 100 is refused in either flow.) And a share that is neither a number
from 0 to 100 nor `"auto"` is an error naming the child, instead of a `NaN` width.

attributes.name: gap
attributes.doc: The default space between children, overridable per plan entry.

docSegs.md: The default space between children, overridable per plan entry.

attributes.name: align
attributes.doc:
Where children sit **across the flow** — `y` in a row, `x` in a stack: `start` (the
default), `center`, `end`, or `baseline`. A bare literal here; a plan entry overrides
it with a string (`align: "center"`). `center` and `end` work in the **band**: the
view's own cross content extent, or the tallest (widest) laid child on a view that sizes
itself from these very children — the same band as `SimpleLayout`'s `align`.
`baseline` sits every child of a row on one text line, each child declaring its own
(a `Text` does; a composite says which part carries it), and is refused on a stack
tier, which has no line. **There is no `none`**: this layout places the cross axis in
every tier, so it always says where.

methods.name: place
methods.doc:
Selects the active plan from the **view's own width — never the window's** — and
arranges accordingly: both axes of every child, along the flow by the plan and across
it by `align` and `offset`. That is what makes nesting work: the parent's plan decides how much
room a child gets, and the child's own plan answers to the room it got, automatically. A
plan can only name direct children; managing a grandchild is the child's plan's business.

example.name: ResponsiveLayout
example.title: Two arrangements, one width rule
example.lead: A `plan` is a storyboard: the largest `from` that fits wins. Wide, three panels share the row; narrow, they stack and the actions panel is hidden by a share of 0. Drag the slider to change the box's width and watch the plan switch.

tree.name: Spacer
tree.doc:
When a row (or stack) does not fill its container, the leftover space has to
go somewhere. A Spacer says where, structurally: put one between two groups
and they push apart ("logo left, actions right"); put one on each side of a
run and it centers; put one first and the run right-aligns. Several spacers
split the slack evenly. When there is no slack — a plan whose shares fill the
width, an auto-sized container — a Spacer is simply zero and invisible in
effect.

It is nothing but an empty view that flexes: `Spacer [ ]` is
`View [ flexes = true ]`, named for what it is for. Any view can flex the same
way (`View.flexes`); a Spacer is the one with nothing in it. It paints nothing
and has no size of its own; it declares a baseline of 0, so a baseline row
takes it like any other child. For a minimum height (a strut), use an empty view:
`View [ width = 0, height = 44 ]`.

tree.name: Table
tree.doc:
The list collection, componentized: the selection-bearing, scroll-owning frame around a replicated (or
written) collection, carrying the selection model so no app hand-rolls it again:

- **Selection is the Table's value** — `selected` (the primary item) and
  `selection` (all of them, presented order), holding **items**: the record
  for a replicated row, the row view itself for a written one. App-ownable via
  `input`; identity by the usual ladder (a record's `id` by convention, else
  the object itself — the reconciler's own rule).
- **The three facts**: selection, the anchor (where ranges extend from), and
  the keyboard position `active` — moved by arrows, extended by shift,
  walked alone by ⌘ with Space toggling (discontiguous keyboard selection).
- **`selects` declares the mode**: `none | single | multi` (default single).
- Rows are TableRow instances — the RadioGroup discipline: direct children
  reaching their table as `parent`, replicated over data or written by hand.
  The row template stays free of any selection wiring.
- Windowing composes: put `virtualize` on the row template and selection,
  ranges, and keyboard travel keep working — items are read from the data
  through any row's cursor, never from instances, so an unmaterialized row
  can be range-selected and arrow travel scrolls it into existence (rows are
  assumed uniform in height).

    Table [ width = 300, height = 400, datapath = { app.d.value },
        selects = "multi", input(sel: object) { app.chosen = sel },
        TableRow [ datapath = :rows[], height = 30,
            t: TextLabel [ x = 8, text = :label ] ] ]

```declare
App [ width = 320, height = 200,
    d: Dataset { { "rows": [ { "id": 1, "label": "Ada" },
                             { "id": 2, "label": "Grace" },
                             { "id": 3, "label": "Alan" } ] } },
    t: Table [ x = 20, y = 20, width = 200, height = 100, datapath = { d.value },
        selects = "multi",
        TableRow [ datapath = :rows[], height = 26,
            Text [ x = 8, y = center, text = :label ]
            ]
        ],
    Text [ x = 20, y = 140, text = { (t.selection ?? []).length + " selected" } ]
    ]
```

```declare
        TableRow [ datapath = :rows[], height = 28,
            Text [ x = 8, y = center, text = { :label + (parent.selected ? "  ✓" : "") } ]
            ]
        ],
    Text [ x = 20, y = 110, text = "Click a row: its own selected fact follows." ]
    ]
```

tree.name: Combobox
tree.doc:
Filter-as-you-type over a collection: a text field owning a **query** plus a
dismissable option list owning a **choice** — a derived selection over data.
Composition, not invention: `TextInput` for the entry, the `Menu` machinery for
the list (overlay, raise, light-dismiss, Escape closes — the whole dismissal
discipline rides along), and the matches are a derived collection — a
constraint over the items array, so the live match count is free and no
rendered row is ever scanned.

    Combobox [ width = 240, placeholder = "Assignee",
        items = { app.people }, input(v: object) { app.assignee = v } ]

- **Items are members** (the selection model's currency): records — shown by
  their `label` (or `id`) — or plain strings. `value` holds the chosen member;
  `input(v)` is the delivery seam: the default writes `value`, a use-site
  override redirects and the attribute stays untouched.
- **Typing filters live** (case-insensitive substring); opening without typing
  shows the full list (the disclosure-button path). Picking echoes the label
  into the field and closes; editing again re-filters from the new text.
- **Keyboard**: arrows rove the list (the Menu rover), Enter picks the roved
  row — or the first match when none is roved (the type-then-Enter path);
  Escape closes the list (then a second Escape leaves the control — the
  focus-scope ascent). The list is never a tab stop of its own.
- The list is a collection like any other — bind 100k options and
  `virtualize` applies to it the same way (via the Menu it composes).

```declare
App [ width = 320, height = 160, picked: string = "",
    people: array = { ["Ada Lovelace", "Grace Hopper", "Alan Turing", "Barbara Liskov"] },
    Combobox [ x = 20, y = 20, width = 240, placeholder = "Assignee",
        items = { app.people },
        input(v: object) { app.picked = "" + v }
        ],
    Text [ x = 20, y = 80, text = { app.picked == "" ? "—" : app.picked } ]
    ]
```

tree.name: ContextMenu
tree.doc:
The right-click / long-press menu: `Menu`'s machinery whole — overlay, raise,
pointer-anchored placement with viewport clamping, the Mac light-dismiss rule
(an outside press closes **and** is swallowed), Escape closes the chain — with
a gesture-opened entry. It has no overlay machinery of its own; whatever it
does, `Menu` does.

Declared once, opened by many. **The serving view declares the gesture** — that
declaration is what routes it (the claim model: `contextMenu` engages the
right-click/two-finger path, `hold` is the touch long-press gate, and each
engages only where a handler is declared). The whole wiring is two lines on
the view the menu serves:

    rowMenu: ContextMenu [ items = { … }, picked(id: string) { … } ],
    …
    Row [ …,
        onContextMenu(e: PointerEvent) { app.rowMenu.open(this, e) },
        onHold(e: PointerEvent) { app.rowMenu.open(this, e) } ]

`open(v, e)` anchors at the pointer (view-relative event coordinates walked to
root space) and clamps inside the app — Menu's own placement discipline. Items
are the standard Menu records — written lists or derived from the opener
(`items = { … opener … }` for per-row menus with zero per-row instances);
picking delivers through `picked(id)` and closes.

Everything else — `items`, `opener`, `picked`, the rover, the cascade, dismissal — is
`Menu`'s, documented there.

```declare
App [ width = 320, height = 130, chose: string = "",
    rowMenu: ContextMenu [ items = { [ ({ id: "open", label: "Open" }),
                                      ({ id: "rename", label: "Rename" }),
                                      ({ divider: true }),
                                      ({ id: "delete", label: "Delete" }) ] },
        picked(id: string) { app.chose = id }
        ],
    card: View [ x = 20, y = 20, width = 200, height = 44, cornerRadius = 8, fill = darkslategray,
        onContextMenu(e: PointerEvent) { app.rowMenu.open(this, e) },
        onHold(e: PointerEvent) { app.rowMenu.open(this, e) },
        Text [ x = 12, y = center, text = "Right-click or hold me" ]
        ],
    Text [ x = 20, y = 80, text = { app.chose == "" ? "—" : app.chose } ]
    ]
```

tree.name: DataGrid
tree.doc:
Records as rows, one column per field you choose: headers that sort, reorder and resize by
drag (touch-correct), selection and keyboard travel from `Table`, and a windowed collection,
so ten thousand rows cost a screenful of views.

A DataGrid has **no children**. What it shows comes from two attributes: `items`, the
records, one row each; and `columns`, plain records, one column each.

```declare
App [ width = 440, height = 220,
    d: Dataset { { "rows": [ { "id": 1, "title": "Fix the rail",      "state": "open" },
                             { "id": 2, "title": "Draft the chapter", "state": "done" },
                             { "id": 3, "title": "Measure the grid",  "state": "open" } ] } },
    DataGrid [ x = 20, y = 50, width = 400, height = 130, selects = "multi",
        items = { app.d.value.rows },
        columns = { [ { id: "id",    title: "ID",    width: 50 },
                      { id: "title", title: "Title", width: 220 },
                      { id: "state", title: "State", width: 110 } ] } ]
    ]
```

Drag a header sideways to reorder; drag the divider between two headers to resize; click a
header to sort.

- **Items** are records, kept matched to their rows by each record's `id`. Taken from a
  `Dataset`, they are the dataset's own records: an edit made in a cell writes the record,
  and everything that reads it follows.
- **Columns** are records with an `id` (the field the column shows, and its name), a
  `title`, a `width`, and optionally a `cell` or `edit`. Being data, they can be built,
  stored, or chosen by the person, like any records.
- **A cell** shows its field as text, unless its column names a class: `cell: "DoneCell"`
  draws that class in every row of the column, each copy bound to its own row's record (so
  `:done` is that row's `done`). Cells in one column can differ by row: the class decides
  how to look for its record, with a `State` or a `classFor` inside it.
- **`edit: true`** makes a column's cells text fields that write the record as you type,
  with a spreadsheet's keys: Enter, F2 or a typed character starts the edit, Up and Down
  move it a row, Esc puts the text back.
- **A heading row** is a record with a `heading` field — `{ id: "g1", heading: "Overdue" }` —
  drawn across the full width, with no cells, passed over by selection and the arrow keys.
  `headingClass` names a class of your own to draw it.
- **Sorting names a derivation.** A header click sets `sortOn` and `sortDir`; your app
  derives the sorted items from them, and the grid shows the order it is given.
- **Order and widths** are the grid's state, `order` and `widths`, delivered through
  `arrangeInput` and `resizeInput`, so an app can persist a person's layout.

tree.name: SearchField
tree.doc:
A text field for searching, that a screen reader announces as a search field, with "Search"
as its placeholder until you give it your own. Its look is the theme's: a stadium — round at
both ends, `searchFieldCornerRadius = "round"` — unless the theme gives that token a radius (a
square-cornered house style gives it its `fieldCornerRadius`), with `searchFieldHeight`, `searchFieldPadding`, and
`searchFieldFill` and `searchFieldStroke` (the theme's `surface` and `line` when unset).
Everything else is `TextInput`'s: `text`, `onInput`, `onEnter`, the value pattern.

```declare
App [ width = 400, height = 100, q: string = "",
    find: SearchField [ x = 20, y = 20, width = 260, placeholder = "Search messages",
        onInput(t: string) { app.q = "" + t } ],
    Text [ x = 20, y = 64, text = { app.q == "" ? "type to search" : "searching for " + app.q } ]
    ]
```

tree.name: Segmented
tree.doc:
A row of mutually exclusive choices — the control you reach for when the options
are few, named, and worth showing all at once. Its choices are **data**, like
`Menu`'s items and `DataGrid`'s columns:

```declare-fragment
Segmented [ width = 300, value = { app.page },
    choices = { [ ({ id: "controls", label: "Controls" }),
                 ({ id: "table",    label: "Table" }),
                 ({ id: "grid",     label: "DataGrid" }) ] },
    input(v: string) { app.page = v }
    ]
```

### Tabs

A segmented control that switches what is shown below it — pages, panes — is a row of
tabs: use a `TabBar`, which is a `Segmented` in every other way and is heard as tabs.

### Why data, and not `Segment` children

Because the sliding highlight cannot be built any other way. The pill has to know
which choice is selected and how wide each one is, and a constraint may not ask
the view tree that: `childViews` carries **set membership only**, so `.length` is
live while anything reaching into the collection is refused —
`aggregation over a reactive node collection … derive from data [DECLARE7001]`.
The compiler names the answer.

### Equal widths

Segments divide the control's width evenly — a segmented control divides evenly,
where a row of buttons sizes to its content. Equal width keeps the convention that
segment labels are short and similar in length, and it lets the pill travel at
constant width between segments. So **a `Segmented` does not size itself to its
labels**: set `width`, or accept `segMin × choices.length`.

### The pill

The highlight springs a **normalized lane** — a float index — not pixels. `x` is
then `lane × segW`, so a resize recomputes `segW` and the pill **snaps** to the
right place instead of skating across the bar on every layout change. The chosen
segment wears a raised `surface` pill with a hairline.

```declare
App [ width = 340, height = 130, page: string = "one",
    Segmented [ x = 20, y = 20, width = 300, value = { app.page },
        choices = { [ ({ id: "one", label: "One" }),
                     ({ id: "two", label: "Two" }),
                     ({ id: "three", label: "Three" }) ] },
        input(v: string) { app.page = v }
        ],
    Text [ x = 20, y = 74, text = { "showing: " + app.page } ]
    ]
```

attributes.name: choices
attributes.doc:
The segments, as **records**: `{ id, label }` or `{ id, icon }` — the same vocabulary
`Menu`'s items use. A choice shows a label **or** an icon, never both. A choice may also
carry a `location`, which makes that segment a real link (see `SegmentedItem.location`).

docSegs.md:
The segments, as **records**: `{ id, label }` or `{ id, icon }` — the same vocabulary
`Menu`'s items use. A choice shows a label **or** an icon, never both. A choice may also
carry a `location`, which makes that segment a real link (see `SegmentedItem.location`).

attributes.name: value
attributes.doc:
The active choice. Constrain it to your own state and override `input` to own the
destination, or leave it alone and read `value` back — a `Segmented` works
standalone. Compared against each choice's `id` by identity, so any value type
works.

docSegs.md:
The active choice. Constrain it to your own state and override `input` to own the
destination, or leave it alone and read `value` back — a `Segmented` works
standalone. Compared against each choice's `id` by identity, so any value type
works.

attributes.name: disabled
attributes.doc:
Disables the whole control. **A segment is not separately disable-able** — a disabled
group leaves the tab order entirely rather than offering unreachable stops.

docSegs.md:
Disables the whole control. **A segment is not separately disable-able** — a disabled
group leaves the tab order entirely rather than offering unreachable stops.

attributes.name: rad
attributes.doc:
The control's corner radius, from the theme's `segmentedCornerRadius` (8 by default); the
pill and each segment's hover sit 2 inside it.

docSegs.md:
The control's corner radius, from the theme's `segmentedCornerRadius` (8 by default); the
pill and each segment's hover sit 2 inside it.

attributes.name: segMin
attributes.doc:
The per-segment width used when you set no `width` on the control. Because a
`Segmented` **does not self-size to its labels**, this is what decides the default
width: `segMin × choices.length`.

docSegs.md:
The per-segment width used when you set no `width` on the control. Because a
`Segmented` **does not self-size to its labels**, this is what decides the default
width: `segMin × choices.length`.

attributes.name: count
attributes.doc: How many choices there are, floored at 1 so the width arithmetic never divides by zero.

docSegs.md: How many choices there are, floored at 1 so the width arithmetic never divides by zero.

attributes.name: segW
attributes.doc:
One segment's width — the control's width divided by the count. What the pill and every
segment position from.

docSegs.md:

attributes.name: idx
attributes.doc:
Which choice is live, as an index into `choices`, from the **data** — the only place the
question can be asked. `−1` (nothing selected) parks the pill at 0 and hides it rather
than springing to a phantom slot.

attributes.name: lane
attributes.doc:
The pill's position as a **float index**, sprung toward `idx`. The whole reason the pill
is correct at any size: `x` is `lane × segW`, so a resize recomputes the width and the
pill **snaps** to the right place instead of skating across the bar on every layout
change.

attributes.name: focusScope
attributes.doc:
`stop`: the control is one Tab stop — Tab lands on the selected segment and the next
Tab leaves; the arrows move among the segments, wrapping, as in any stop. Space or Enter
picks where they land, so **an inactive choice is reachable and selectable entirely from
the keyboard**, and nothing changes until it is asked to — a choice that is a place is
followed on Enter, as a link is, not on the arrow.

Tab leaves; the arrows move among the segments, wrapping, as in any stop. Space or Enter
picks where they land, so **an inactive choice is reachable and selectable entirely from
the keyboard**, and nothing changes until it is asked to — a choice that is a place is
followed on Enter, as a link is, not on the arrow.

between segments; one beside the pill fades as the pill reaches it, so they part around the
selection as it slides.

tree.name: TextSizeSwitch
tree.doc:
The reading-size control: three sizes — smaller, the default, larger — each shown as
the letter A at that size, with the size in use marked. It is a `Segmented`, so it
holds its value the way every segmented control does, Tab reaches it as one stop, and
the arrows move between the sizes.

The value is a scale, one of `sizes`. An app keeps the scale it reads its text at and
binds the switch to it:

```declare-fragment
App [ fontScale: number = 1,
    TextSizeSwitch [ value = { app.fontScale },
        input(v: object) { app.fontScale = v as number } ],
    Text [ fontSize = { 15 * app.fontScale }, text = "Read me" ]
    ]
```

docSegs.md:

the letter A at that size, with the size in use marked. It is a `Segmented`, so it
holds its value the way every segmented control does, Tab reaches it as one stop, and
the arrows move between the sizes.

The value is a scale, one of `sizes`. An app keeps the scale it reads its text at and

```declare-fragment

    ]
```

tree.name: ChevronIcon
tree.doc:
The **disclosure** mark: a menu drops, a pane opens, a select expands. Every
disclosure in the chrome is this one class turned by its `dir`, which is what makes
them agree. For a direction that is itself the state — a sort order, a trend — reach
for `ArrowIcon` instead; the two must not look alike.

docSegs.md:

disclosure in the chrome is this one class turned by its `dir`, which is what makes
them agree. For a direction that is itself the state — a sort order, a trend — reach
for `ArrowIcon` instead; the two must not look alike.

attributes.name: dir
attributes.doc:
The resting orientation: `"down"` (the default), `"up"`, `"left"` or `"right"`. Sugar
over `angle`.

docSegs.md:

attributes.name: angle
attributes.doc:
The rotation in radians, and **the primitive, so it can be sprung** — an `Accordion`
twisty turns in step with its pane sliding open rather than snapping between two
states. The turn lives in the recording deliberately: the mark rotates inside its
16-box while the box stays put. (The View-level `rotation` attribute turns the whole
box — the wrong tool for a glyph whose frame should not move.)

        ]

tree.doc:

local**: a menu row inverts its check on the highlighted row while a checkbox always
uses the accent text color, so the host sets `ink` rather than the icon assuming it.

tree.name: Icon
tree.doc:
A small monochrome mark, **drawn** rather than typed. A font's glyphs are not
marks: they are not guaranteed to be present, they rasterize differently on
every platform, and the ones that exist are the wrong shapes — a `✓` sits on the
text baseline and reads like a square-root sign, not like a checkmark. The
library's own marks — `Checkbox.mark`, `Menu.check`, the `Combobox` disclosure —
are all `Icon`s.

An icon is placed like any view. In a row, the row's `align = center` centers it with
the text beside it; placed by hand, it takes `y = center` as any view does.

### Writing one

Subclass and override `draw`. Author the shape in a **16×16 box** — `unit`
converts it to whatever size the host asked for:

```declare-fragment
class SparkIcon extends Icon [
    draw(d: Draw) {
        d.scale(unit, unit)
        d.strokeStyle = ink; d.lineWidth = weight / unit
        d.beginPath(); d.moveTo(8, 1); d.lineTo(8, 15); d.stroke()
        }
    ]
```

Overriding a **method** is how a subclass refines an icon — a subclass cannot
re-declare a child it inherits (the compiler refuses it) — so the shape lives in
`draw` and everything adjustable is an attribute.

### Size changes the drawing, not the shape

Every icon is **one path**. There are no per-size variants, no thresholds, nothing
redrawn at a breakpoint: `unit` scales the 16-box to whatever the host asked for,
so a 64px icon is the 16px icon at 4×, exactly.

The **stroke** is the deliberate exception. `d.lineWidth = weight / unit` sits
*inside* `d.scale(unit, unit)`, so the two cancel and the line lands at a constant
`weight` in **device pixels at every size**. An icon's line therefore matches the
1px rules and text weights it sits among, instead of fattening as it grows.

The cost is that the stroke-to-size ratio falls: 1.6px is 10% of a 16px icon, 5%
at 32, 2.5% at 64. Across 14–18px — chrome sizes — that is invisible. Past ~32
an icon starts reading as a fine-line drawing rather than a mark — so **this set
is built for chrome sizes**, and a large display icon (an empty-state mark, an
about-box graphic) would want the opposite: `d.lineWidth = weight` *outside* the
scale, so the line grows with the drawing.

### What is not an Icon

Application art. The desktop's dock icons are the case to look at before
reaching for this class: they rest at 56px and grow under the magnification
swell, they are polychrome (`gradient(hue1, hue2)` behind a hue-parameterised
drawing), and their **width animates every frame**. Each of those alone rules
them out — the constant stroke that suits a 16px mark is 2.9% of a 56px one and
reads spindly; `ink` is a single colour; and an animated width is the one thing
this set forbids.

The line is not "drawn versus not drawn" — dock art is drawn too. It is
**chrome vocabulary versus identity**. A mark that says *close*, *expand*,
*checked*, *this is the dark theme* belongs here, at a size the host states.
A mark that says *this is Calendar* does not, and belongs to the app that owns
the identity.

Desktop has both, which is what makes it the clarifying example: its menu rows
take `WindowIcon` and `CodeIcon` from this set, while its dock keeps `DockIcon`.

### Two rules

**Scale inside the body, never with the View's `scale`.** A recording rasterizes
into a canvas sized to its own ink bounds at device resolution, while `scale` is
a transform applied *after* — so `scale = { width / 16 }` would rasterize 16
pixels and stretch them. Crisp at exactly 16, soft at every other size, which is
most of them. Scaling inside the recording allocates the raster at true size
instead.

**Never animate an icon's `width`.** Reading size inside `draw` makes the
recording size-dependent: an animated size re-records **and** reallocates the
backing canvas every frame, which drops a magnifying dock of icons from 60 to
~25fps. A static size re-records once and costs nothing after: 120 icons
re-recording their *content* every frame run frame-bound at 16.6ms.

Colour is not a rule — `ink` follows the provided text colour, so an icon beside
a muted label goes muted on its own, and a host that needs a different ink (a
menu row's check inverting on the hot row) simply sets it.

tree.name: IconHost
tree.doc:
Turns an icon's class name into a live view. A control names its icon
(`iconLeft = "TrashIcon"`) rather than nesting one: a control is a leaf, and a name is
the one form that is the same whether it is written or read from data. `IconHost`
builds the named icon with `createView`, as a menu record's `icon` field does.

It reserves no space when empty, so a control's `contentWidth` measures only the slots
that are filled and an icon-less button needs no special case.

**The name is read once, when the host is built.** A name read from data gives each row
of a toolbar its own icon, but changing the name later does not swap the icon. An icon that
must change at runtime — a play/pause toggle — is two icons, each with `visible`
constrained.

authored directly**, which is why it carries almost nothing of its own. It is a full

inactive choice and select it.

these, not a fill of its own** — which is exactly what lets the pill travel between

sit adjacent — a sort-direction control beside a sort-menu popper — and one shape for
both reads as a mistake.

tree.name: AppearanceSwitch
tree.doc:
The light/dark control: one icon that shows the appearance you are in — a sun in
light, a moon in dark — and a press flips to the other. Two states, not three.

The third state other switches carry, "follow the system", is not a choice here but
the **default**: an app derives its appearance from its environment (the OS, or the
host it is embedded in) until the reader presses the switch, and from then on keeps
what the reader chose. That is the rule the platform's own apps follow, and it is
why the control needs no Auto button: nobody has to choose to follow the system,
because until they choose anything else, they already are.

```declare-fragment
App [ themeMode: string = "auto",                     // "auto" until the reader chooses
    isDark: boolean = { app.themeMode == "auto" ? app.dark : app.themeMode == "dark" },
    theme = { app.isDark ? SanFranciscoDark : SanFrancisco },
    AppearanceSwitch [ dark = { app.isDark },
        input(v: boolean) { app.themeMode = v ? "dark" : "light" } ]
    ]
```
