tree.name: Floating
tree.doc:
The base of every overlay in the library — `Popover`, `Sheet`, `Dialog`, `Toast`, and the
menus — and of a program's own (`class Viewer extends Dialog [ … ]`). It is declared where it
belongs, in its owner, and paints above everything in its context: in the overlay layer the
nearest `Window` provides, else in the App's own layers — overlays in the order they open,
toasts above them.
It carries, once, what every overlay needs:

- **Opening and closing** — `show()` and `close()`; `shown` says whether it is open now. A
  closed overlay builds no view of its own until it is first shown.
- **Motion** — it animates in and out on `openT` (0 closed, 1 open), and stays built until
  its closing motion lands: closing stops it taking input at once.
- **Input** — `pressPolicy` and `scrollPolicy` say what a press and a scroll aimed past it do
  (`outsidePress`, `scrollBelow`), while it is open. An outside press that dismisses closes it.
- **Keys and focus** — while open it holds the keyboard (a key it uses does not also reach
  the program's `Keys` members); Esc closes the topmost open overlay; one that takes focus
  focuses its first stop on opening and gives focus back on closing.
- **Anchoring** — `anchorBox(v)` is a view's box in the overlay's frame, for an overlay that
  opens next to something; `toLayer(v, x, y)` maps a point the same way, through a window
  turned or scaled; `keepOnApp(x, y, w, h)` moves a box back onto the App.

```declare
App [ width = 420, height = 220,
    Button [ x = 20, y = 20, label = "Show", onClick() { app.note.show() } ],
    note: Popover [ anchorTo = { app.children[0] as View },
        Text [ text = "A popover is a Floating." ]
        ]
    ]
```

tree.name: Popover
tree.doc:
A bubble anchored to a view, holding your own content — a picker, a few settings, an info
card. It opens next to its anchor (below, else above where there is no room), follows it as
it moves, and closes when you press anywhere outside it, the press going on to what you
pressed. On a phone-width screen it presents as a sheet rising from the bottom instead.

```declare
App [ width = 420, height = 240,
    b: Button [ x = 20, y = 20, label = "Font…", onClick() { app.pick.showFor(this) } ],
    pick: Popover [
        Text [ text = "Size" ],
        Slider [ width = 180 ]
        ]
    ]
```

It is a `Floating`: it takes focus on opening (its first control) and gives it back on
closing; Tab stays inside it; Esc closes it.

tree.name: Sheet
tree.doc:
A modal panel attached to an edge of its context — a form, a detail, a set of choices. On
a phone-width screen it rises from the bottom, and a downward swipe on its handle puts it
away; on a wide screen it slides in from the end edge (`edge = "end"`) or, for a sheet whose
edge is the bottom, floats as a card in the middle. A sheet at the start edge
(`edge = "start"`) is a navigation drawer: it slides in from the start edge at every width,
and a swipe back toward that edge on its trailing edge puts it away. Behind it the context
dims; a press there closes the sheet, and nothing behind it scrolls while it is open. Tab stays inside it;
Esc closes it; focus goes to its first control when it opens and back when it closes.

```declare
App [ width = 640, height = 420,
    Button [ x = 20, y = 20, label = "New entry…", onClick() { app.entry.show() } ],
    entry: Sheet [ edge = "end",
        Text [ fontWeight = bold, text = "New entry" ],
        TextInput [ width = 100%, accessibilityLabel = "Title" ],
        Button [ label = "Save", primary = true, onClick() { app.entry.close() } ]
        ]
    ]
```

tree.name: Shortcuts
tree.doc:
Keyboard shortcuts, declared as data: records with the key that triggers each, the label a
person reads, and the id the action receives. A set covers the view it is declared on and
everything inside it. A key press is looked up from the focused view outward: the nearest
set that declares that key takes it, and the press goes no further. The walk goes on past the
program — a program running in a desktop window reaches the desktop's shortcuts — so a host
offers its keys to whatever runs inside it without passing anything down.

```declare
App [ width = 520, height = 240,
    saved: number = 0,
    keys: Shortcuts [ title = "Notes",
        items = { [ ({ id: "save", key: "⌘S", label: "Save" }), ({ id: "clear", key: "⇧⌘K", label: "Clear" }) ] },
        picked(id: string) { if (id == "save") app.saved = app.saved + 1 }
        ],
    Text [ x = 20, y = 20, text = { "Saved " + app.saved + " times — press ⌘S" } ]
    ]
```

A key with a command modifier (⌘, ⌃, ⌥) or a function key works anywhere; a plain key
(`"?"`) does not fire while a text field has focus — typing is the field's. While an open
menu, dialog or sheet holds the keyboard its keys are its own: a set declared inside it is in
force — a form in a sheet keeps its own keys — and every set outside it stands down. A shortcut's chord is
not also the browser's (⌘S does not save the page) — except those the browser keeps for
itself, such as ⌘W and ⌘N in Safari, which a label may still show.

A `MenuBar` declares the keys of its items for its whole program: the menu bar is the
program's shortcut table, and nothing is declared twice. `Keys.shortcutsInForce()` lists what
is in force where focus is — a panel of the available shortcuts reads it.

tree.name: Window
tree.doc:
A window inside a program: a raised surface with a title bar you drag it by and a button at
its end that closes it — and, when `resizable`, edges that resize it. It is the theme's
surface, hairline, rounding and shadow, as a dialog or a popover is, with the title bar the
same surface and a hairline under it.

It is also a world of its own. A menu, popover, dialog or sheet declared inside it opens
over it: above its content and past its edges, turning and scaling with it. A toast belongs
to the whole program and shows at the bottom of the App. Tab stays among the window's
controls; F6 moves to the next window, Shift-F6 back; a press inside it gives it the
keyboard, back on the control that last had focus there, and brings it to the front. A
dialog or sheet open in it holds back presses aimed at this window only — another window,
or what lies behind, still takes them. Esc closes it when focus is inside it and nothing
open inside it takes Esc first.

Its children go into its body, the pane below the title bar, and place themselves there as
in any view — give one a layout or a `padding` of its own. Whether it is open is state, by
the value pattern: `open` on its own, or `open = { … }` with `input` writing where your
state lives. Its `x`, `y`, `width` and `height` are its own to move and resize, so set them
as literals.

```declare
App [ width = 640, height = 360, fill = { provided("theme").background },
    notesOpen: boolean = true,
    Button [ x = 20, y = 316, label = "Show notes", disabled = { app.notesOpen },
        onClick() { app.notesOpen = true } ],
    Window [ x = 30, y = 30, width = 280, height = 190, title = "Settings",
        more: Menu [ items = { [ ({ id: "reset", label: "Reset" }), ({ id: "copy", label: "Copy settings" }) ] } ],
        View [ width = 100%, padding = 16,
            layout: SimpleLayout [ axis = y, spacing = 12 ],
            Checkbox [ label = "Show line numbers" ],
            Checkbox [ label = "Wrap long lines" ],
            Button [ label = "More", menu = { parent.parent.more } ]
            ]
        ],
    Window [ x = 330, y = 60, width = 280, height = 220, title = "Notes", resizable = true,
        open = { app.notesOpen }, input(v: boolean) { app.notesOpen = v },
        View [ width = 100%, padding = 16,
            layout: SimpleLayout [ axis = y, spacing = 10 ],
            TextInput [ width = 100%, placeholder = "Title" ]
            ]
        ]
    ]
```

`frame = false` keeps the world and drops the frame: no surface, title bar, close button or
resize edges, and no bringing itself forward or closing on Esc — its fill, stroke, shadow
and rounding are yours, and so are moving, sizing and stacking it (`raise()` brings it to the
front). What a program with windows of its own design builds on — the Desktop app's are
these.

```declare
App [ width = 560, height = 260, fill = #E6E9EE,
    Window [ x = 40, y = 40, width = 240, height = 160, rotation = -4, frame = false, title = "Tilted",
        cornerRadius = 10, fill = white, shadow = { shadow(0, 6, 20, 0x00000033) },
        Text [ x = 16, y = 16, text = "A window of its own design" ],
        TextInput [ x = 16, y = 52, width = 200, accessibilityLabel = "Note" ]
        ]
    ]
```

tree.name: Tree
tree.doc:
An outline whose rows open and close to show their children — a file browser, the
sidebar of a mail program or a Finder window. Like `Segmented`'s choices and `Menu`'s
items, what it shows is **data**: nested records, each `{ id, label, icon?, children? }`.

```declare-fragment
Tree [ width = 240, accessibilityLabel = "Files",
    items = { app.folders },
    value = { app.picked }, input(v: string) { app.picked = v },
    expanded = { app.openFolders }, expandInput(ids: array) { app.openFolders = ids }
    ]
```

The Tree holds two values, and both follow the value pattern: **`value`**, the id of the
selected row, and **`expanded`**, the ids of the rows that are open. Neither is written
into the records — the records say what the outline holds, the two values say where the
person is in it — so the same records can stand under two trees open in different
places. Each value works standalone, or is owned by the program through `input` and
`expandInput`.

The rows on screen are the open part of the outline, flattened into a dataset and
replicated as `TreeRow`s. Every row is built, none virtualized: a tree is for tens or
hundreds of rows, not hundreds of thousands. For a long flat collection use a `Table`.

### Keyboard

The Tree is **one Tab stop**: Tab lands on the selected row (else the first) and the
next Tab leaves. Focus itself moves from row to row, so a screen reader announces each:

- **Up** and **Down** move to the previous and next visible row; **Home** and **End** to
  the first and last.
- **Right** opens a closed row; on an open one it moves to its first child.
- **Left** closes an open row; on any other it moves to the row's parent.
- **Enter** and **Space** select the row focus is on.

With the pointer, a click selects a row, a click on its chevron opens or closes it
without selecting, and a second click on a row with children opens or closes it.

### Naming it

A tree is something a person moves through, so a screen reader needs its name: set
`accessibilityLabel` where you place it ("Files", "Mailboxes"). The rows are named by
their labels.

```declare
App [ width = 320, height = 300, picked: string = "notes",
    Tree [ x = 20, y = 20, width = 280, accessibilityLabel = "Documents",
        expanded = ["docs"],
        value = { app.picked }, input(v: string) { app.picked = v },
        items = { [
            ({ id: "docs", label: "Documents", children: [
                ({ id: "notes", label: "Notes.txt" }),
                ({ id: "plans", label: "Plans", children: [
                    ({ id: "q3", label: "Third quarter" }),
                    ({ id: "q4", label: "Fourth quarter" }) ] }) ] }),
            ({ id: "pics", label: "Pictures", children: [
                ({ id: "beach", label: "Beach.jpg" }) ] }),
            ({ id: "todo", label: "To do" }) ] }
        ],
    Text [ x = 20, y = 260, text = { "selected: " + app.picked } ]
    ]
```

attributes.name: items
attributes.doc:
The outline, as **records**: `{ id, label, icon?, children? }`, where `children` is an
array of the same records, nested to any depth. `id` is a string and unique across the
whole tree — selection and the open rows are held by it. `icon` names an icon class, as
`Menu`'s items do (`icon: "CheckIcon"`); a name computed at run time needs
`use [ Name ]` to survive the build. A row with a `children` array is a parent even when
the array is empty.

methods.name: flatten
methods.doc:
The visible rows, in order: the outline walked from the top, descending only into open
rows. Each row record wraps its source record (`item`) and adds what the row shows from
the outline — `level` (1 at the top), `hasChildren`, `open`, the `parent` row's id, and
its place among its siblings, `pos` of `size`. The tree's own dataset of these rows,
re-derived whenever `items` or `expanded` changes, is what the `TreeRow`s replicate over;
the rows stack flush.

tree.name: TreeRow
tree.doc:
One row of a `Tree`, **materialized from the tree's visible rows — never authored
directly**. It is a `Control`, so focus lands on the row itself and a screen reader
announces it as a tree item, with its level, whether it is open, and whether it is
selected.

A row is the library's row look: a rounded highlight, `controlHovered` under the pointer
and `controlSelected` when selected, the label in the theme's `text` at the menu's size.
A row with children leads with a chevron that turns on a spring as it opens and closes,
the same turn as an `Accordion` pane's; a row without one leaves the space blank, so
labels at one level line up.

```declare
App [ width = 280, height = 140,
    Tree [ x = 20, y = 20, accessibilityLabel = "Mailboxes", expanded = ["in"],
        items = { [ ({ id: "in", label: "Inbox", children: [
                        ({ id: "work", label: "Work" }), ({ id: "home", label: "Home" }) ] }),
                    ({ id: "sent", label: "Sent" }) ] }
        ]
    ]
```

tree.name: Splitter
tree.doc:
The divider between two panes — a mail list and the message beside it, a sidebar and the
page — that a person drags to give one pane more room. **It is only the divider**: you
arrange the panes yourself, and the pane before it reads `value` for its size. Drag it,
or Tab to it and use the arrow keys; it keeps `value` inside `min`…`max` either way.

```declare
App [ width = 600, height = 300, fill = { provided("theme").surface },
    row: View [ width = 100%, height = 100%,
        layout: SimpleLayout [ axis = x ],
        side: View [ width = { app.row.split.value }, height = 100%, fill = { provided("theme").background },
            Text [ x = 16, y = 16, text = "Mailboxes" ] ],
        split: Splitter [ value = 200, min = 120, max = 400, accessibilityLabel = "Sidebar width" ],
        main: View [ width = { app.row.width - app.row.side.width - app.row.split.width }, height = 100%,
            Text [ x = 16, y = 16, text = "Message" ] ]
        ]
    ]
```

At rest it is a hairline in the theme's `line`; under the pointer, while dragged and while
focused from the keyboard it becomes a 2 px line in `accent`. Its own footprint along the
axis is the slim strip a pointer can catch (`thickness`), with the line centred in it.

The same value pattern as every control: standalone it owns `value`, as above; constrained
to your own state it needs `input` with it —
`Splitter [ value = { app.sideW }, input(v: number) { app.sideW = v } ]`.

tree.name: DatePicker
tree.doc:
A field that shows a date and opens a month to pick one from. Press it — or Enter,
Space or Down on it — and a `Popover` opens below it holding a `MonthCalendar`, with the
focus on the chosen day; picking a day sets it and closes, and the focus goes back to
the field. Esc, or a press past it, closes without picking.

```declare
App [ width = 340, height = 380, due: string = "",
    DatePicker [ x = 20, y = 20, value = { app.due },
        input(v: string) { app.due = v } ],
    Text [ x = 20, y = 70, text = { app.due == "" ? "no date" : "due " + app.due } ]
    ]
```

It looks like a `Combobox`'s field: the theme's field fill and line, its height and
corners, a chevron at the end. The date shows in the program's language
(`app.language`) at medium length, "Oct 18, 2026".

tree.name: MonthCalendar
tree.doc:
A month of days to pick one from: the month and year with buttons to the months either
side, a row of weekday initials, and six weeks of days. Days of the months either side
fill the first and last weeks, in muted ink, and pressing one picks it and shows its
month. Today wears a ring; the chosen day is filled.

Its value is a date as an ISO string, `"YYYY-MM-DD"`, or `""` for none — the value
pattern, as every control has it: standalone it keeps its own, constrained it delivers
through `input`.

```declare
App [ width = 300, height = 340, day: string = "2026-10-18",
    MonthCalendar [ x = 20, y = 20, value = { app.day }, min = "2026-10-05",
        input(v: string) { app.day = v } ],
    Text [ x = 20, y = 310, text = { app.day } ]
    ]
```

The days are one Tab stop, as a screen reader's grid: Tab lands on the chosen day, else
today, else the 1st. The arrows move a day left and right and a week up and down, into
the next or previous month when they cross its edge; Page Up and Page Down move a month
(with Shift, a year); Home and End go to the start and end of the week; Enter or Space
picks. The month buttons are Tab stops of their own, before the days.

Names come from the program's language (`app.language`): the month, the weekday
initials, and each day's full date, which is what a screen reader says on it.

tree.name: Disclosure
tree.doc:
A section that opens and closes under a line that names it — "Advanced options", "Show
details". Press the line and the section slides open below it, its chevron turning as it
goes; press again and it slides shut. `Accordion` is a stack of these that keeps one open;
a `Disclosure` stands alone, and any number may be open.

The content is the disclosure's ordinary children, present through the whole slide and
carried by the disclosure's clip, exactly as an `Accordion`'s `Pane` carries its own:

```declare
App [ width = 320, height = 200,
    Disclosure [ x = 20, y = 20, width = 280, label = "Advanced options",
        Checkbox [ label = "Keep a log" ],
        Checkbox [ label = "Check for updates" ]
        ]
    ]
```

To a screen reader the line is a button that says whether it is expanded; Tab reaches the
content only while it is open.

tree.name: Stepper
tree.doc:
A number you change a step at a time — a quantity, a font size, a count of copies. It
shows the value between a − and a + on the same rounded track a `Segmented` sits on, and
is one Tab stop:

```declare
App [ width = 300, height = 100, copies: number = 2,
    Stepper [ x = 20, y = 20, value = { app.copies }, min = 1, max = 99,
        accessibilityLabel = "Copies",
        input(v: number) { app.copies = v } ],
    Text [ x = 160, y = 26, text = { app.copies + " copies" } ]
    ]
```

From the keyboard, Up and Down step it, Page Up and Page Down move ten steps, and Home and End
go to `min` and `max`. To a screen reader it is a spin button, named at its use site, saying
its value and range; its adjust gesture steps it the same way. − and + are for the pointer,
and dim at the ends of the range.

tree.name: Toolbar
tree.doc:
A row of commands that is one Tab stop — a text editor's Bold, Italic and Underline, a
drawing app's tools. Tab lands on its first command (or the one last used), the arrows move
along the row, Home and End go to its ends, and the next Tab leaves it, so a long row of
commands costs one stop. It sits on the same rounded track a `Segmented` does, its
`ToolButton`s quiet until hovered:

```declare
use [ PlusIcon, MinusIcon ]

App [ width = 360, height = 100, bold: boolean = false, italic: boolean = false,
    Toolbar [ x = 20, y = 20, accessibilityLabel = "Formatting",
        ToolButton [ label = "B", toggle = true, on = { app.bold }, input(v: boolean) { app.bold = v },
            accessibilityLabel = "Bold" ],
        ToolButton [ label = "I", toggle = true, on = { app.italic }, input(v: boolean) { app.italic = v },
            accessibilityLabel = "Italic" ],
        ToolbarDivider [ ],
        ToolButton [ icon = "PlusIcon", label = "Add" ],
        ToolButton [ icon = "MinusIcon", label = "Remove" ]
        ]
    ]
```

Its children are yours: `ToolButton`s, a `ToolbarDivider` between groups, or any control —
a `Segmented`, a `Stepper` — which the arrows reach like the rest. To a screen reader it is a
toolbar, named at its use site.


tree.name: Breadcrumb
tree.doc:
The path to where you are — Home › Guide › Layout — each step a way back up. The steps are
**records**, outermost first; the last is where you are, shown in the stronger ink and not
pressable. A step with a `location` is a real link (⌘-click, copy link, the crawler); one
without is a button that hands its `id` to `input`:

```declare
App [ width = 400, height = 80, at: string = "layout",
    Breadcrumb [ x = 20, y = 20,
        items = { [ ({ id: "home", label: "Home" }),
                    ({ id: "guide", label: "Guide" }),
                    ({ id: "layout", label: "Layout" }) ] },
        input(id: string) { app.at = id } ]
    ]
```

To a screen reader it is a navigation landmark named "Breadcrumb", its steps links or
buttons, the last one the current page. Each step is a Tab stop, as links are.

tree.doc:

code path: Cupertino metrics — compact controls, 6px
radii, the tight hairline focus halo hugging the control (gap 0), a muted

theme token.

tree.name: ThemeDefaults
tree.doc:
The value every **optional** library token takes when the theme in force does not
state it. The runtime lays any provided theme over this record, so a library class
reads `provided("theme").segmentedHeight` and always gets a number: a theme states
only what it changes, and no read site carries a fallback of its own.

The **required** tokens — the palette (`accent`, `surface`, `text`, `line`,
`control` and their states) and `controlCornerRadius`, `focusRingStyle` — are not
here: a missing colour is an error to see, never a light default under a dark theme.

A token whose natural default is another token (`trackFill` is `control` unless a
theme says otherwise) has no value here; its reader says so with `??`. One that no
preset states is listed as `null` all the same, so every token a theme can carry is
declared somewhere and reading one that is not is a compile error. This record is
not a preset: no program names it.

tree.name: Redmond
tree.doc:
The Fluent-fidelity record (Windows 11): 4px radii on everything, the
Windows accent blue (light-on-dark flips to the pale #4CC2FF with dark
text on it), compact 32px buttons, the 40×20 toggle with its 12px
off-thumb, the round slider grabber with the accent dot
(`sliderHandleStyle = "dot"`), and Fluent's two-tone focus **rectangle** — a 2px
outer stroke over a 1px inner separator (`focusRingInnerWidth`), black
over white in light, white over black in dark. Windows focus does not
fly: `focusRingStyle = "rest"` — the indicator appears in place and stays. An
accent button's hover and pressed tones are Fluent's secondary and tertiary
accent fills — the accent at 90% and 80% over the page.
Segoe UI is the consuming app's `fontFamily`, not a theme token.

tree.name: SanFrancisco
tree.doc:
Declare's own look — named for where Declare is made — and the theme a widget
renders when nothing provides one: `control.declare` defaults `theme` to
`SanFrancisco` (the light record), so an app that never mentions a theme is San
Francisco light, always. These declarations are the preset itself, written in the
language; the runtime serves them by name.

A record is **complete**, not a delta: every token the standard library consults is
stated, so a preset reads whole with nothing to chase. A control's hover and pressed
step darker in light and lighter in dark. The accent steps darker in both: it is the
fill behind white labels, which a lighter blue would wash out. Links are blue on the
page itself, so they take their own `linkColor`, lighter than the accent in dark.

Declare's own look — named for where Declare is made — and the theme a widget
renders when nothing provides one: `control.declare` defaults `theme` to
`SanFrancisco` (the light record), so an app that never mentions a theme is San
Francisco light, always. These declarations are the preset itself, written in the
language; the runtime serves them by name.

A record is **complete**, not a delta: every token the standard library consults is
stated, so a preset reads whole with nothing to chase. A control's hover and pressed
step darker in light and lighter in dark. The accent steps darker in both: it is the
fill behind white labels, which a lighter blue would wash out. Links are blue on the
page itself, so they take their own `linkColor`, lighter than the accent in dark.

# How it ships

Delivery, hosting, and the honest posture — the promises about running and
shipping a Declare program.

### SATOR-1 — Programs are data
A compiled program is data the toolchain can read, so one compiler powers the
documentation system, static extraction for crawlers, and live editing alike —
not three separate pipelines.
*Held in:* FAQ ("programs are data — the same compiler powers the documentation system, static extraction for crawlers, and live editing").

### SATOR-2 — What a visitor sees and what a crawler sees can never drift
Static extraction is built into the compiler: it runs the program headlessly to
its settled state and serializes the actual content as semantic HTML — real
headings, paragraphs, links — baked into the page at build time. A crawler (or an
AI reading the web) reads that; a person gets the live app that replaces it at
boot. No server-side rendering, no hydration — it works on a plain static host.
*Held in:* FAQ ("How do Declare-written sites handle crawlers and SEO"); the "why" essay ("what a visitor sees and what a crawler sees can never drift").

### SATOR-3 — In-browser compilation, and no build step to develop
Because the compiler runs in the page, a page can edit and re-run itself: every
sample is live-editable, and view-source culture is restored. Development needs no
build step — the dev server and the browser use the *same* compiler with
byte-identical output.
*Held in:* FAQ ("What benefits does in-browser compilation bring"); getstarted ("no build step").

### SATOR-4 — You don't ship the compiler
For production, `declarec` precompiles everything into a small, self-contained
artifact — a set of static files you can host anywhere, with no trace of the
toolchain and no compiler aboard.
*Held in:* FAQ ("For production you don't ship the compiler").

### SATOR-5 — The program's URL is the app's address
A program is addressed by its own URL: on the dev server, browse to a `.declare`
file's URL and get the running app. The address is the program, not a route
registered elsewhere.
*Held in:* getstarted ("the program URL is the app's address"); FAQ.

### SATOR-6 — Small, and fast where it counts
A full application ships small — the flagship calendar, application *and* runtime,
at roughly 153 KB gzipped (machine-stamped from
the measured artifact): a compact runtime, practical on a phone over a slow network.
Input latency is low — there is no virtual-DOM pass between gesture and pixels — and
animation runs at the display's full rate. The homepage reports the live size figures,
measured from the deployed artifacts and regenerated with them on every publication.
*Held in:* FAQ ("What should I expect in terms of performance").

### SATOR-7 — Honest about the trades and the gaps
The promises come with their limits stated plainly: a framework with no in-browser
compiler wins the very first cold load (the production path closes the gap by
precompiling); Declare is young and the repository *is* the distribution and the
source of truth; an npm package and a dedicated editor extension are named, unhidden
gaps; and the canvas renderer does not yet carry the accessibility the DOM renderer does.
*Held in:* FAQ ("Startup" trade; "How mature is Declare?"; "Is Declare accessible?"; "Is there editor support?").

### SATOR-8 — Open, MIT, entirely public
The complete source — compiler, runtime, standard library, documentation, and the
site itself — is public under the MIT license.
*Held in:* FAQ ("What license is Declare offered under?").

# The wager

Why the language is shaped the way it is: built for the era when much code is
written by machines, and bet on verifiability over familiarity.

### AREPO-1 — Built for machine-written code
When machines write the code, familiarity matters less and *verifiability* matters
more. Declare is designed around that shift, not retrofitted to it.
*Held in:* homepage hero ("a UI language for you and your AI"); FAQ ("Declare is built for the era when much code is written by machines").

### AREPO-2 — The whole language fits in a model's context
The declarative surface is small, closed, and regular — its *entire* definition is
one file (`docs/declare.md`, on the order of 13,000 tokens). No model has
trained on Declare, and none needs to: a model can hold the complete spec while it
writes.
*Held in:* declare.md preamble ("the language, in one file … no LLM has been trained on it"); FAQ; the "why" essay.

### AREPO-3 — Comprehension leverage, not corpus leverage
Declare competes on the kind of leverage a new language *can* have: a language
small enough to hand a model whole, regular enough to be analyzed rather than
pattern-matched, backed by a compiler that turns each mistake into a precise
correction. With less code passing under human eyes, the language and its compiler
are the one reviewer always present.
*Held in:* the "why" essay ("Two kinds of leverage").

### AREPO-4 — Type-checking is mandatory, and trustworthy
Every `{ }` body is type-checked on every compile, with no opt-out, and the
checker is held to **zero false positives** across the repository's own corpus —
every app, component, and doc example it ships. So an error always means something
is genuinely wrong.
*Held in:* FAQ ("Mandatory type-checking … zero false positives").

### AREPO-5 — Diagnostics name the fix
A compiler message is written to steer the *next* attempt — it states the rule and
names the rewrite that fixes it, including "did you mean" guidance for instincts
carried from other frameworks. The primary reader of a diagnostic, now, is a model
deciding what to do next.
*Held in:* FAQ ("Diagnostics that name the fix"); the "why" essay.

### AREPO-6 — No magic
Declare consistently chooses predictability over cleverness: dependencies are
extracted statically, events don't bubble, there is one way to say most things.
Where it looks familiar it behaves as you'd assume; where it is genuinely new it
*looks* new — a cue to consult the spec rather than autocomplete from memory.
*Held in:* FAQ ("No magic"); the "why" essay.

### AREPO-7 — Tested against models, not assumed
The claim that Declare suits LLMs is tested: an evaluation harness gives
model tiers application-building tasks cold, one-shot and iterated, and failures
feed back into the language, the diagnostics, and the docs. The documentation
doubles as training material — every code fence in the teaching docs is
compiled by the test suite, so nothing a model reads is stale or wrong.
*Held in:* FAQ ("What has been done during Declare's development to optimize for LLM usage").

### AREPO-8 — The human owns intent; the toolchain keeps the text honest
The workflow the language is designed around: a person directs and reviews; a
model writes the text; the compiler stays in the loop. The flagship calendar
reports its own number — zero lines written by hand.
*Held in:* FAQ ("The calendar says '0 lines written by hand'").

# The standing model

Reactivity and continuity — the central idea the whole language is arranged
around.

### TENET-1 — A binding is a standing relationship the runtime keeps true
Read a reactive value inside a binding and you are subscribed; assign to one and
everything bound to it updates. That is the defining idea, and it holds with no
re-render, no diffing, no dependency array, and no hook — the relationship is
kept true for you, not re-run by you.
*Held in:* declare.md §1.

### TENET-2 — Reactivity is derived by the compiler, not guessed at runtime
The compiler works out what every binding depends on, statically. Behavior is
therefore predictable and analyzable by tools rather than discovered as the
program runs — the model reasons about exactly what the compiler verifies.
*Held in:* FAQ ("reactivity is *derived by the compiler*, not guessed at runtime"); the "why" essay.

### TENET-3 — Continuity is the grain, not the garnish
Layout, states, springs, and data all derive from the same constraints, so a view
doesn't switch so much as *become* the next one — and the continuous version of
an interface is often *less* code than the discrete one. The prized, usually
bespoke layer of UX moves into the declarative, analyzable layer.
*Held in:* README ("continuity is the grain, not the garnish"); the "why" essay ("Declare makes continuity the grain, not the garnish").

### TENET-4 — Motion, layout, and modes are all just values
Motion is physics on an attribute — a `Spring` toward where a thing belongs, with
interruption just the target changing. Layout is a reactive slot you can swap,
derive, or animate. A mode is a reversible bundle of overrides that cannot leak,
so modes compose and interrupt cleanly.
*Held in:* declare.md §1, §5, §8.

### TENET-5 — State derives from data and location, not from control flow
Screens follow data state (`shown = { data.loaded }`), not navigation code. There
is no router object: `location` is an attribute wired to the URL fragment, and
state *derives* from it the same way everything else derives — a deep link is
just an initial value.
*Held in:* declare.md §7; FAQ ("There's no router object — location is an attribute, like everything else").

# How you write it

The shape of the language and how programs compose — the promises about the
authoring surface.

### OPERA-1 — Two delimiters carry the whole model
`[ … ]` is the view tree — a component's attributes, children, and declarations,
its bracket nesting *being* the tree. `{ … }` is TypeScript — a value, a handler
body, a script. Those two are the entire mental model.
*Held in:* declare.md §2; getstarted ("Two delimiters carry the whole model").

### OPERA-2 — All real logic is ordinary TypeScript
Everything inside `{ }` is ordinary TypeScript — no new expression language to
learn — type-checked with full knowledge of every component's attributes. What
you (or a model) already know about TypeScript carries over — at full expression
strength; type annotations and declarations live on attributes, not in bodies.
*Held in:* README ("with all real logic in ordinary TypeScript"); FAQ ("There is no new expression language to learn").

### OPERA-3 — No CSS, by design
Styling is part of the language: paint attributes on views, and provided values in
place of the cascade. A value a node provides — a theme record, the text face — is
read below it with `provided(…)`, explicitly, so one theme reskins a whole subtree
from one place and a subtree can extend the theme above it. No cascade, no
specificity, no selectors. CSS *knowledge* transfers — colors, font stacks, shadows
read the same — but there is no stylesheet, which is also what makes a non-DOM
renderer possible.
*Held in:* FAQ ("Can I use CSS to style a Declare app? No — and that's a feature").

### OPERA-4 — Values derive down, information travels up, internals stay private
A component is a class; its attributes are its public interface, and values
*derive down* through constraints. Information travels back *up* through events a
component declares and fires — delivered to the handler that declared interest,
never bubbled through the tree. Inside, code reaches other parts only through
explicit scopes (`this`, `parent`, `classroot`, `app`), so a component's
internals stay its own.
*Held in:* FAQ ("How do encapsulation and composition work"); declare.md.

### OPERA-5 — The library is written in Declare, with no privileged API
The entire standard library is written in Declare itself, in readable source you
can open and live-edit. There is no privileged component API underneath: library
components are the same kind of thing your components are, used identically —
including replication over data.
*Held in:* FAQ ("How are Declare's UI components created?").

### OPERA-6 — Data binds declaratively
Data enters the way everything else does: a `Dataset` or fetched `DataSource`, a
`datapath` cursor whose descendants read relative to it, replication per element
of a bound array, and two-way binding for editable fields. Large collections can declare a
windowed materialization (`virtualize`, opt-in) rather than building everything.
*Held in:* FAQ ("How do I get data into an app?").

# What Declare is

The nature of the thing — the promises about what kind of language it is.

### ROTAS-1 — A language, not a framework
Declare is a domain-specific language for user interfaces — the way SQL is a DSL
for queries — not a library inside JavaScript. There is no framework runtime to
orchestrate, no lifecycle to manage.
*Held in:* homepage hero; FAQ ("It's a language, not a framework inside JavaScript").

### ROTAS-2 — The UI is a standing structure, not a re-run function
An interface is a standing tree that values flow through when things change —
never a function the platform re-runs and diffs. There is no re-render, no
virtual-DOM pass, no reconciliation.
*Held in:* declare.md §1 ("A binding is a relationship, not a callback … standing expressions the runtime keeps true"); FAQ ("the UI is a *standing structure* … nothing re-renders because nothing was ever a render").

### ROTAS-3 — One program, any renderer
One source tree renders to managed DOM or directly to pixels on a canvas — and
runs headlessly, no screen at all — with the same layout and input handling. The
language owns its semantics; no DOM assumptions leak into a program. The DOM and
canvas renderers are held equal, verified pixel-for-pixel, and the native Mac host is held
to both by a conformance suite. (The Mac host is a renderer, first-class and complete for
what it does; it is not yet a way to deliver an offline desktop application, which needs
integration the host does not have.)
*Held in:* FAQ ("renderer-independence"); the guide's Renderers chapter.

### ROTAS-4 — One tree, one language
Structure, style, and behavior are one tree in one language — not the HTML/CSS/JS
trinity. There is no separate stylesheet, template, and script to keep in sync.
*Held in:* FAQ ("There is also no HTML/CSS/JS trinity — structure, style, and behavior are one tree in one language").

### ROTAS-5 — Compiled, everywhere
Declare is a compiled language, and the compiler runs anywhere the program does —
in Node and in the browser, the same compiler with byte-identical output.
*Held in:* FAQ ("The compiler itself runs anywhere — in Node, or in the browser"); declare.md §1.

### ROTAS-6 — A successor that kept the convictions
Declare is a from-the-ground-up successor to OpenLaszlo (2002): it keeps the
declarative tree, constraint-based reactivity, and a real compiler, and rebuilds
everything else — keyword-free syntax, TypeScript for logic, DOM and canvas
renderers, in-browser compilation — for the modern, LLM era.
*Held in:* FAQ ("Where does Declare come from?").

forms.gist: Inside rich-text content, a **self-closing tag whose name is a view class the program declares** is one real view of that class, placed in the flowing line as an atomic box the words wrap around.

forms.gist: Sets an attribute the class already has.

forms.gist: Declares a new reactive attribute — the way state enters a program.

forms.gist: A child is a member that is itself an instance.

forms.gist: A method is a typed signature, name first, and a statement body.

forms.gist: A handler is a method named `on` + an event this node fires — `onClick`, `onPointerMove`, `onInit`, `onKeyDown` — and it is a method in every respect: a subclass's `onInit` replaces its base's, and reaches it with `super.onInit()` when it wants the base's to run.

forms.name: super.name(…)
forms.gist: A method a subclass declares replaces the base's method of the same name, handlers included.
The return-type marker in a signature, and the arrow of a function type.
Braces hold TypeScript, and as an attribute's value the expression is a **constraint** — re-evaluated when, and only when, something it reads changes, and kept true from then on.

forms.name: :path
forms.gist: A colon-prefixed path reads from bound data, relative to the nearest enclosing `datapath`.

forms.name: key

Two-way binding, opt-in and for leaf editors only.

forms.name: gradient(…) · stroke(…) · shadow(…) · frost(…)
forms.gist: The value constructors build the composite values decoration attributes take: a gradient, a stroke, a shadow, a frosted backdrop, a gradient `stop`.

forms.name: 12 · 50% · center · navy · #336699 · "text" · true
forms.gist: The bare-value vocabulary the compiler owns: numbers, percents, the position literals `center` and `end`, colors by name or hex, strings, booleans, `null`, and the enum tokens each attribute names.

forms.name: provided("name")
forms.gist: The one explicit **up-the-tree read**: `provided("name")` is the value the nearest ancestor makes available under that name — bare in `[ ]` like `gradient(…)`, or a call in `{ }`.

forms.name: this · parent · classroot · app
forms.gist: A bare name resolves outward through the enclosing brackets, innermost first — the brackets are the scope exactly as they are the tree — and the compiler rewrites the read to an explicit path at compile time.

forms.name: include
forms.gist: Merges another file's **top-level declarations** — its classes, scripts, styles, themes, schemas — into this program, once, however many times it is named.

forms.name: use
forms.gist: Keeps classes the production build would otherwise drop.

forms.name: ship
forms.gist: States what a **self-contained package** of this program must carry beyond what its source names.

forms.name: defaultFlags
forms.gist: The program's own defaults for the platform's flags, the same ones a request names in its URL (`?render=canvas`) and `declarec` takes (`--render=canvas`), with the same values.

forms.name: script
forms.gist: A top-level block of plain TypeScript, wholly outside the reactive system: pure functions of their arguments (date arithmetic, formatting, parsing), stateful helpers, whole libraries.

forms.name: font
forms.gist: A typeface is an **object in the tree**, not a top-level declaration: a `Font` with `FontFace` children, usually on the App, or a `Font [ family = "…" ]` with no faces for a system font.

forms.name: style
forms.gist: A named **record of text attributes** — the style of a run of text that has no view of its own.

forms.name: theme
forms.gist: A theme is a **named record of tokens** — colours, sizes, decorations — declared at the top level like a class or a schema.

forms.name: schema
forms.gist: A named data shape, declared at the top level like a class, and a **type** in the one type system: use the name in any type position — a declared attribute, a parameter, a return, a field of another schema — and declare a dataset's document with it.

app.name: App [ … ]
app.lead:
A program is one tree, and `App [ … ]` is its root — one per program. With `width` and
`height` unset it fills its host, which is the common case: the page, the window, the
island it is mounted in. Everything else nests inside its brackets, and `app` (lower case)
names the running instance from any depth — which makes it the place for the few values
the whole app shares, such as the current selection or a mode.

Any instance may declare its own members, the App included — attributes, methods,
handlers, children — with no class at all; the compiler synthesizes an anonymous subclass.
The top-level forms (`class`, `include`, `use`, `script`, `style`, `theme`, `schema`,
`ship`, `defaultFlags`) may come before or after it, in any order. Records belong in a `Dataset`, and state
that is a thing in its own right in a model class (a class with no `extends`) — the App is
not meant to hold every value.

example.name: form-app
example.title: The one root
example.lead: `App [ … ]` fills its host when its size is unset. It may declare members of its own — a fact here, read by a text below through `app`, the instance's name from any depth.
example.source:
App [ fill = 0xF6F8FA, textColor = 0x172530, fontSize = 14,
    visits: number = 0,
    onClick() { visits = visits + 1 },
    Text [ x = 20, y = 20, text = { "the app is " + app.width + " × " + app.height + " — click anywhere" } ],
    deep: View [ x = 20, y = 50,
        Text [ text = { "clicks reach the root's fact: " + app.visits } ]
        ]
    ]

instance.name: Type [ … ]
instance.lead:
Square brackets hold a node's members — attributes, declarations, methods, handlers,
children — and the nesting of brackets *is* the tree. Naming a type with a bracketed body
instantiates it: `Text [ text = "OK" ]` is a Text, `bg: View [ … ]` a View reachable as `bg`.
Every member inside is one of the five shapes (set, declare, child, method, handler),
separated by commas.

An instance is a full node in its own right: it may declare new attributes and methods
without a class, because the compiler synthesizes an anonymous subclass for it. Name a
`class` when you instantiate it more than once or need to name its type — or when a long
instance declaration makes its parent hard to read, so pulling it out (possibly into its
own file) keeps the program's structure visible.

example.name: form-instance
example.title: Brackets are the tree
example.lead: Each `[ ]` is an instance; nesting them nests views. A named child is reachable by its name; an anonymous one is placed and painted. The instance in the middle declares a member of its own with no class in sight.
example.source:
App [ fill = 0xF6F8FA, textColor = 0x172530, fontSize = 14,
    card: View [ x = 20, y = 20, width = 300, height = 110, cornerRadius = 10, fill = 0xFFFFFF,
        stroke = stroke(1, 0xDCE3E9),
        taps: number = 0,                      // declared on the instance, no class
        onClick() { taps = taps + 1 },
        title: Text [ x = 16, y = 14, fontWeight = semibold, text = "A card" ],
        Text [ x = 16, y = 40, textColor = 0x6A7883, text = { "anonymous child, reading the card: " + parent.taps } ],
        Text [ x = 16, y = 66, textColor = 0x6A7883, text = { "the title is " + parent.title.text.length + " characters" } ]
        ]
    ]

class.name: class
syntax: class Name extends Base [ members ]       // any other base
class.syntaxText:
class Name [ members ]                    // a view
class Name extends Base [ members ]       // any other base
class.lead:
This is the one way to define a class. Everything inside the
brackets is a **member**: `name = value` sets an attribute the base already has,
`name: Type = value` declares a new one, `name: Type [ … ]` is a named child, `name() { … }`
a method, `onThing() { … }` a handler for an event the node fires. Instantiate the class by
naming it with a `[ ]` body, as many times as you like; each instance may set any attribute
and add members of its own.

A class is not a file and not a module. It is a top-level declaration, and a program is one
tree of them — `include` merges another file's classes into the same program, and there is
nothing to export. Any instance may declare members with no class at all, because the
compiler synthesizes an anonymous subclass. Name a class when you instantiate it more than
once or need to name its type, or when pulling a long instance out keeps its parent readable.

With no `extends`, the base is `View`: a class that draws. A class with no view names its
base: `extends Node`, or `extends Dataset` for a document.

extends.name: extends
extends.lead:
Single inheritance from another class — a library class or one of your own. The
subclass sees every attribute, child, method, and event of the base. Re-stating an
attribute with `name = value` **overrides** its default; re-stating a method replaces it;
and a base's named child is reached by name, not redeclared. Omit `extends` altogether and
the base is `Node` — a model class with no box.

`extends` is not a top-level form in its own right: it is part of a `class` declaration.
The base may be declared later in the file, or in an included one. Any concrete built-in is
a base — `View`, `Node`, `Layout` and `TweenLayout`, `Dataset`, `Spring`, `Keys`, `State` and
the rest — as is any class descending from one; only the abstract bases (`Stream`, `Media`,
`Editor`) are refused.

inlineview.name: <Class/>
syntax: <Chip key='a' label='docs'/>                 // key: this view's identity across a content change
inlineview.syntaxText:
HTMLText [ html = "Filed under <Chip label='docs'/> today." ]
Markdown [ text = "Fixed by <Issue id='142'/>." ]
<Chip key='a' label='docs'/>                 // key: this view's identity across a content change
inlineview.lead:
Inside rich-text content, a **self-closing tag whose name is a view class the program
declares** is one real view of that class, placed in the flowing line as an atomic box the
words wrap around. There is no whitelist to extend and no attribute to set: the class
existing is what makes the tag mean it, matched by the name exactly as written, in both
formats (`HTMLText`'s `html` and `Markdown`'s `text`). A tag naming no class of yours keeps
the meaning it already had — the HTML whitelist, an autolink, a literal `<` — and a
`<span class>` stays a style, never a view.

The tag's attributes are the class's, each converted from its string by the attribute's
**declared** type, exactly as a source literal is: `id='142'` is the number in a `number`
attribute, `tint='#DDF4E4'` a `Color`, `align='center'` an enum member, `width='50%'` a percent of
the width the text flows in, a bare `open` is `true`. The tag **is the use site**, so an
attribute takes use-site precedence over what the class body sets for that attribute — a literal
or a `{ }` constraint — and only the winner installs; an attribute the tag does not mention keeps
the class's own behaviour. `x`/`y` are refused — the flow places the view, as a layout places
its children — and an unknown attribute, a value that will not convert, a read-only attribute, or
a percent on an attribute with no axis goes to the class's `unsupported` policy. The view owns
its `width`/`height` while the flow owns its `x`/`y`, it never splits
across a line, a taller one grows its line, a size change re-flows the text, and it reads the
surrounding run's text face as provided values. Content is reactive: a tag still present keeps
its view and its state, with only changed attributes rewritten (a tag that gains or loses an
attribute is built again, since what it claims is settled at build), and `key='…'` fixes that
identity when the order moves. Markup carries no expressions, so a live value is either
concatenated into the content (with `escapeHtml` around every interpolated value) or derived
inside the class from an identity the content names.

set.name: name = value
set.lead:
Sets an attribute the class already has. The right-hand side is one of three things,
and the spelling says which: a **bare literal** (a number, a percent, a color, a string, a
keyword — set once), a **`{ }` constraint** (TypeScript that stays true), or a **`:path`**
read from bound data. A bare `[ … ]` list fills an array-typed attribute.

One family of names may be set on a node that does not declare them: the built-in
**provided values** — the text face (`fontSize`, `fontFamily`, `fontWeight`, `textColor`,
`letterSpacing`), `theme`, `iconSize`, and the rich-text attributes. Setting one on a container
*provides* it to every descendant that reads it (see `provided`).

A set attribute with a `{ }` is **owned by its constraint**: the runtime keeps it current, and a direct
write to it is refused with a message naming the fix — derived state is never assigned;
change its inputs. In a handler, `name = value` is the setter: the write lands when the
handler returns, together with every other write it made, in one settle.

declare.name: name: Type = value
syntax: name: Type                                 // no default: undefined until written
panel: Menu? = null                         // a class — the attribute holds an instance
declare.syntaxText:
name: Type = value
name: Type                                 // no default: undefined until written
rows: Row[] = []
panel: Menu? = null                         // a class — the attribute holds an instance
declare.lead:
Declares a new reactive attribute — the way state enters a program. The type is a
TypeScript type, the same vocabulary a signature uses: TypeScript's built-ins (`number`,
`string`, `Map<string, Row>`), Declare's own (`Color`, `Length`, `Radius`), a class, a
declared schema, a literal union (`"open" | "closed"`), an array, a tuple, or a function
type. The default is a bare literal or a `{ }` expression.

A declaration's `{ }` default is only a **formula**: reading it inlines the
expression, and an assignment simply replaces it — the right tool for a value you may take
over later, which is how `TextInput.initial` differs from its read-only `text = { … }` twin.
Compare `set`: a set attribute is owned by its `{ }` and refuses assignment.

child.lead:
A child is a member that is itself an instance. Named, it is reachable from its siblings and
its class as `name`; anonymous, it is placed and painted but never addressed. Children paint
in declaration order — later siblings on top; there is no z-index — and a parent with a
`layout:` member arranges them, while one without positions them by their own `x`/`y`.

A child is also how anything that is not a view joins the tree: a `Dataset`, a `Spring`, a
`Keys` or `Focus` service, a stream. A source of events is a child, so it lives and dies with
the node that declares it; there is nothing to subscribe to and nothing to unregister.

name() { statements }

method.lead:
A method is a typed signature, name first, and a statement body. Every parameter carries a
written type — a primitive, a class, an event payload, a function type
(`f: (id: string) -> void`), or an array of one; a `?` after the type says the value may be
absent, and the body must check. Omit `-> R` for a method that returns nothing.

A method runs when called; an attribute stays true. A computed *value* is therefore not a
method but a declaration with a `{ }` default. A constraint that calls a method stays live
through it: every read inside the method is a wired dependency, rebased onto what you passed
— which is the difference between a method and a `script { }` function, whose body the
compiler never reads.

rules.rule: Parameters are typed; a bare name has no type.
rules.says: parameter 'a' has no type — a signature is typed name-first: 'f(a: number)'

rules.rule: An attribute's value is one expression; statements live in methods.
rules.says: an attribute value is one expression, not statements; move the logic into a method and call it (e.g. { classroot.compute() })

example.name: form-method
example.title: A typed method, and a constraint that calls it
example.lead: `price()` is a method with typed parameters and a return type. The total is a constraint that calls it — and stays live through it, because the compiler reads the method's body.

handler.name: onEvent(e: Payload) { … }
handler.lead:
A handler is a method named `on` + an event this node fires — `onClick`, `onPointerMove`,
`onInit`, `onKeyDown` — and it is a method in every respect: a subclass's `onInit` replaces
its base's, and reaches it with `super.onInit()` when it wants the base's to run. The payload, when there is one, is typed by the event, and the
compiler names the type when you write the wrong one. Handlers only assign attributes; every
constraint that reads those attributes follows, which is the whole update model. The `on`
prefix is a convention: a method so named that answers no event of its node is an ordinary
method, and the compiler warns, naming the handler when the name is one slip from it.

Nothing bubbles. A handler runs on the node that declares it, for events that node fires;
a parent that wants a child's click declares the handler on the child (or the child calls
up through `parent` or `classroot`). Events from outside the tree come through a member you
declare — a `Keys [ onKeyUp(e: KeyEvent) { … } ]` gives a node app-wide keyboard handling.

A handler is a method named `on` + an event this node fires — `onClick`, `onPointerMove`,
`onInit`, `onKeyDown` — and it is a method in every respect: a subclass's `onInit` replaces
its base's, and reaches it with `super.onInit()` when it wants the base's to run. The payload, when there is one, is typed by the event, and the
compiler names the type when you write the wrong one. Handlers only assign attributes; every
constraint that reads those attributes follows, which is the whole update model. The `on`
prefix is a convention: a method so named that answers no event of its node is an ordinary
method, and the compiler warns, naming the handler when the name is one slip from it.

Nothing bubbles. A handler runs on the node that declares it, for events that node fires;
a parent that wants a child's click declares the handler on the child (or the child calls
up through `parent` or `classroot`). Events from outside the tree come through a member you
declare — a `Keys [ onKeyUp(e: KeyEvent) { … } ]` gives a node app-wide keyboard handling.

handler.gist: A handler is a method named `on` + an event this node fires — `onClick`, `onPointerMove`, `onInit`, `onKeyDown` — and it is a method in every respect: a subclass's `onInit` replaces its base's, and reaches it with `super.onInit()` when it wants the base's to run.

rules.says: 'onMouseDown' is 'onPointerDown' here

example.name: form-handler
example.title: Handlers only assign
example.lead: `onPointerMove` gets a typed payload; the handler writes two facts, and the texts that read them follow. Nothing bubbles: the pad's handler sees only the pad's moves.
example.source:
App [ fill = 0xF6F8FA, textColor = 0x172530, fontSize = 14,
    px: number = 0,
    py: number = 0,
    inside: boolean = false,
    pad: View [ x = 20, y = 20, width = 220, height = 120, cornerRadius = 8, fill = 0xE9EFF4,
        onPointerMove(e: PointerEvent) { app.px = e.x; app.py = e.y },
        onPointerOver() { app.inside = true },
        onPointerOut() { app.inside = false }
        ],
    Text [ x = 256, y = 24, text = { app.inside ? "pointer at " + Math.round(app.px) + ", " + Math.round(app.py) : "move over the pad" } ],

super.name: super.name(…)
super.syntaxText:
name(v: T) { super.name(v) }
fetch() { log = log + "fetching"; super.fetch() }
super.lead:
A method a subclass declares replaces the base's method of the same name, handlers included.
`super.name(args)` calls the one it replaced: the nearest method of that name beneath the
body in the `extends` chain. It is an ordinary call, so the body decides where it goes —
before its own work, after it, in the middle, conditionally, or not at all — and passes
whatever arguments it likes. Inside the base's method, `this` is still the instance, so the
base's own calls reach the subclass's overrides, as in any class language. A built-in's own
runtime methods are replaced and reached the same way: `class Fetcher extends DataSource [
fetch() { …; super.fetch() } ]` wraps the DataSource's fetch rather than rewriting it, and the
runtime's own calls to `fetch()` land on the override.

A use site that overrides a class's method (`Stepper [ input(v: number) { … } ]`) reaches the
class's with `super` the same way. A constraint that calls a method stays live through
`super` too: the base body's reads are wired like the override's.

example.name: form-super
example.title: A subclass reaches its base's method
example.lead: `Counter.bump()` adds one. `Capped` replaces it and decides for itself whether the base runs: below the cap it calls `super.bump()`, at the cap it never does. Nothing else about the method changes — `super` is an ordinary call, placed wherever the body wants it.

syntax: f: (id: string) -> void                   // a function type, in a parameter or a declaration
arrow.syntaxText:
name(a: T) -> R { … }
f: (id: string) -> void                   // a function type, in a parameter or a declaration
arrow.lead:
The return-type marker in a signature, and the arrow of a function type. `quant(v: number)
-> number { … }` returns a number; omit it for a method that returns nothing. In a type
position, `(a: T) -> R` is a function type — a parameter that takes a callback, or a
declared attribute holding one.

It is not a lambda arrow and not a binding operator: inside a `{ }` body or a `script`
block, `=>` is ordinary TypeScript. The language's other arrow, `<->`, is the two-way
binding operator on a text field's value.

rules.rule: Parameters in a function type are typed like a method's.
rules.says: parameter 'a' has no type — a signature is typed name-first: 'f(a: number)'

example.name: form-arrow
example.title: Two arrows in a signature
example.lead: `-> string` is a method's return type; `(n: number) -> string` is a function type, here the type of a parameter. A handler passes a formatter to `render`, which applies it — ordinary TypeScript in a handler, where a callback is just a value.

constraint.lead:
Braces hold TypeScript, and as an attribute's value the expression is a **constraint** —
re-evaluated when, and only when, something it reads changes, and kept true from then on. `width = {
parent.width - 40 }` stays true through every resize; nothing subscribes, diffs, or
re-renders. Dependencies are extracted statically by the compiler, which reads *through* the
methods you call — a script function is the one opaque call.

Inside the braces you are in plain TypeScript at full expression strength: ternaries,
template literals, array chains, closures, casts. The bare-value vocabulary stops at the
brace — a color is `0x4169E1`, not `navy`; a size is computed from the parent, not written
as a percent. A `:path` may appear inside a body, which is how anything conditional over
replicated data is written.

rules.says: there are no percentages: read the parent and scale, so 100% is { parent.width * 1 }

rules.rule: No `#hex` in braces: a color in TypeScript is a number.
rules.says: inside { } a color is written 0x336699, not #336699 (the #… and named-color forms work only as bare values)

rules.rule: No named colors in braces either; the message gives the number.
rules.says: 'navy' is a named color — the name form works only as a bare value; inside { } write it as 0x000080.

rules.rule: A body is one expression; statements belong in a method.
rules.says: an attribute value is one expression, not statements; move the logic into a method and call it (e.g. { classroot.compute() })

rules.rule: An attribute may not derive from itself — that is a cycle by construction; derive from a base.
rules.says: 'width' reads itself — a { } cannot depend on the attribute it defines; name the base it derives from instead

rules.rule: A bare name must resolve: a member up the enclosing brackets, a parameter, or one of the few globals a body may use.
rules.says: cannot resolve 'nothingHere' — not a member of t: Text → App, a parameter, or one of the globals a body may use (Math, JSON, Date, URL, console, …)

rules.says: 'n' is mutable state in a script { } block — nothing can notice a module variable change; hold the value in a reactive attribute (declare it on the app) and read that instead

example.title: A relationship that stays true

example.lead: The first total calls a method: the compiler reads through it, so the total follows `rate` too. The second calls a script function with the same inputs: it depends only on what it is passed. Change the rate and watch which one moves.

datapath.name: :path
syntax: text = :title                              // a read, relative to the nearest datapath
View [ datapath = :rows[], … ]             // [] replicates: one instance per record
text = { :on ? :title : "—" }              // a read inside a body
input(v: boolean) { :done = v }            // a write, in a handler or method
Text [ datapath = :tags[], text = :@ ]     // :@ — the record itself
text = { "" + :@[(classroot.field)] }      // [( … )] — a key computed by TypeScript
datapath.syntaxText:
text = :title                              // a read, relative to the nearest datapath
View [ datapath = :rows[], … ]             // [] replicates: one instance per record
text = { :on ? :title : "—" }              // a read inside a body
input(v: boolean) { :done = v }            // a write, in a handler or method
Text [ datapath = :tags[], text = :@ ]     // :@ — the record itself
text = { "" + :@[(classroot.field)] }      // [( … )] — a key computed by TypeScript
datapath.lead:
A colon-prefixed path reads from bound data, relative to the nearest enclosing `datapath`.
`datapath` selects a place in a dataset; descendants read fields relative to it; and a path
ending in `[]` **replicates** its node — one instance per record, reconciled by the record's
`id`. This is what replaces `items.map(…)`: a collection of children comes from data, never
from code in the tree.

Between the root and the `[]`, a path may select in the JSONPath subset — `[0]`, `[-1]`,
`[1:4]`, `[*]`, `['quoted key']`. A `:path` in a value is a read. In a handler or method,
`:field = v` (and `+=`, `++`) writes that field of the record the node is attached to,
through the dataset's `set` — a field, a nested field or a non-negative index; a slice,
wildcard or `[]` is refused, and so is an assignment inside a `{ }` value. A text field's
`<->` is the other write, with a draft and validation.

`:@` is the record itself — JSONPath's current node — for a record that is a plain value
(a string in a list of tags) or to hand a whole record to a method. `[( expr )]` is a key
computed by TypeScript, anywhere in a path: `:@[(field)]` reads the field `field` names,
`:rows[(i)].title` the title of the record `i` indexes, and both follow the expression as
well as the data. Plain `[ ]` stays JSONPath; the parentheses mark the computed form, which
needs braces — `text = { :@[(k)] }`. Both are written like any path: `:@[(k)] = v`, and
`:@ = r` replaces the record. Without a schema a path is dynamic: an unresolved read yields
`null` and the bound attribute falls back to its default; with one, every path is checked at
compile time.

example.name: form-datapath
example.title: One instance per record
example.lead: `datapath = :rows[]` replicates the row view per record; inside it, `:name` and `:score` read the record's fields. Add a record and a row appears — the tree follows the data.

example.name: form-datapath-select
example.title: Selecting along the path
example.lead: A path may select before it replicates: `[0]` the first, `[-1]` the last, `[1:3]` a range. Each instance is cursored at its real index, so `:name` still reads its own record.

App [ fill = 0xF6F8FA, textColor = 0x172530, fontSize = 14,
    d: Dataset { { "rows": [ { "name": "one" }, { "name": "two" }, { "name": "three" }, { "name": "four" } ] } },
    col: View [ x = 20, y = 16, width = 320, datapath = { d.value },
        layout: SimpleLayout [ axis = y, spacing = 8 ],
        Text [ text = { "first: " + :rows[0].name + " · last: " + :rows[-1].name } ],
        Text [ fontSize = 12, textColor = 0x6A7883, text = ":rows[1:3][] replicates the middle two:" ],
        View [ datapath = :rows[1:3][], height = 22, width = 320,
            Text [ x = 12, text = { "— " + :name } ]
            ]
        ]
    ]

key.name: key
key.lead:
Replication reuses an instance across sorts, filters and edits when it can tell which
record is which. By convention that is the record's `id` field, with nothing declared.
When a collection's identity lives under another name, `key = :field` on the replicated
node names it — a single `:path`, read per record. It is replication metadata, so it is
legal only beside a many-path `datapath`.

example.name: form-key
example.title: Identity by name
example.lead: Reconciliation reuses an instance across sorts, filters and edits when it can tell which record is which. That is the record's `id` by convention; when identity lives under another name, `key = :field` on the replicated node says which. Re-sort and watch the rows keep their tint: the instances survived, only their order moved.

App [ fill = 0xF6F8FA, textColor = 0x172530, fontSize = 14,
    d: Dataset { { "people": [ { "email": "ada@x.io", "name": "Ada" },
                               { "email": "grace@x.io", "name": "Grace" },

        layout: SimpleLayout [ axis = y, spacing = 8 ],

            tint: number = { 0xDCE8DC + Math.floor(Math.random() * 0x2000) },   // set once per INSTANCE
            fill = { tint },
            Text [ x = 10, y = 6, text = { :name + "  ·  " + :email } ]

    ]

syntax: TextInput [ text <-> { fieldName } ]       // a { } yielding a field name
twoway.syntaxText:
TextInput [ text <-> :title ]
TextInput [ text <-> { fieldName } ]       // a { } yielding a field name
twoway.lead:
Two-way binding, opt-in and for leaf editors only. The left side is an editor's value;
the right names a **place in data** — a `:path`, or a `{ }` yielding a field name — resolved
against the nearest enclosing `datapath`. Edits in the field write back through the cursor,
and a change in the data shows in the field. It is the only arrow in the language that
writes.

Deliberately narrow: to drive an ordinary attribute from a control, use the value pattern —
derive down with `text = { app.note }`, deliver up with `input(v: string) { app.note = v }` —
so data flow stays traceable. One-way `:path` everywhere else.

constructors.name: gradient(…) · stroke(…) · shadow(…) · frost(…)
syntax: fill = gradient(#F8F8F8, #D8D8D8)          // bare: colors in the bare vocabulary
stroke = stroke(1, #B0B0B0)                // drawn inside the box
stroke = [ stroke(1, #B0B0B0), null, stroke(1, #B0B0B0), null ]   // per side, top first
shadow = shadow(0, 4, 12, #00000033)       // dx, dy, blur, color
constructors.syntaxText:
fill = gradient(#F8F8F8, #D8D8D8)          // bare: colors in the bare vocabulary
fill = { gradient("180deg", 0xF8F8F8, 0xD8D8D8) }
stroke = stroke(1, #B0B0B0)                // drawn inside the box
stroke = [ stroke(1, #B0B0B0), null, stroke(1, #B0B0B0), null ]   // per side, top first
shadow = shadow(0, 4, 12, #00000033)       // dx, dy, blur, color
backdrop = frost(26, 1.5)                  // blur, saturate
constructors.lead:
The value constructors build the composite values decoration attributes take: a gradient, a
stroke, a shadow, a frosted backdrop, a gradient `stop`. They are the only call forms a bare
value admits, and each has one shape — the message names it when the call is wrong. Inside
a `{ }` the same names are ordinary functions, with colors written as numbers.

Their names are reserved: no member may be called `gradient`, `stroke`, `shadow`, `stop`,
or `frost`. A stroke is drawn **inside** the box, so it never enlarges the layout; a shadow
is cast outside it, escaping any clip, as a CSS box-shadow does. A `stroke` attribute also takes
**four** of them — `[top, right, bottom, left]`, clockwise from the top, `null` for a bare
side — which is the one-or-four shape `cornerRadius` and `padding` share. All three take
either form from a `{ }` constraint as readily as from a literal, which is how a border in a
theme token is written: `stroke = { [ stroke(1, provided("theme").line), null,
stroke(1, provided("theme").line), null ] }` rules a row top and bottom.

theme token is written: `stroke = { [ stroke(1, provided("theme").line), null,
stroke(1, provided("theme").line), null ] }` rules a row top and bottom.

literals.lead:
The bare-value vocabulary the compiler owns: numbers, percents, the position literals
`center` and `end`, colors by name or hex, strings, booleans, `null`, and the enum tokens
each attribute names. A bare literal is the value itself, set once. Inside `{ }` none of this
exists — there you are in TypeScript, where a color is `0x336699` and a size is arithmetic
on the parent.

A `"…"` string ends at its line; long text is a `"""` block. An 8-digit `0x` literal is an
alpha color, never a number — which is why `#RRGGBBAA` and `0xRRGGBBAA` mean the same thing
and a Length refuses it.

scope.name: this · parent · classroot · app
syntax: this.width                                 // the node the code is written on
classroot.label                            // the instance of the class being defined
scope.syntaxText:
this.width                                 // the node the code is written on
parent.width                               // its parent
classroot.label                            // the instance of the class being defined
app.theme                                  // the running application
scope.lead:
A bare name resolves outward through the enclosing brackets, innermost first — the brackets
are the scope exactly as they are the tree — and the compiler rewrites the read to an
explicit path at compile time. Four reserved words say it explicitly: **`this`**, the node
the code is written on; **`parent`**; **`classroot`**, the instance of the class being
defined, from any depth inside it; and **`app`**, the running application, from anywhere.

Built-ins never resolve outward: every view carries `width`, so a bare `width` is always
*this* node's. `classroot` is legal only inside a `class` body. Two structural members every
View carries, `root` (what `app` compiles to) and `children`, are reserved as well — a child
or attribute named `root` would shadow every `app.…` in the same class.

include.name: include
include.lead:
Merges another file's **top-level declarations** — its classes, scripts, styles, themes,
schemas — into this program, once, however many times it is named. It is not a
module system: there are no exports, no namespacing, and no root instance comes across.
Everything merges into one program, and a class in an included file may extend one declared
here.

The path resolves relative to the including file. The standard library needs no include —
its classes are auto-included by name — but a library file may be included explicitly,
as the library's own files include each other.

use.name: use
use.lead:
Keeps classes the production build would otherwise drop. The build tree-shakes anything
no tag instantiates; a class your code constructs **by name** at runtime —
`app.createView("Badge")`, an icon named by a string in a control's `iconLeft` — is mentioned
nowhere in the tree, so it would be removed. `use` says it is still needed.

The symptom without it is a class that works in dev, where everything is present, and
is missing from the built app. A menu's `kind` or `icon` record field, an `IconHost`'s
`kind`, and every `createView` call are the places to look.

ship.name: ship
ship.syntaxText:
ship [ islands = ["name", "../../other/other"] ]
ship [ files = ["../../docs/model.json", "app.declare"] ]
ship [ compiler = true, inspector = true ]
ship.lead:
States what a **self-contained package** of this program must carry beyond what its source
names. A production build (`declarec`) reads the block; the dev server and the static site,
which carry every source and a compiler, read none of it. Each member is a fact about the
program, never a build option:

- `islands` — the programs an `AppIsland` may mount when its `program` is *computed*
  (`program = { app.current }`), spelled as `program` spells them. Each is compiled ahead and
  shipped beside the app with everything it would carry alone — its data, its own islands,
  its own `ship` block — once, however many hosts name it. A literal `program = "name"`
  needs no entry.
- `files` — what the program reads that no literal names, or that lives outside its folder:
  a docs model two levels up, its own source for a viewer. Each is copied into the package and
  served from there; the program's paths are untouched. A `.declare` source ships with its
  highlighted reader form too, so a viewer in the package reads it as on the site. A literal `url = "data.json"` beside
  the program needs no entry.
- `compiler = true` — the program compiles source at run time (live editing, programs typed
  in). The package carries the compiler and the library's source; otherwise it carries
  neither, and an island naming an unbuilt program is a reported error.
- `inspector = true` — the program answers questions about itself in production: the
  Inspector (compiled ahead), the `__declare` bridge, source positions, and error prose all
  ship. It does not imply the compiler.

The block may appear before or after the root, and an included class may carry its own —
a help panel that reads the docs model says so where it lives — and the program's merged
block is the union.

defaultFlags.name: defaultFlags
defaultFlags.syntaxText:
defaultFlags [ render = canvas ]
defaultFlags [ kernel = js, crawler = true ]
defaultFlags.lead:
The program's own defaults for the platform's flags, the same ones a request names in its
URL (`?render=canvas`) and `declarec` takes (`--render=canvas`), with the same values. A flag the request
or the command names wins; one it leaves out, the program's block decides; one neither names
takes the platform's default.

- `render` — `dom` or `canvas`: the renderer a browser runs the program on. A program whose
  screen is all drawing, redrawn every frame — a game — can run smoother as one canvas.
- `kernel` — `wasm` or `js`: the reactive kernel a production build carries.
- `crawler` — `true` or `false`: whether a production build, or a run page on the dev server,
  embeds the program's crawled content for readers that don't run it.
- `accessibility` — `true` or `false`: whether the program carries its accessibility layer —
  what screen readers are given, the accessibility warnings, reduced motion. A game drawn
  every frame, with nothing a screen reader could use, sets it false and pays nothing for it.

The block is read before the program runs, so it says nothing about how the program behaves,
and the program runs the same whichever values a host uses. A program running as another's
`AppIsland` takes the outer program's renderer and kernel, and the Mac host runs its own.

A program has at most one block. It may sit in any of the program's files, before or after
the root.
