script.name: script
syntax: script [ "file.ts" ]                       // the same, from a file
script.syntaxText:
script { … }                               // inline TypeScript
script [ "file.ts" ]                       // the same, from a file
script.lead:
A top-level block of plain TypeScript, wholly outside the reactive system: pure
functions of their arguments (date arithmetic, formatting, parsing), stateful helpers,
whole libraries. A program may hold any number of blocks,
inline and files mixed; they share one scope in source order. A file is written
module-style (`export` allowed); an inline block refuses `export`, since its top-level names
are already visible to every `{ }`. A block may `import` ES modules — a relative file, or an
npm package by bare specifier — bundled at compile by a Node host (the dev server, `declarec`,
`verify`); the in-browser compile refuses imports by name.

A constraint may call into script, **opaquely**: it depends on the values it passes, never on
what the function does inside. So pass values, not nodes, and hold state that changes in an
attribute — nothing notices a script `let` change. This is where arithmetic, formatting, and imported
JavaScript live, so the tree stays about the tree.

What does **not** belong here is anything the program's look or model depends on. A
color, a font list or a size used in more than one place is a theme token read with
`provided("theme")`, a `style`, or an attribute — a script constant cannot be themed,
switched for dark mode, or read by `explain`. A derivation over the app's data — an
order's total, a running balance — is a **method** on the node that holds the data. The compiler
reads through a method, so its dependencies are known and `explain` can show them; it
cannot see inside a script function, and its results arrive untyped.

example.name: form-script
example.title: Plain TypeScript, outside the tree
example.lead: A script block holds a constant and two functions; every `{ }` may call them. A constraint that calls `fmt` depends on what it passes — the amount — never on what `fmt` does inside.

font.name: font
syntax: brand: Font [ FontFace [ src = "brand-400.woff2" ], FontFace [ src = "brand-700.woff2", weight = bold ] ]
font.lead:
A typeface is an **object in the tree**, not a top-level declaration: a `Font` with `FontFace`
children, usually on the App, or a `Font [ family = "…" ]` with no faces for a system font.
A family attribute holds it — `fontFamily = { app.brand }`, or a list in a `{ }`,
`{ [app.brand, "sans-serif"] }` — so switching fonts is an assignment. `loaded` and
`failed` are the font's facts; `wait` and `late` say what loading is worth. A FontFace's
`weight` is a keyword, a number 1–1000, or `range(lo, hi)` for a variable font file. See
the `Font` and `FontFace` classes.

example.name: form-font
example.title: A typeface is an object in the tree
example.lead: `serif: Font [ … ]` and `mono: Font [ … ]` live on the App; a family attribute takes one in a { }, alone or first in a fallback list. `fontFamily` is provided, so the App's choice reaches every Text below until one overrides it — and a raw family string is still allowed.

syntax: HTMLText [ html = "class" ] // a run wears the bundle by name

style.lead:
A named **record of text attributes** — the style of a run of text that has no view of its
own. `<span class='Keyword'>` inside `HTMLText` or `Markdown` wears it, and a drawing's
`d.fillText` / `d.strokeText` and `measureText` take it. Its name is a value in any `{ }`,
typed by the fields it sets (`Keyword.textColor`).

Like a theme record, a bundle holds **literal values only**: it has no place in the tree, so
nothing in it can depend on where it is used. A look that should follow something — the
theme, dark mode — is written where it is used: a `textStyles = { … }` map on the rich text,
or a spread in a drawing, `{ ...Keyword, textColor: provided("theme").accent }`. Top-level
declared names are capitalized by convention.

For whole views there is no bundle: reuse a look by **subclassing** (`class Tile [ … ]`,
or `class Tile extends Card [ … ]`), and provide values downward with `theme` and the face attributes.

theme.name: theme
syntax: theme Brand [ accent = #CC3333, surface = #FFF7F5 ]     // a named token record
App [ theme = Brand ]                                    // PROVIDE it — a plain set, no keyword
fill = { provided("theme").surface }                     // READ a token anywhere below

theme.syntaxText:
theme Brand [ accent = #CC3333, surface = #FFF7F5 ]     // a named token record
App [ theme = Brand ]                                    // PROVIDE it — a plain set, no keyword
fill = { provided("theme").surface }                     // READ a token anywhere below

theme.lead:
A theme is a **named record of tokens** — colours, sizes, decorations — declared at the top
level like a class or a schema. Token names are free; values are plain literals, value
constructors, or lists of them. The library ships presets in scope by name (`SanFrancisco`, `Cupertino`,
`MountainView`, `Redmond`, each with a `…Dark` companion), and `theme Brand [ … ]` declares
your own.

Providing and reading are the two halves of **provided values**. `theme = Brand` on the App
provides the record to the whole tree — a plain set, no keyword. `provided("theme").accent`
reads a token from the nearest provider; the standard library reads it *for* you (a `Button`
styles off `provided("theme")` inside `Control`), so an app that only sets `theme` never
writes the read. Because `theme` is an ordinary reactive value, dark mode is one expression
— `theme = { app.dark ? BrandDark : Brand }` — and a subtree re-skins partially by providing
a spread copy lower down. The library reads specific token names, so build a theme from a
preset rather than an empty record.

provided.name: provided("name")
syntax: provided("name")                           // the nearest ancestor's value under name
provided("name", default)                  // … or the default when no ancestor provides one
density: number = 2                        // PROVIDE: declare a typed value on an ancestor
fontSize = 13                              // a built-in provided name is set bare on any container
provided.syntaxText:
provided("name")                           // the nearest ancestor's value under name
provided("name", default)                  // … or the default when no ancestor provides one
density: number = 2                        // PROVIDE: declare a typed value on an ancestor
fontSize = 13                              // a built-in provided name is set bare on any container
provided.lead:
The one explicit **up-the-tree read**: `provided("name")` is the value the nearest ancestor
makes available under that name — bare in `[ ]` like `gradient(…)`, or a call in `{ }`.
*Providing* is just holding a value: declare a typed attribute on an ancestor
(`density: number = 2`) and every descendant may read it; the built-in provided names —
the text face, `theme`, `iconSize`, the rich-text attributes — need no declaration at all, so
`fontSize = 13` on a container provides it to every `Text` beneath. A value set locally
always outranks a provided one.

It is explicit on purpose: the read reaches past this node, and a non-local dependency is
worth showing. You rarely write it — `Text` and the library widgets read the face and theme
values for you; you write it where your own code wants a value from above. A read that
finds no provider falls to its default, else fails at boot naming the value.

syntax: schema Task [ id: string, done: boolean, status: "open" | "closed", note?: string ]
d: DataSource [ url = "tasks.json", schema = [ tasks[]: Task ] ]
sel: Task? = null                           // the name in any type position
schema.syntaxText:
schema Task [ id: string, done: boolean, status: "open" | "closed", note?: string ]
d: DataSource [ url = "tasks.json", schema = [ tasks[]: Task ] ]

schema.lead:
A named data shape, declared at the top level like a class, and a **type** in the one type
system: use the name in any type position — a declared attribute, a parameter, a return, a
field of another schema — and declare a dataset's document with it. The dataset's `.value`
is then typed, so a misspelled field dies at compile time; the runtime enforces the same
declaration at every boundary — arrival, the literal body, and the mutation verbs — so
malformed data yields `.failed` rather than `undefined` three steps downstream.

Field markers: `[]` for an array, `?` for optional. Field types are `string`, `number`,
`boolean`, `any`, a literal union of strings or numbers, another schema's name, or a nested
`[ … ]`. Extra keys always pass — a schema declares what the program relies on, not
everything the document carries.

docSegs.md: Every form the grammar accepts — 29 of them, in 5 groups. Each is a page: its syntax, what it is, live usage, the rules the compiler enforces in the checker's own words, and what it relates to. `declare.md` is the same language in one file, in order; these are its forms one at a time, for the reader who arrived with a keyword.

types.name: AccessibilityLive
types.gist: How a change to a live view is announced.

types.name: AccessibilityRole
types.gist: What a view is to assistive technology — the closed vocabulary every platform's accessibility API shares, so a program is written for none of them in particular.

types.name: AccessibilitySort
types.gist: Which way the column a `columnHeader` heads is sorted, as a screen reader says it with the header's name: `none` (not the sorted column), `ascending` or `descending`.

types.name: Axis
types.gist: Which way an arrangement runs.

types.name: Backface
types.gist: What a view shows once a rotation turns it more than 90° about X or Y.

types.name: Blend
types.gist: The W3C blend modes, in camelCase, naming how a view lands against what has already painted beneath it.

types.name: Claim
types.gist: The axis a declared drag takes for itself.

types.name: Credentials
types.gist: Whether a request carries cookies, TLS client certificates and authentication headers.

types.name: CrossAlign
types.gist: Where a laid child sits across the flow — `y` on a row, `x` on a stack.

types.name: Direction
types.gist: The direction a view's text runs in, and what it holds: `ltr`, `rtl`, or `auto` (from the first strong letter of the text); `inherit`, the default, takes the nearest ancestor's.

types.name: Edges
types.gist: How an app meets the device's **own** chrome — a notch, a home-indicator bar.

types.name: EditorJudgeOn
types.gist: When a field first says what is wrong with its draft (`Editor.judgeOn`): `edit` at every edit, `leave` once the field has been left — or `judge()` asked — and at every edit after.

types.name: FitAlign
types.gist: Which end of the box an aspect-preserving fit keeps, one axis at a time.

types.name: FocusScope
types.gist: What Tab does at a view's edge.

types.name: FontLate
types.gist: What a face that finishes loading **after** the text is already painted does to text already on screen.

types.name: FontWeight
types.gist: The named weights, and a **number from 1 to 1000 is the same attribute** — the keywords are the names of the hundreds.

types.name: Justify
types.gist: How a finished row sits along the direction of flow.

types.name: Motion
types.gist: The shape of an interpolation over its duration: which fraction of the travel has been covered at each fraction of the time.

types.name: Numerals
types.gist: The **shape** of the digits in a face that carries more than one set.

types.name: NumeralWidth
types.gist: The **advance** of the digits, which is a different question from their shape.

types.name: OutsidePress
types.gist: What a press aimed past an open overlay does: `dismiss` (the overlay closes; the press goes no further — a menu), `dismissAndDeliver` (it closes; the press goes on — a popover), `block` (the press goes nowhere; the overlay stays — a dialog), `ignore` (the press goes on as if the overlay were not there — a toast).

types.name: Process
types.gist: Whether the members of an `AnimatorGroup` run one after another or all at once.

types.name: Purpose
types.gist: What a text field holds — an email address, a password, a card number, a line of an address — said once on `TextInput.purpose`, so the platform can help: autofill and password managers recognise the field, a phone brings up the keyboard that suits it, and a password is hidden.

types.name: Scaling
types.gist: How a view's images and drawings look when they are shown larger or smaller.

types.name: ScrollAnchor
types.gist: What a scroller keeps still while its content changes size.

types.name: ScrollBelow
types.gist: What a scroll aimed past an open overlay does: `block` (nothing behind it scrolls — a menu, a dialog), `allow` (it goes on — a popover, a toast), `dismiss` (the overlay closes and the scroll goes on — a tooltip).

types.name: Scrolls
types.gist: Which axes of interior overflow a view scrolls.

types.name: StreamStatus
types.gist: A live connection's lifecycle as one read-only fact, the same shape a `DataSource`'s `loaded` / `loading` / `failed` facts has for a fetch.

types.name: Stretch
types.gist: How a bitmap fills a box whose size differs from its natural size.

types.name: TextAlign
types.gist: Horizontal alignment of wrapped lines inside the run's own width.

types.name: TextTransform
types.gist: Reshapes the painted glyphs **without changing `text`**: selection, find-in-page and `$data` all see the original string, exactly as CSS `text-transform` behaves.

types.name: Tick
types.gist: How often a `Time` fires, from the display's own rate up to a calendar boundary.

types.name: Color
types.gist: A color as `0xRRGGBB`, or with alpha as the runtime's own encoding (see `colorWithAlpha`).

types.name: Fill
types.gist: What a fill slot holds: a flat color, or a gradient.

types.name: Gradient
types.gist: A gradient value, as `gradient`, `radialGradient` and `conicGradient` build it.

types.name: Length
types.gist: What a geometry slot takes: a number in the view's own units, or a percent of the parent on that axis.

types.name: Percent
types.gist: A percentage literal — what `width = 50%` becomes.

types.name: Radius
types.gist: A corner rounding: one number for all four corners, or `[topLeft, topRight, bottomRight, bottomLeft]` to round only some.

types.name: Inset
types.gist: A room-inside: one number insets all four sides, or `[top, right, bottom, left]` to inset only some.

types.name: Shape
types.gist: A clip path, as the `clip` slot takes it: an SVG path string in the view's own coordinates, or `null` for the plain rectangle.

types.name: Stroke
types.gist: A border, built by `stroke(width, color)`.

types.name: BoxStroke
types.gist: What the `stroke` slot holds: ONE Stroke on all four sides, or four — `[top, right, bottom, left]`, clockwise from the top, `null` for a bare side.

types.name: Outline
types.gist: A stroke around the edges of the GLYPHS, built by `outline(width, color)` — the value `Text.outline` takes.

types.name: Shadow
types.gist: A drop shadow, built by `shadow(dx, dy, blur, color)`.

types.name: Filter
types.gist: One entry in a filter list: a blur, one of the amount filters, a hue rotation, a colorize, or a shadow.

types.name: Backdrop
types.gist: What lies BENEATH a view, filtered: the same list `filter` takes, applied to the backdrop instead of the view's own paint.

types.name: Theme
types.gist: A token record — every color and metric an app names once.

types.name: MotionCurve
types.gist: An easing curve, built by `cubicBezier`, `back`, `steps` or `laszlo` — what an `Animator`'s `motion` takes, alongside the named tokens.

types.name: Cursor
types.gist: The data a `:path` reads against — a view's place in the bound data, its `datapath` plus its position under replication.

types.name: TextMeasure
types.gist: What measureText reports — a Text's own fact names.

types.name: IslandPost
types.gist: One message across the island boundary — what `post` sends and `onPost` receives between an embedded app and its host.

types.name: IslandNavigation
types.gist: A navigation the embedded app asked for — what an island's `onNavigate` receives: `to`, the address made absolute; `program`, the Declare program it names ("" when none); `location`, the place after its `#`; `newWindow`, whether it asked for a window of its own (`openWindow`).

types.name: DelayHandle
types.gist: What `afterDelay(ms, fn)` returns: `cancel()` drops the wait if it has not run.

types.name: TextStyle
types.gist: The style of one run of text that has no view — a `style` bundle, or an inline record with the same fields.

types.name: TextStyles
types.gist: The palette a `<span class>` names: style name → that style's fields.

types.name: BlockGeometry
types.gist: One block type's geometry in a rich-text flow: a measure to cap its width at (0 = the full track), a `[left, right]` margin, and how it sits in what is left.

types.name: RichTextLayout
types.gist: Per-BLOCK-TYPE geometry for a rich-text flow: block name → that block's `BlockGeometry`.

types.name: PointerEvent
types.gist: A pointer's position, in both frames.

types.name: PointerUpEvent
types.gist: A release, plus the one fact a drag handler must not miss: `canceled` is true when the browser reclaimed the gesture — a touch that became a scroll.

types.name: TouchEvent
types.gist: The multi-finger stream: every finger down (`touches`) and the ones this event moved (`changed`).

types.name: Touch
types.gist: One finger in a multi-finger gesture: a stable id for its lifetime, and a point.

types.name: WheelEvent
types.gist: A wheel or trackpad scroll, by axis: how far is `deltaX` and `deltaY` (from PointerEvent), in pixels.

types.name: PinchEvent
types.gist: A resolved two-finger zoom: the accumulated `scale` (1 at `onPinchStart`) and the point between the fingers it pivots about.

types.name: KeyEvent
types.gist: A key, both ways: `code` is the physical key regardless of layout (what a shortcut wants), `key` is the character it produced (what typing wants).

types.name: FocusGeometry
types.gist: Where the focus indicator should be, and where it came from — the rect and radius to draw, the view and root it belongs to, the scroller it sits in, and the `home…` fields it is travelling from.

types.name: TooltipEvent
types.gist: A tooltip's request: the text, and the rect of the view asking, so a custom tip can place itself against the thing it describes.

types.name: StreamMessage
types.gist: One message from an `EventStream` or `Socket`: its payload, its type, and its id.

types.name: ChangeEvent
types.gist: What `onChange` receives: every value this node named in `trackChanges` that ended the settle different, in list order, once per settle.

types.name: ValueChange
types.gist: One value that ended a settle different from where it started — its name, and what it was and is.

types.name: FilesOver
types.gist: Files dragged over a view: how many (0 when the browser does not say), and where, in the view's own coordinates.

types.name: FilesDrop
types.gist: Files dropped on a view: the files — a dropped folder's, every file in it, each with its path — and where, in the view's own coordinates.

types.name: File
types.gist: A file the person chose (`Files.pick`) or dropped (`onFilesDrop`): its name, size in bytes, MIME type, when it last changed (ms since 1970), its path within a chosen or dropped folder ("" for a file on its own), and a `url` that reads it — an `Image`'s `source`, a `DataSource`'s `url` — or, in a `DataSource` body, uploads it.

types.name: PickOptions
types.gist: What `Files.pick` offers: the types (MIME types or extensions), more than one file, or a whole folder.

types.name: Draw
types.gist: The canvas drawing context a `draw(d: Draw)` body receives — a Canvas2D- shaped recorder whose operations every renderer replays (runtime/src/draw.ts).

types.name: DrawGradient
types.gist: A gradient built INSIDE a drawing, by `d.createLinearGradient` and its kin — the Canvas2D shape, stops added by call.

types.name: DrawImageSource
types.gist: What `d.drawImage` accepts: any `Image` view, by its loading facts.

types.name: TraceSettle
types.gist: One settle, as the wake trace recorded it: its number; when it opened (`at`, ms since the trace started) and how long it ran (`ms`); the user code that ran before it (`origin`); how many rules the kernel ran (`runs`); the writes that opened it (`triggers`) and what it changed in response (`changes`); and `unnamed`, cells that moved but belong to no addressable attribute.

types.name: TraceChange
types.gist: One attribute the wake trace saw change: the view it lives on (`path`) and the attribute, its value before and after, and — for a change the settle made — the rule that wrote it (`by`; null for a plain write).

types.name: Headers
types.gist: A response's headers — `get(name)`.

types.name: AbortSignal
types.gist: The cancellation handle an `AbortController` issues.

types.name: AbortController
types.gist: Cancel an in-flight `fetch` — pass `.signal`, call `.abort()`.

types.name: RequestInit
types.gist: The options `fetch` takes — `method`, `headers`, `body`, `signal`.

types.name: Response
types.gist: What `fetch` resolves to — `ok`, `status`, `json()`, `text()`.

types.name: Blob
types.gist: A binary body.

types.name: FormData
types.gist: A multipart body.

types.name: URLSearchParams
types.gist: A query string as a map — `get`, `set`, `append`, `toString()`.

types.name: URL
types.gist: Parse or build a URL — `new URL(path, base)`, then `.searchParams`, `.pathname`, `.href`.

AccessibilityLive.name: AccessibilityLive
AccessibilityLive.doc:
How a change to a live view is announced. `off`: it is not. `polite`: at the next pause, without
interrupting. `assertive`: at once, interrupting what is being read — for what cannot wait.
AccessibilityLive.gist: How a change to a live view is announced.

AccessibilityRole.name: AccessibilityRole
AccessibilityRole.doc:
What a view is to assistive technology — the closed vocabulary every platform's accessibility
API shares, so a program is written for none of them in particular. Each word is a contract: it
names the facts the role reads and the methods its actions call, and the compiler holds a class
that declares it to them. `none` is transparent — the view is read as part of its parent.
AccessibilityRole.gist: What a view is to assistive technology — the closed vocabulary every platform's accessibility API shares, so a program is written for none of them in particular.

AccessibilitySort.name: AccessibilitySort
AccessibilitySort.doc:
Which way the column a `columnHeader` heads is sorted, as a screen reader says it with the
header's name: `none` (not the sorted column), `ascending` or `descending`.
AccessibilitySort.gist: Which way the column a `columnHeader` heads is sorted, as a screen reader says it with the header's name: `none` (not the sorted column), `ascending` or `descending`.

Axis.name: Axis
Axis.doc:
Which way an arrangement runs. It is a **bare token, not a string** — `axis = x`
names the axis, and the `x` here is unrelated to the position attribute of the same
name. Every stacking layout takes one, and `y` is the house default, so a column is
what you get by naming no axis at all.

Backface.name: Backface
Backface.doc:
What a view shows once a rotation turns it more than 90° about X or Y. `hidden`
takes the turned-away face out of the picture **and out of hit-testing**, so a
pointer passes through to whatever is behind it; `visible` keeps painting the
mirrored face.
Backface.gist: What a view shows once a rotation turns it more than 90° about X or Y.

Blend.name: Blend
Blend.doc:
The W3C blend modes, in camelCase, naming how a view lands against what has
already painted beneath it. The operator is not a filter on the view: it reaches
down to the nearest **isolating** ancestor, so what a `multiply` chip blends with
depends on where the isolation is, not on how deeply it is nested. `normal` is no
blending at all, and the value every view has until one is named.
Blend.gist: The W3C blend modes, in camelCase, naming how a view lands against what has already painted beneath it.

Claim.name: Claim
Claim.doc:
The axis a declared drag takes for itself. `both` (the default) gives the drag the
whole gesture; `x` or `y` leaves the other axis to the enclosing scroller, so a
horizontal column-drag and a vertical page scroll can share one finger. It
**scopes** a drag that already exists and never creates one — a view with no
pointer handler ignores it.
Claim.gist: The axis a declared drag takes for itself.

Credentials.name: Credentials
Credentials.doc:
Whether a request carries cookies, TLS client certificates and authentication
headers. These are the Fetch API's three modes as tokens, so `sameOrigin` is the
camelCase spelling of the wire's `same-origin`. `include` is the only one that
reaches another origin, and it works **only** when that origin's CORS response
names your origin back — a wildcard `*` cannot combine with it.
Credentials.gist: Whether a request carries cookies, TLS client certificates and authentication headers.

CrossAlign.name: CrossAlign
CrossAlign.doc:
Where a laid child sits across the flow — `y` on a row, `x` on a stack. `none`
leaves the cross placement to the child, which is what lets an ordinary
`y = center` keep working; `start | center | end` place every child for you. Pick
`baseline` only where each child can report one: a `Text` does by itself, and a
composite must **declare** which of its parts carries it.
CrossAlign.gist: Where a laid child sits across the flow — `y` on a row, `x` on a stack.

Direction.name: Direction
Direction.doc:
The direction a view's text runs in, and what it holds: `ltr`, `rtl`, or `auto` (from the
first strong letter of the text); `inherit`, the default, takes the nearest ancestor's.
A right-to-left paragraph is laid out from the right — its lines start there unless its
`textAlign` says otherwise — and a field types from the right.
Direction.gist: The direction a view's text runs in, and what it holds: `ltr`, `rtl`, or `auto` (from the first strong letter of the text); `inherit`, the default, takes the nearest ancestor's.

Edges.name: Edges
Edges.doc:
How an app meets the device's **own** chrome — a notch, a home-indicator bar.
`safe` keeps the app inside the safe region and every `safe*` inset then reads 0,
because there is nothing left to handle. `cover` is the edge-to-edge opt-in: the
box extends under the system chrome and the insets carry real numbers, which is
what pinned chrome needs to place itself.
Edges.gist: How an app meets the device's **own** chrome — a notch, a home-indicator bar.

EditorJudgeOn.name: EditorJudgeOn
EditorJudgeOn.doc:
When a field first says what is wrong with its draft (`Editor.judgeOn`): `edit` at every
edit, `leave` once the field has been left — or `judge()` asked — and at every edit after.
EditorJudgeOn.gist: When a field first says what is wrong with its draft (`Editor.judgeOn`): `edit` at every edit, `leave` once the field has been left — or `judge()` asked — and at every edit after.

FitAlign.name: FitAlign
FitAlign.doc:
Which end of the box an aspect-preserving fit keeps, one axis at a time. It is
read only by `contain` (which letterboxes on one axis) and `cover` (which crops on
one) — under a distorting stretch there is nothing left over to align, and the
value is ignored.
FitAlign.gist: Which end of the box an aspect-preserving fit keeps, one axis at a time.

FocusScope.name: FocusScope
FocusScope.doc:
What Tab does at a view's edge. `none`: its stops are its parent's. `stop`: it is one Tab stop
and the arrows move inside (a radio group, a list). `capture`: Tab walks in and through its
stops (an entry form). `region`: one stop from outside, a cycle of its own inside, left with
F6 (a window, a pane). `modal`: Tab wraps inside and never leaves (a dialog).
FocusScope.gist: What Tab does at a view's edge.

FontLate.name: FontLate
FontLate.doc:
What a face that finishes loading **after** the text is already painted does to
text already on screen. `swap` changes to the real face — one redraw, and the
usual answer. `keep` leaves the fallback in place for the rest of the run, which
is how a reflow mid-read is avoided; a face kept this way reports `loaded = false`
for the life of the run.
FontLate.gist: What a face that finishes loading **after** the text is already painted does to text already on screen.

FontWeight.name: FontWeight
FontWeight.doc:
The named weights, and a **number from 1 to 1000 is the same attribute** — the
keywords are the names of the hundreds. That is what puts a variable font's weight
axis in reach at any point between the names — `fontWeight = 480` is as legal as
`fontWeight = regular`, and there is no second attribute to learn for it.
FontWeight.gist: The named weights, and a **number from 1 to 1000 is the same attribute** — the keywords are the names of the hundreds.

Justify.name: Justify
Justify.doc:
How a finished row sits along the direction of flow. `start`, `center` and `end`
move the row; `fill` does not — it spreads the row's slack into the gaps between
its children, so every full row ends flush. As in justified text, the **last row
stays at `start`** under `fill`, and a row holding one child has no gap to widen.
Justify.gist: How a finished row sits along the direction of flow.

Motion.name: Motion
Motion.doc:
The shape of an interpolation over its duration: which fraction of the travel has
been covered at each fraction of the time. Read a token as a family plus a
direction — `In` bends at the start, `Out` at the end, `Both` at each end with the
fastest part in the middle.

The polynomial families bend progressively harder in this order: `sine`, `quad`,
`cubic`, `quart`, `quint`, `expo`, `circ` — so `quadOut` is a gentle settle and
`expoOut` a sharp one. `easeIn`, `easeOut` and `easeBoth` are the `quad` family
under an older set of names, and `ease` on its own is the CSS default curve, not a
member of any family. `back` overshoots the target and comes back, which reads as
weight. `laszlo` is the one curve that reads how far the animator is actually
travelling, so its bend adapts to the distance rather than being fixed by the
token. `linear` is no easing at all.
Motion.gist: The shape of an interpolation over its duration: which fraction of the travel has been covered at each fraction of the time.

Numerals.name: Numerals
Numerals.doc:
The **shape** of the digits in a face that carries more than one set. `normal` is
whatever the face does by itself, and faces differ on that, so it is worth naming
the one you want rather than relying on the default. A face with a single set
ignores the value, silently and correctly.
Numerals.gist: The **shape** of the digits in a face that carries more than one set.

NumeralWidth.name: NumeralWidth
NumeralWidth.doc:
The **advance** of the digits, which is a different question from their shape.
`tabular` gives every digit the same width, so a column of figures lines up and a
counter does not jitter as it counts; `proportional` lets each digit take its
natural width and reads better in prose. `normal` defers to the face, and faces
disagree about which of the two that is.
NumeralWidth.gist: The **advance** of the digits, which is a different question from their shape.

OutsidePress.name: OutsidePress
OutsidePress.doc:
What a press aimed past an open overlay does: `dismiss` (the overlay closes; the press goes
no further — a menu), `dismissAndDeliver` (it closes; the press goes on — a popover), `block`
(the press goes nowhere; the overlay stays — a dialog), `ignore` (the press goes on as if the
overlay were not there — a toast). `none` is every ordinary view.
OutsidePress.gist: What a press aimed past an open overlay does: `dismiss` (the overlay closes; the press goes no further — a menu), `dismissAndDeliver` (it closes; the press goes on — a popover), `block` (the press goes nowhere; the overlay stays — a dialog), `ignore` (the press goes on as if the overlay were not there — a toast).

Process.name: Process
Process.doc:
Whether the members of an `AnimatorGroup` run one after another or all at once. It
is the group's own control — nothing else in the language reads it — and it is
what makes a group more than a list of animators started together.
Process.gist: Whether the members of an `AnimatorGroup` run one after another or all at once.

Purpose.name: Purpose
Purpose.doc:
What a text field holds — an email address, a password, a card number, a line of an
address — said once on `TextInput.purpose`, so the platform can help: autofill and
password managers recognise the field, a phone brings up the keyboard that suits it,
and a password is hidden. `text`, the default, says nothing.
Purpose.gist: What a text field holds — an email address, a password, a card number, a line of an address — said once on `TextInput.purpose`, so the platform can help: autofill and password managers recognise the field, a phone brings up the keyboard that suits it, and a password is hidden.

Scaling.name: Scaling
Scaling.doc:
How a view's images and drawings look when they are shown larger or smaller. `smooth`
blends neighbouring pixels, which suits photographs and an ordinary interface under a
zoom. `pixelated` shows every pixel as a solid block, so pixel art stays sharp. A view's
whole subtree follows its setting.
Scaling.gist: How a view's images and drawings look when they are shown larger or smaller.

ScrollAnchor.name: ScrollAnchor
ScrollAnchor.doc:
What a scroller keeps still while its content changes size. `content` keeps the
reader's place: the view at the top edge stays where it is, and a pane at its very
start stays at its start. `end` is for a pane read from the bottom, such as a
terminal or a build's output: at its end it stays at the end as content grows, and away
from the end it keeps the reader's place. `none` leaves the offset alone.
ScrollAnchor.gist: What a scroller keeps still while its content changes size.

ScrollBelow.name: ScrollBelow
ScrollBelow.doc:
What a scroll aimed past an open overlay does: `block` (nothing behind it scrolls — a menu,
a dialog), `allow` (it goes on — a popover, a toast), `dismiss` (the overlay closes and the
scroll goes on — a tooltip). `none` is every ordinary view.
ScrollBelow.gist: What a scroll aimed past an open overlay does: `block` (nothing behind it scrolls — a menu, a dialog), `allow` (it goes on — a popover, a toast), `dismiss` (the overlay closes and the scroll goes on — a tooltip).

Scrolls.name: Scrolls
Scrolls.doc:
Which axes of interior overflow a view scrolls. Overflow along a declared axis
becomes scroll range; overflow along any other axis is simply out of frame,
because a scroller clips to its box either way. The value is a token **string** in
a `{ }` body, so compare it explicitly — `"none"` is truthy, and a bare truth test
says every view scrolls.
Scrolls.gist: Which axes of interior overflow a view scrolls.

StreamStatus.name: StreamStatus
StreamStatus.doc:
A live connection's lifecycle as one read-only fact, the same shape a `DataSource`'s `loaded` / `loading` / `failed` facts
has for a fetch. `retrying` is the one worth planning for: it covers both the
platform's own recovery and a declared retry waiting to re-dial, and it is the
difference between a stream that is coming back and `failed`, which is not.
StreamStatus.gist: A live connection's lifecycle as one read-only fact, the same shape a `DataSource`'s `loaded` / `loading` / `failed` facts has for a fetch.

Stretch.name: Stretch
Stretch.doc:
How a bitmap fills a box whose size differs from its natural size. The axis values
— `width`, `height`, `both` — **distort by design**; the aspect-preserving fits
never do: `contain` puts the whole picture in the box and letterboxes the
remainder, `cover` fills the box and crops the overflow. `none` paints at natural
size. Both fits center the picture until `FitAlign` says otherwise.
Stretch.gist: How a bitmap fills a box whose size differs from its natural size.

TextAlign.name: TextAlign
TextAlign.doc:
Horizontal alignment of wrapped lines inside the run's own width. It only means
anything once the run **has** a width to align within — a `Text` that sizes itself
to its content is already exactly as wide as its longest line, so every value
looks the same.
TextAlign.gist: Horizontal alignment of wrapped lines inside the run's own width.

TextTransform.name: TextTransform
TextTransform.doc:
Reshapes the painted glyphs **without changing `text`**: selection, find-in-page
and `$data` all see the original string, exactly as CSS `text-transform` behaves.
The measurer shapes the transformed glyphs, so an `uppercase` run still wraps
correctly at its real width on every renderer.
TextTransform.gist: Reshapes the painted glyphs **without changing `text`**: selection, find-in-page and `$data` all see the original string, exactly as CSS `text-transform` behaves.

Tick.name: Tick
Tick.doc:
How often a `Time` fires, from the display's own rate up to a calendar boundary.
The calendar tiers aim at the **boundary** — aligned and drift-free, so an
hour-ticking clock changes on the hour rather than an hour after it started —
while `frame` follows the display and is the one to reach for when something is
being animated rather than counted. A number instead of a token is a period in
milliseconds — `tick = 30000` — counted from when the `Time` starts, for a repeating
job that is not about the time of day.
Tick.gist: How often a `Time` fires, from the display's own rate up to a calendar boundary.

Color.name: Color
Color.doc: A color as `0xRRGGBB`, or with alpha as the runtime's own encoding (see `colorWithAlpha`). `null` means NO color — an unfilled view, an unstroked box — which is why it is part of the type rather than a sentinel. In a bare slot the CSS names and `#RRGGBB` are also legal; inside `{ }` a color is a number.
Color.gist: A color as `0xRRGGBB`, or with alpha as the runtime's own encoding (see `colorWithAlpha`).

usedBy.label: conicGradient
usedBy.detail: conicGradient(cx: number, cy: number, angle: number, ...stops: (Color | { offset: number | null; color: Color })[]): Gradient

usedBy.label: gradient
usedBy.detail: gradient(...args: (Color | string | { offset: number | null; color: Color })[]): Gradient

usedBy.label: radialGradient
usedBy.detail: radialGradient(cx: number, cy: number, r: number, ...stops: (Color | { offset: number | null; color: Color })[]): Gradient

usedBy.label: shadow
usedBy.detail: shadow(dx: number, dy: number, blur: number, color: Color): Shadow

usedBy.label: stop
usedBy.detail: stop(offset: number, color: Color): { offset: number; color: Color }

Fill.name: Fill
Fill.doc: What a fill slot holds: a flat color, or a gradient. `null` is no fill at all.
Fill.gist: What a fill slot holds: a flat color, or a gradient.

usedBy.label: Switch.fill
usedBy.detail: = { checked ? provided("theme").accent : hovered || pressed ? provided("theme").controlSelected : ((provided("theme").trackFill ?? provided("theme").control)) }

Gradient.name: Gradient
Gradient.doc: A gradient value, as `gradient`, `radialGradient` and `conicGradient` build it. Any `Fill` slot takes one, and a drawing can too. Write it through a constructor rather than by hand: the shape is published so a program can read one back.
Gradient.gist: A gradient value, as `gradient`, `radialGradient` and `conicGradient` build it.
Gradient.syntax:
interface Gradient {
    kind?: "linear" | "radial" | "conic"
    angle: number
    cx?: number
    cy?: number
    r?: number
    stops: readonly { offset: number | null
    color: Color }[]
}
Gradient.syntaxText:
interface Gradient {
    kind?: "linear" | "radial" | "conic"
    angle: number
    cx?: number
    cy?: number
    r?: number
    stops: readonly { offset: number | null
    color: Color }[]
}

usedBy.label: conicGradient
usedBy.detail: conicGradient(cx: number, cy: number, angle: number, ...stops: (Color | { offset: number | null; color: Color })[]): Gradient

usedBy.label: gradient
usedBy.detail: gradient(...args: (Color | string | { offset: number | null; color: Color })[]): Gradient

usedBy.label: radialGradient
usedBy.detail: radialGradient(cx: number, cy: number, r: number, ...stops: (Color | { offset: number | null; color: Color })[]): Gradient

Length.name: Length
Length.doc: What a geometry slot takes: a number in the view's own units, or a percent of the parent on that axis. There is no unit vocabulary — no px, em or rem — because there is one coordinate space and the renderer owns the device pixels.
Length.gist: What a geometry slot takes: a number in the view's own units, or a percent of the parent on that axis.

usedBy.label: Menu.width
usedBy.detail: = { Math.max(minWidth, widestCustom, textEdge + widestLabel + (widestKey > 0 ? 26 + widestKey + 16 : hasSubs ? 34 : 18)) }

usedBy.label: OverlayStrata.height
usedBy.detail: = { this.parent == app && app.hostHeight > 0 ? Math.min(app.height, app.hostHeight) : (this.parent as View).height }

usedBy.label: OverlayStrata.width
usedBy.detail: = { this.parent == app && app.hostWidth > 0 ? Math.min(app.width, app.hostWidth) : (this.parent as View).width }

usedBy.label: Popover.x
usedBy.detail: = { this.asSheet ? 0 : Math.max(8, Math.min(this.hostW - this.width - 8, this.ab.x + this.ab.w / 2 - this.width / 2)) }

usedBy.label: Popover.y
usedBy.detail:
= { this.asSheet ? this.hostH - this.height * this.openT
: this.below ? this.ab.y + this.ab.h + this.gap : this.ab.y - this.gap - this.height }

usedBy.label: Sheet.height
usedBy.detail: = { this.form == "end" || this.form == "start" ? this.hostH : Math.min(this.body.contentHeight + (this.form == "bottom" ? 20 : 0), this.form == "bottom" ? this.footY - 24 : this.hostH - 48) }

usedBy.label: Sheet.x
Sheet.y
usedBy.detail:
= { this.form == "bottom" ? this.footY - this.height * this.openT + this.dragY
: this.form == "center" ? (this.hostH - this.height) / 2 + 16 * (1 - this.openT) : 0 }

Percent.name: Percent
Percent.doc: A percentage literal — what `width = 50%` becomes. Resolved against the parent on each axis, reactively, so a percent is a live relationship and not a number computed once.

Radius.name: Radius
Radius.doc: A corner rounding: one number for all four corners, or `[topLeft, topRight, bottomRight, bottomLeft]` to round only some.
Radius.gist: A corner rounding: one number for all four corners, or `[topLeft, topRight, bottomRight, bottomLeft]` to round only some.
Radius.syntax: type Radius = number | readonly [number, number, number, number]
Radius.syntaxText: type Radius = number | readonly [number, number, number, number]

Inset.name: Inset
Inset.doc: A room-inside: one number insets all four sides, or `[top, right, bottom, left]` to inset only some. The same literal shape as a `Radius` and a different meaning — a radius rounds corners and counts from the top-LEFT, an inset holds edges away and counts from the TOP.
Inset.gist: A room-inside: one number insets all four sides, or `[top, right, bottom, left]` to inset only some.
Inset.syntax: type Inset = number | readonly [number, number, number, number]
Inset.syntaxText: type Inset = number | readonly [number, number, number, number]

Shape.name: Shape
Shape.doc: A clip path, as the `clip` slot takes it: an SVG path string in the view's own coordinates, or `null` for the plain rectangle. `clip = true` is the box; a shape is for everything else.
Shape.gist: A clip path, as the `clip` slot takes it: an SVG path string in the view's own coordinates, or `null` for the plain rectangle.

Stroke.name: Stroke
Stroke.doc: A border, built by `stroke(width, color)`. It is drawn INSIDE the box, so a stroke never changes a view's size — there is no `borderWidth` to add to a layout.

usedBy.label: TableRow.stroke
usedBy.detail: = { active && (parent as Table).focusVisible ? stroke(1, provided("theme").accent) : null }

BoxStroke.name: BoxStroke
BoxStroke.doc: What the `stroke` slot holds: ONE Stroke on all four sides, or four — `[top, right, bottom, left]`, clockwise from the top, `null` for a bare side. The one-or-four shape is the house pattern for anything said per side (see `Radius`), and the slot reads back what was written, so a body that reaches into a stroke asks which form it has first: `Array.isArray(v.stroke)`, or `v.stroke && "width" in v.stroke`. `null` is no border at all.
BoxStroke.gist: What the `stroke` slot holds: ONE Stroke on all four sides, or four — `[top, right, bottom, left]`, clockwise from the top, `null` for a bare side.
BoxStroke.syntax: type BoxStroke = Stroke | readonly [Stroke | null, Stroke | null, Stroke | null, Stroke | null] | null
BoxStroke.syntaxText: type BoxStroke = Stroke | readonly [Stroke | null, Stroke | null, Stroke | null, Stroke | null] | null

Outline.name: Outline
Outline.doc: A stroke around the edges of the GLYPHS, built by `outline(width, color)` — the value `Text.outline` takes. It rides under the fill, so a filled letter shows a thin ring and an unfilled one reads hollow; it is not a box around the run.
Outline.gist: A stroke around the edges of the GLYPHS, built by `outline(width, color)` — the value `Text.outline` takes.

Shadow.name: Shadow
Shadow.doc: A drop shadow, built by `shadow(dx, dy, blur, color)`. It is also a `Filter`, so it composes in a filter list; on `textShadow` it shadows the glyphs.
Shadow.gist: A drop shadow, built by `shadow(dx, dy, blur, color)`.
Shadow.syntax:
interface Shadow {
    fn: "shadow"
    dx: number
    dy: number
    blur: number
    color: Color
}
Shadow.syntaxText:
interface Shadow {
    fn: "shadow"
    dx: number
    dy: number
    blur: number
    color: Color
}

usedBy.label: shadow
usedBy.detail: shadow(dx: number, dy: number, blur: number, color: Color): Shadow

Filter.name: Filter
Filter.doc: One entry in a filter list: a blur, one of the amount filters, a hue rotation, a colorize, or a shadow. `filter` applies the list to the view's own paint as a GROUP (so a subtree blurs together, not child by child); `backdrop` applies the same list to what lies beneath. There is no CSS `filter` string: the tokens are functions, so a misspelling is a compile error rather than a silent no-op.
Filter.gist: One entry in a filter list: a blur, one of the amount filters, a hue rotation, a colorize, or a shadow.
Filter.syntax: type Filter = { fn: "blur"; radius: number } | { fn: "brightness" | "contrast" | "saturate" | "grayscale" | "invert" | "sepia"; amount: number } | { fn: "hueRotate"; degrees: number } | { fn: "colorize"; color: Color } | Shadow
Filter.syntaxText: type Filter = { fn: "blur"; radius: number } | { fn: "brightness" | "contrast" | "saturate" | "grayscale" | "invert" | "sepia"; amount: number } | { fn: "hueRotate"; degrees: number } | { fn: "colorize"; color: Color } | Shadow

Backdrop.name: Backdrop
Backdrop.doc: What lies BENEATH a view, filtered: the same list `filter` takes, applied to the backdrop instead of the view's own paint. `frost` is the common one.
Backdrop.gist: What lies BENEATH a view, filtered: the same list `filter` takes, applied to the backdrop instead of the view's own paint.

Theme.name: Theme
Theme.doc: A token record — every color and metric an app names once. Provided down the tree (`provided("theme")`), spread to override a token, and declared at the top level with `theme Name [ … ]`. Its keys are open by design: a record whose keys the program chooses cannot be closed without firing on correct code. A read of `provided("theme")` is closed all the same, over every token some theme declares, so a misspelled token is a compile error.
Theme.gist: A token record — every color and metric an app names once.

MotionCurve.name: MotionCurve
MotionCurve.doc: An easing curve, built by `cubicBezier`, `back`, `steps` or `laszlo` — what an `Animator`'s `motion` takes, alongside the named tokens. Opaque by design: a curve is a value you pass, not a shape you inspect.
MotionCurve.gist: An easing curve, built by `cubicBezier`, `back`, `steps` or `laszlo` — what an `Animator`'s `motion` takes, alongside the named tokens.

Cursor.name: Cursor
Cursor.doc: The data a `:path` reads against — a view's place in the bound data, its `datapath` plus its position under replication. You rarely name the type: a `:path` reads through it for you.
Cursor.gist: The data a `:path` reads against — a view's place in the bound data, its `datapath` plus its position under replication.

TextMeasure.doc: What measureText reports — a Text's own fact names.
TextMeasure.gist: What measureText reports — a Text's own fact names.

    readonly height: number
    readonly baseline: number
    readonly capHeight: number
    readonly lines: number

IslandPost.name: IslandPost
IslandPost.doc: One message across the island boundary — what `post` sends and `onPost` receives between an embedded app and its host.
IslandPost.gist: One message across the island boundary — what `post` sends and `onPost` receives between an embedded app and its host.

IslandNavigation.name: IslandNavigation
IslandNavigation.doc: A navigation the embedded app asked for — what an island's `onNavigate` receives: `to`, the address made absolute; `program`, the Declare program it names ("" when none); `location`, the place after its `#`; `newWindow`, whether it asked for a window of its own (`openWindow`).
IslandNavigation.gist: A navigation the embedded app asked for — what an island's `onNavigate` receives: `to`, the address made absolute; `program`, the Declare program it names ("" when none); `location`, the place after its `#`; `newWindow`, whether it asked for a window of its own (`openWindow`).

DelayHandle.name: DelayHandle
DelayHandle.doc: What `afterDelay(ms, fn)` returns: `cancel()` drops the wait if it has not run.
DelayHandle.gist: What `afterDelay(ms, fn)` returns: `cancel()` drops the wait if it has not run.

TextStyle.doc: The style of one run of text that has no view — a `style` bundle, or an inline record with the same fields. Each field is the `Text` attribute of that name; a field left out takes its plain default, never an inherited value.
TextStyle.gist: The style of one run of text that has no view — a `style` bundle, or an inline record with the same fields.

    fontWeight?: FontWeight

TextStyles.name: TextStyles
TextStyles.doc: The palette a `<span class>` names: style name → that style's fields. The KEYS are open — content chooses them — and the VALUES are closed, so a misspelled field is caught in the record form exactly as it is in a `style` bundle. This is the one record slot that can be narrowed without firing on correct code: only the value side has a declared shape.
TextStyles.gist: The palette a `<span class>` names: style name → that style's fields.

BlockGeometry.name: BlockGeometry
BlockGeometry.doc: One block type's geometry in a rich-text flow: a measure to cap its width at (0 = the full track), a `[left, right]` margin, and how it sits in what is left. Every field is optional; what a block does not state it takes from the map's `default` entry, field by field.
BlockGeometry.gist: One block type's geometry in a rich-text flow: a measure to cap its width at (0 = the full track), a `[left, right]` margin, and how it sits in what is left.

RichTextLayout.name: RichTextLayout
RichTextLayout.doc: Per-BLOCK-TYPE geometry for a rich-text flow: block name → that block's `BlockGeometry`. The keys are the block types a document has — `default` for all of them, then `code`, `p`, `h1`, `blockquote` and the rest by name — so a reading measure with full-bleed code is two entries: `richTextLayout = { { default: { maxWidth: 560 }, code: { maxWidth: 0 } } }`. A `pre` with no entry of its own follows `code`. Keys open, values closed: a misspelled field is caught, a block type you invent is not.
RichTextLayout.gist: Per-BLOCK-TYPE geometry for a rich-text flow: block name → that block's `BlockGeometry`.

PointerEvent.name: PointerEvent
PointerEvent.doc: A pointer's position, in both frames. `x`/`y` are in this view's own coordinates (through its whole transform); `rootX`/`rootY` are in root space — the frame a drag reads, since it does not move with the dragged view (and the one `app.viewAt` takes). `deltaX`/`deltaY` are how far the pointer has moved, in root space, since the press (0 with no press; on a wheel, the scroll amount).
PointerEvent.gist: A pointer's position, in both frames.
PointerEvent.syntax:
interface PointerEvent {
    x: number
    y: number
    rootX: number
    rootY: number
    deltaX: number
    deltaY: number
}
PointerEvent.syntaxText:
interface PointerEvent {
    x: number
    y: number
    rootX: number
    rootY: number
    deltaX: number
    deltaY: number
}

PointerUpEvent.name: PointerUpEvent
PointerUpEvent.doc: A release, plus the one fact a drag handler must not miss: `canceled` is true when the browser reclaimed the gesture — a touch that became a scroll. Commit on release only when it is false, or an interruption reads as a drop.
PointerUpEvent.gist: A release, plus the one fact a drag handler must not miss: `canceled` is true when the browser reclaimed the gesture — a touch that became a scroll.

TouchEvent.name: TouchEvent
TouchEvent.doc: The multi-finger stream: every finger down (`touches`) and the ones this event moved (`changed`). Declaring a touch handler claims every finger, so the app then owes its own zoom.
TouchEvent.gist: The multi-finger stream: every finger down (`touches`) and the ones this event moved (`changed`).

Touch.name: Touch
Touch.doc: One finger in a multi-finger gesture: a stable id for its lifetime, and a point. The id is what lets you follow the same finger across moves.
Touch.gist: One finger in a multi-finger gesture: a stable id for its lifetime, and a point.

WheelEvent.name: WheelEvent
WheelEvent.doc: A wheel or trackpad scroll, by axis: how far is `deltaX` and `deltaY` (from PointerEvent), in pixels. A trackpad PINCH arrives here too, with `pinch` true — the browser reports it as a wheel event with a modifier, and hiding that would make a zoom impossible to write.
WheelEvent.gist: A wheel or trackpad scroll, by axis: how far is `deltaX` and `deltaY` (from PointerEvent), in pixels.

PinchEvent.name: PinchEvent
PinchEvent.doc: A resolved two-finger zoom: the accumulated `scale` (1 at `onPinchStart`) and the point between the fingers it pivots about. `center` is that point in ROOT space (the same as `rootX`/`rootY`); `x`/`y` are the same point in this view's own coordinates — what zooming "about the fingers" on this view wants.
PinchEvent.gist: A resolved two-finger zoom: the accumulated `scale` (1 at `onPinchStart`) and the point between the fingers it pivots about.

KeyEvent.name: KeyEvent
KeyEvent.doc: A key, both ways: `code` is the physical key regardless of layout (what a shortcut wants), `key` is the character it produced (what typing wants). Plus the four modifiers and whether the key is repeating.
KeyEvent.gist: A key, both ways: `code` is the physical key regardless of layout (what a shortcut wants), `key` is the character it produced (what typing wants).
KeyEvent.syntax:
interface KeyEvent {
    code: string
    key: string
    shift: boolean
    ctrl: boolean
    alt: boolean
    meta: boolean
    repeat: boolean
}

children.name: 1 SATOR
children.label: Tenet
children.doc:
# How it ships

Delivery, hosting, and the honest posture — the promises about running and
shipping a Declare program.

### SATOR-1 — Programs are data
A compiled program is data the toolchain can read, so one compiler powers the
documentation system, static extraction for crawlers, and live editing alike —
not three separate pipelines.
*Held in:* FAQ ("programs are data — the same compiler powers the documentation system, static extraction for crawlers, and live editing").

### SATOR-2 — What a visitor sees and what a crawler sees can never drift
Static extraction is built into the compiler: it runs the program headlessly to
its settled state and serializes the actual content as semantic HTML — real
headings, paragraphs, links — baked into the page at build time. A crawler (or an
AI reading the web) reads that; a person gets the live app that replaces it at
boot. No server-side rendering, no hydration — it works on a plain static host.
*Held in:* FAQ ("How do Declare-written sites handle crawlers and SEO"); the "why" essay ("what a visitor sees and what a crawler sees can never drift").

### SATOR-3 — In-browser compilation, and no build step to develop
Because the compiler runs in the page, a page can edit and re-run itself: every
sample is live-editable, and view-source culture is restored. Development needs no
build step — the dev server and the browser use the *same* compiler with
byte-identical output.
*Held in:* FAQ ("What benefits does in-browser compilation bring"); getstarted ("no build step").

### SATOR-4 — You don't ship the compiler
For production, `declarec` precompiles everything into a small, self-contained
artifact — a set of static files you can host anywhere, with no trace of the
toolchain and no compiler aboard.
*Held in:* FAQ ("For production you don't ship the compiler").

### SATOR-5 — The program's URL is the app's address
A program is addressed by its own URL: on the dev server, browse to a `.declare`
file's URL and get the running app. The address is the program, not a route
registered elsewhere.
*Held in:* getstarted ("the program URL is the app's address"); FAQ.

### SATOR-6 — Small, and fast where it counts
A full application ships small — the flagship calendar, application *and* runtime,
at roughly 153 KB gzipped (machine-stamped from
the measured artifact): a compact runtime, practical on a phone over a slow network.
Input latency is low — there is no virtual-DOM pass between gesture and pixels — and
animation runs at the display's full rate. The homepage reports the live size figures,
measured from the deployed artifacts and regenerated with them on every publication.
*Held in:* FAQ ("What should I expect in terms of performance").

### SATOR-7 — Honest about the trades and the gaps
The promises come with their limits stated plainly: a framework with no in-browser
compiler wins the very first cold load (the production path closes the gap by
precompiling); Declare is young and the repository *is* the distribution and the
source of truth; an npm package and a dedicated editor extension are named, unhidden
gaps; and the canvas renderer does not yet carry the accessibility the DOM renderer does.
*Held in:* FAQ ("Startup" trade; "How mature is Declare?"; "Is Declare accessible?"; "Is there editor support?").

### SATOR-8 — Open, MIT, entirely public
The complete source — compiler, runtime, standard library, documentation, and the
site itself — is public under the MIT license.
*Held in:* FAQ ("What license is Declare offered under?").

children.name: 2 AREPO
children.label: Tenet
children.doc:
# The wager

Why the language is shaped the way it is: built for the era when much code is
written by machines, and bet on verifiability over familiarity.

### AREPO-1 — Built for machine-written code
When machines write the code, familiarity matters less and *verifiability* matters
more. Declare is designed around that shift, not retrofitted to it.
*Held in:* homepage hero ("a UI language for you and your AI"); FAQ ("Declare is built for the era when much code is written by machines").

### AREPO-2 — The whole language fits in a model's context
The declarative surface is small, closed, and regular — its *entire* definition is
one file (`docs/declare.md`, on the order of 13,000 tokens). No model has
trained on Declare, and none needs to: a model can hold the complete spec while it
writes.
*Held in:* declare.md preamble ("the language, in one file … no LLM has been trained on it"); FAQ; the "why" essay.

### AREPO-3 — Comprehension leverage, not corpus leverage
Declare competes on the kind of leverage a new language *can* have: a language
small enough to hand a model whole, regular enough to be analyzed rather than
pattern-matched, backed by a compiler that turns each mistake into a precise
correction. With less code passing under human eyes, the language and its compiler
are the one reviewer always present.
*Held in:* the "why" essay ("Two kinds of leverage").

### AREPO-4 — Type-checking is mandatory, and trustworthy
Every `{ }` body is type-checked on every compile, with no opt-out, and the
checker is held to **zero false positives** across the repository's own corpus —
every app, component, and doc example it ships. So an error always means something
is genuinely wrong.
*Held in:* FAQ ("Mandatory type-checking … zero false positives").

### AREPO-5 — Diagnostics name the fix
A compiler message is written to steer the *next* attempt — it states the rule and
names the rewrite that fixes it, including "did you mean" guidance for instincts
carried from other frameworks. The primary reader of a diagnostic, now, is a model
deciding what to do next.
*Held in:* FAQ ("Diagnostics that name the fix"); the "why" essay.

### AREPO-6 — No magic
Declare consistently chooses predictability over cleverness: dependencies are
extracted statically, events don't bubble, there is one way to say most things.
Where it looks familiar it behaves as you'd assume; where it is genuinely new it
*looks* new — a cue to consult the spec rather than autocomplete from memory.
*Held in:* FAQ ("No magic"); the "why" essay.

### AREPO-7 — Tested against models, not assumed
The claim that Declare suits LLMs is tested: an evaluation harness gives
model tiers application-building tasks cold, one-shot and iterated, and failures
feed back into the language, the diagnostics, and the docs. The documentation
doubles as training material — every code fence in the teaching docs is
compiled by the test suite, so nothing a model reads is stale or wrong.
*Held in:* FAQ ("What has been done during Declare's development to optimize for LLM usage").

### AREPO-8 — The human owns intent; the toolchain keeps the text honest
The workflow the language is designed around: a person directs and reviews; a
model writes the text; the compiler stays in the loop. The flagship calendar
reports its own number — zero lines written by hand.
*Held in:* FAQ ("The calendar says '0 lines written by hand'").

children.name: 3 TENET
children.label: Tenet
children.doc:
# The standing model

Reactivity and continuity — the central idea the whole language is arranged
around.

### TENET-1 — A binding is a standing relationship the runtime keeps true
Read a reactive value inside a binding and you are subscribed; assign to one and
everything bound to it updates. That is the defining idea, and it holds with no
re-render, no diffing, no dependency array, and no hook — the relationship is
kept true for you, not re-run by you.
*Held in:* declare.md §1.

### TENET-2 — Reactivity is derived by the compiler, not guessed at runtime
The compiler works out what every binding depends on, statically. Behavior is
therefore predictable and analyzable by tools rather than discovered as the
program runs — the model reasons about exactly what the compiler verifies.
*Held in:* FAQ ("reactivity is *derived by the compiler*, not guessed at runtime"); the "why" essay.

### TENET-3 — Continuity is the grain, not the garnish
Layout, states, springs, and data all derive from the same constraints, so a view
doesn't switch so much as *become* the next one — and the continuous version of
an interface is often *less* code than the discrete one. The prized, usually
bespoke layer of UX moves into the declarative, analyzable layer.
*Held in:* README ("continuity is the grain, not the garnish"); the "why" essay ("Declare makes continuity the grain, not the garnish").

### TENET-4 — Motion, layout, and modes are all just values
Motion is physics on an attribute — a `Spring` toward where a thing belongs, with
interruption just the target changing. Layout is a reactive slot you can swap,
derive, or animate. A mode is a reversible bundle of overrides that cannot leak,
so modes compose and interrupt cleanly.
*Held in:* declare.md §1, §5, §8.

### TENET-5 — State derives from data and location, not from control flow
Screens follow data state (`shown = { data.loaded }`), not navigation code. There
is no router object: `location` is an attribute wired to the URL fragment, and
state *derives* from it the same way everything else derives — a deep link is
just an initial value.
*Held in:* declare.md §7; FAQ ("There's no router object — location is an attribute, like everything else").

children.name: 4 OPERA
children.label: Tenet
children.doc:
# How you write it

The shape of the language and how programs compose — the promises about the
authoring surface.

### OPERA-1 — Two delimiters carry the whole model
`[ … ]` is the view tree — a component's attributes, children, and declarations,
its bracket nesting *being* the tree. `{ … }` is TypeScript — a value, a handler
body, a script. Those two are the entire mental model.
*Held in:* declare.md §2; getstarted ("Two delimiters carry the whole model").

### OPERA-2 — All real logic is ordinary TypeScript
Everything inside `{ }` is ordinary TypeScript — no new expression language to
learn — type-checked with full knowledge of every component's attributes. What
you (or a model) already know about TypeScript carries over — at full expression
strength; type annotations and declarations live on attributes, not in bodies.
*Held in:* README ("with all real logic in ordinary TypeScript"); FAQ ("There is no new expression language to learn").

### OPERA-3 — No CSS, by design
Styling is part of the language: paint attributes on views, and provided values in
place of the cascade. A value a node provides — a theme record, the text face — is
read below it with `provided(…)`, explicitly, so one theme reskins a whole subtree
from one place and a subtree can extend the theme above it. No cascade, no
specificity, no selectors. CSS *knowledge* transfers — colors, font stacks, shadows
read the same — but there is no stylesheet, which is also what makes a non-DOM
renderer possible.
*Held in:* FAQ ("Can I use CSS to style a Declare app? No — and that's a feature").

### OPERA-4 — Values derive down, information travels up, internals stay private
A component is a class; its attributes are its public interface, and values
*derive down* through constraints. Information travels back *up* through events a
component declares and fires — delivered to the handler that declared interest,
never bubbled through the tree. Inside, code reaches other parts only through
explicit scopes (`this`, `parent`, `classroot`, `app`), so a component's
internals stay its own.
*Held in:* FAQ ("How do encapsulation and composition work"); declare.md.

### OPERA-5 — The library is written in Declare, with no privileged API
The entire standard library is written in Declare itself, in readable source you
can open and live-edit. There is no privileged component API underneath: library
components are the same kind of thing your components are, used identically —
including replication over data.
*Held in:* FAQ ("How are Declare's UI components created?").

### OPERA-6 — Data binds declaratively
Data enters the way everything else does: a `Dataset` or fetched `DataSource`, a
`datapath` cursor whose descendants read relative to it, replication per element
of a bound array, and two-way binding for editable fields. Large collections can declare a
windowed materialization (`virtualize`, opt-in) rather than building everything.
*Held in:* FAQ ("How do I get data into an app?").

children.name: 5 ROTAS
children.label: Tenet
children.doc:
# What Declare is

The nature of the thing — the promises about what kind of language it is.

### ROTAS-1 — A language, not a framework
Declare is a domain-specific language for user interfaces — the way SQL is a DSL
for queries — not a library inside JavaScript. There is no framework runtime to
orchestrate, no lifecycle to manage.
*Held in:* homepage hero; FAQ ("It's a language, not a framework inside JavaScript").

### ROTAS-2 — The UI is a standing structure, not a re-run function
An interface is a standing tree that values flow through when things change —
never a function the platform re-runs and diffs. There is no re-render, no
virtual-DOM pass, no reconciliation.
*Held in:* declare.md §1 ("A binding is a relationship, not a callback … standing expressions the runtime keeps true"); FAQ ("the UI is a *standing structure* … nothing re-renders because nothing was ever a render").

### ROTAS-3 — One program, any renderer
One source tree renders to managed DOM or directly to pixels on a canvas — and
runs headlessly, no screen at all — with the same layout and input handling. The
language owns its semantics; no DOM assumptions leak into a program. The DOM and
canvas renderers are held equal, verified pixel-for-pixel, and the native Mac host is held
to both by a conformance suite. (The Mac host is a renderer, first-class and complete for
what it does; it is not yet a way to deliver an offline desktop application, which needs
integration the host does not have.)
*Held in:* FAQ ("renderer-independence"); the guide's Renderers chapter.

### ROTAS-4 — One tree, one language
Structure, style, and behavior are one tree in one language — not the HTML/CSS/JS
trinity. There is no separate stylesheet, template, and script to keep in sync.
*Held in:* FAQ ("There is also no HTML/CSS/JS trinity — structure, style, and behavior are one tree in one language").

### ROTAS-5 — Compiled, everywhere
Declare is a compiled language, and the compiler runs anywhere the program does —
in Node and in the browser, the same compiler with byte-identical output.
*Held in:* FAQ ("The compiler itself runs anywhere — in Node, or in the browser"); declare.md §1.

### ROTAS-6 — A successor that kept the convictions
Declare is a from-the-ground-up successor to OpenLaszlo (2002): it keeps the
declarative tree, constraint-based reactivity, and a real compiler, and rebuilds
everything else — keyword-free syntax, TypeScript for logic, DOM and canvas
renderers, in-browser compilation — for the modern, LLM era.
*Held in:* FAQ ("Where does Declare come from?").

children.name: App [ … ]
children.subtitle: Structure
children.label: Language form
children.doc:
# App [ … ]

```declare-fragment
App [ members ]
```

A program is one tree, and `App [ … ]` is its root — one per program. With `width` and
`height` unset it fills its host, which is the common case: the page, the window, the
island it is mounted in. Everything else nests inside its brackets, and `app` (lower case)
names the running instance from any depth — which makes it the place for the few values
the whole app shares, such as the current selection or a mode.

Any instance may declare its own members, the App included — attributes, methods,
handlers, children — with no class at all; the compiler synthesizes an anonymous subclass.
The top-level forms (`class`, `include`, `use`, `script`, `style`, `theme`, `schema`,
`ship`, `defaultFlags`) may come before or after it, in any order. Records belong in a `Dataset`, and state
that is a thing in its own right in a model class (a class with no `extends`) — the App is
not meant to hold every value.

children.name: Type [ … ]
children.subtitle: Structure
children.label: Language form
children.doc:
# Type [ … ]

```declare-fragment
Type [ members ]
name: Type [ members ]
```

Square brackets hold a node's members — attributes, declarations, methods, handlers,
children — and the nesting of brackets *is* the tree. Naming a type with a bracketed body
instantiates it: `Text [ text = "OK" ]` is a Text, `bg: View [ … ]` a View reachable as `bg`.
Every member inside is one of the five shapes (set, declare, child, method, handler),
separated by commas.

An instance is a full node in its own right: it may declare new attributes and methods
without a class, because the compiler synthesizes an anonymous subclass for it. Name a
`class` when you instantiate it more than once or need to name its type — or when a long
instance declaration makes its parent hard to read, so pulling it out (possibly into its
own file) keeps the program's structure visible.

children.name: class
children.subtitle: Structure
children.label: Language form
children.doc:
# class

```declare-fragment
class Name [ members ]                    // a view
class Name extends Base [ members ]       // any other base
```

This is the one way to define a class. Everything inside the
brackets is a **member**: `name = value` sets an attribute the base already has,
`name: Type = value` declares a new one, `name: Type [ … ]` is a named child, `name() { … }`
a method, `onThing() { … }` a handler for an event the node fires. Instantiate the class by
naming it with a `[ ]` body, as many times as you like; each instance may set any attribute
and add members of its own.

A class is not a file and not a module. It is a top-level declaration, and a program is one
tree of them — `include` merges another file's classes into the same program, and there is
nothing to export. Any instance may declare members with no class at all, because the
compiler synthesizes an anonymous subclass. Name a class when you instantiate it more than
once or need to name its type, or when pulling a long instance out keeps its parent readable.

With no `extends`, the base is `View`: a class that draws. A class with no view names its
base: `extends Node`, or `extends Dataset` for a document.

children.name: extends
children.subtitle: Structure
children.label: Language form
children.doc:
# extends

```declare-fragment
class Name extends Base [ … ]
```

Single inheritance from another class — a library class or one of your own. The
subclass sees every attribute, child, method, and event of the base. Re-stating an
attribute with `name = value` **overrides** its default; re-stating a method replaces it;
and a base's named child is reached by name, not redeclared. Omit `extends` altogether and
the base is `Node` — a model class with no box.

`extends` is not a top-level form in its own right: it is part of a `class` declaration.
The base may be declared later in the file, or in an included one. Any concrete built-in is
a base — `View`, `Node`, `Layout` and `TweenLayout`, `Dataset`, `Spring`, `Keys`, `State` and
the rest — as is any class descending from one; only the abstract bases (`Stream`, `Media`,
`Editor`) are refused.

children.name: <Class/>
children.subtitle: Structure
children.label: Language form
children.doc:
# <Class/>

```declare-fragment
HTMLText [ html = "Filed under <Chip label='docs'/> today." ]
Markdown [ text = "Fixed by <Issue id='142'/>." ]
<Chip key='a' label='docs'/>                 // key: this view's identity across a content change
```

Inside rich-text content, a **self-closing tag whose name is a view class the program
declares** is one real view of that class, placed in the flowing line as an atomic box the
words wrap around. There is no whitelist to extend and no attribute to set: the class
existing is what makes the tag mean it, matched by the name exactly as written, in both
formats (`HTMLText`'s `html` and `Markdown`'s `text`). A tag naming no class of yours keeps
the meaning it already had — the HTML whitelist, an autolink, a literal `<` — and a
`<span class>` stays a style, never a view.

The tag's attributes are the class's, each converted from its string by the attribute's
**declared** type, exactly as a source literal is: `id='142'` is the number in a `number`
attribute, `tint='#DDF4E4'` a `Color`, `align='center'` an enum member, `width='50%'` a percent of
the width the text flows in, a bare `open` is `true`. The tag **is the use site**, so an
attribute takes use-site precedence over what the class body sets for that attribute — a literal
or a `{ }` constraint — and only the winner installs; an attribute the tag does not mention keeps
the class's own behaviour. `x`/`y` are refused — the flow places the view, as a layout places
its children — and an unknown attribute, a value that will not convert, a read-only attribute, or
a percent on an attribute with no axis goes to the class's `unsupported` policy. The view owns
its `width`/`height` while the flow owns its `x`/`y`, it never splits
across a line, a taller one grows its line, a size change re-flows the text, and it reads the
surrounding run's text face as provided values. Content is reactive: a tag still present keeps
its view and its state, with only changed attributes rewritten (a tag that gains or loses an
attribute is built again, since what it claims is settled at build), and `key='…'` fixes that
identity when the order moves. Markup carries no expressions, so a live value is either
concatenated into the content (with `escapeHtml` around every interpolated value) or derived
inside the class from an identity the content names.

children.name: name = value
children.subtitle: Members
children.label: Language form
children.doc:
# name = value

```declare-fragment
name = literal
name = { expression }
name = :path
```

Sets an attribute the class already has. The right-hand side is one of three things,
and the spelling says which: a **bare literal** (a number, a percent, a color, a string, a
keyword — set once), a **`{ }` constraint** (TypeScript that stays true), or a **`:path`**
read from bound data. A bare `[ … ]` list fills an array-typed attribute.

One family of names may be set on a node that does not declare them: the built-in
**provided values** — the text face (`fontSize`, `fontFamily`, `fontWeight`, `textColor`,
`letterSpacing`), `theme`, `iconSize`, and the rich-text attributes. Setting one on a container
*provides* it to every descendant that reads it (see `provided`).

A set attribute with a `{ }` is **owned by its constraint**: the runtime keeps it current, and a direct
write to it is refused with a message naming the fix — derived state is never assigned;
change its inputs. In a handler, `name = value` is the setter: the write lands when the
handler returns, together with every other write it made, in one settle.

children.name: name: Type = value
children.subtitle: Members
children.label: Language form
children.doc:
# name: Type = value

```declare-fragment
name: Type = value
name: Type                                 // no default: undefined until written
rows: Row[] = []
panel: Menu? = null                         // a class — the attribute holds an instance
```

Declares a new reactive attribute — the way state enters a program. The type is a
TypeScript type, the same vocabulary a signature uses: TypeScript's built-ins (`number`,
`string`, `Map<string, Row>`), Declare's own (`Color`, `Length`, `Radius`), a class, a
declared schema, a literal union (`"open" | "closed"`), an array, a tuple, or a function
type. The default is a bare literal or a `{ }` expression.

A declaration's `{ }` default is only a **formula**: reading it inlines the
expression, and an assignment simply replaces it — the right tool for a value you may take
over later, which is how `TextInput.initial` differs from its read-only `text = { … }` twin.
Compare `set`: a set attribute is owned by its `{ }` and refuses assignment.
