content, and for the App it is the window. On a scrolled page, `transformTo(app)` differs
from `rootTransform()` by the page's scroll: its `y` is less by `app.scrollY` (and its `x`
by `app.scrollX`). The two may be in different programs: the walk
goes on from a hosted program's root through the island that hosts it, so a program in a
desktop window can place a view of its own against one of the host's (what a `Menu` does
when it opens in the window's layer). A one-shot query, like `rootTransform()`.
- `rootOrigin(): { x: number; y: number }` — This view's origin in **root space** (the root's content coordinates — the same space
`viewAt` takes and drag events carry), computed by the one scroll-aware walk the pointer
itself is routed by: translate per level, minus every intermediate scroller's offset, the
root's own scroll back at the boundary. The anchor primitive for overlays — a menu opening
at a pointer, a popover dropping under a control — so they land where the view is *seen*,
at any scroll. Hand-accumulating ancestor `x`/`y` is scroll-blind; call this instead.
- `scrollIntoView(align?: "start" | "nearest", smooth?: boolean, inset?: number): void` — Scrolls this view into the visible region of its nearest `scrolls` ancestor (or the page),
aligning its top to the viewport top — the imperative partner of the declarative jump-index
pattern. Both backends realize it natively (DOM `scrollIntoView`, canvas clamps the scroll
ancestor's `scrollOffset`). A no-op if nothing above it scrolls.
- `scrollTo(y: number | { x?: number; y?: number }, glide?: { duration?: number; motion?: string }): void` — Ask **this scroller** to go to offset `y` — a **request, not an assignment**: the platform
clamps it to the real scroll range, and a pane that cannot take it yet (hidden, or not yet
laid out) holds the request and applies it the moment it can — so `scrollTo(0)` before
showing a pane simply works. A request past the end of content still to arrive waits
for it: the pane goes as far as it can now and follows the content as it grows, until it
reaches `y` — unless the reader scrolls, or another request comes first. **`scrollTo(Infinity)` means the far end** — "scroll to the
bottom" with no magic number; the clamp resolves it against the range the pane has when it
can finally take it. The `scrollY` fact follows the platform's answer. Call it on the
`scrolls` view itself; to reveal a particular *view*, `scrollIntoView()` on the target
finds the scroller for you. A no-op before the view is attached.

**Both axes, or the other one.** `scrollTo({ x, y })` makes one request for both axes of a
`scrolls = both` view, with the same optional glide: `scrollTo({ x: 0, y: 0 })` returns a
large picture to its corner. Leave out an axis to keep it where it is. For the horizontal
axis alone, `scrollToX(x)`.

**The user may be scrolling the same pane.** Scrolling is a process the platform owns, driven
by a hand that does not pause for the program, so a request can arrive mid-gesture and lose —
overridden by momentum, or worse, fighting it. Two habits keep the two from contending. Ask
because something *changed by this much* rather than because the offset is near some value:
a reader who is following the end of a list wants the new content, and a reader who scrolled
up wants to be left alone, and only the first is expressible as growth. And read `scrolling`
before asking, so a request waits for a hand that is still moving. What does not work is
re-asserting a position every frame; the gesture will win, and the program will spend the
whole gesture losing.

**With a glide** — `scrollTo(y, { duration, motion })` — the request moves the pane over
`duration` milliseconds on the platform's own motion: the browser's smooth scroll, the
native host's tween, the canvas runtime's loop. `motion` names a Declare curve
(`"cubicOut"`, the default; any family token) where the provider can honor one. This is
not an Animator: no Animator semantics, no driven attribute — the scroller glides, `scrollY` reports
as it goes, and a **gesture cancels it** (the user always wins). A request that arrives
while a gesture or its momentum owns the pane is dropped.
- `scrollToX(x: number, glide?: { duration?: number; motion?: string }): void` — The horizontal twin of `scrollTo()` — the same clamped, held request against `scrollX`,
for a `scrolls = x` (or `both`) view, with the same optional glide. One difference: a
request past the end stops at the end the content has when it is made, rather than waiting
for more.
- `scrollBy(dx: number, dy: number, glide?: { duration?: number; motion?: string }): void` — A **relative** request — `scrollBy(dx, dy)`, or `scrollBy(dx, dy, { duration, motion })`
— measured from the current facts: `scrollBy(0, -pane.height)` pages up. The same
clamp, hold and glide contract as `scrollTo()`/`scrollToX()`, on both axes at once.
- `createView(tag: string, props?: Record<string, unknown>): View` — Instantiates a class **by tag name** into this view — the receiver is the parent, and
with it the new instance's scope and data anchor. Returns the created view, a full
citizen: constraints installed, `onInit` fired, and the parent's arrangement and auto-size
take it in on arrival. The imperative door, for structure that genuinely cannot be
declared; reach for replication over a datapath first — it reconciles, keys, and tears
down for you.

**The build drops classes nothing statically references**, so a class you only
ever name as a *string* needs `use [ Name ]` at the top level to survive. That is the one
non-obvious requirement, and forgetting it fails at runtime, not compile time. The
returned view is yours: `discard()` it when done.

```declare-fragment
use [ Menu ]
…
onInit() { this.list = app.createView("Menu", ({ })) }
```

The library builds its own overlays exactly this way — a `Menu` cannot declare a `Menu`
child without recursing, so the cascade is created by name at first use (parented to the
`app` root plane, which is why the receiver there is `app` itself).
- `raise(below?: View | null): void` — Moves this view to the **top of its parent's children**, so it paints over its siblings —
stacking is declaration order, and this is the runtime verb for changing it. **The
primitive every overlay needs**: a menu, a popover, or a dialog raises itself on open so
it is not occluded by whatever was declared after it. Pass a sibling to be raised *below*
that view instead, which is how chrome stays above content while staying under an even
higher layer.

```declare-fragment
onPointerDown() { this.raise() }        // click-to-front, e.g. a window in a desktop
```

## Inherited from [Node](declare-docs:Node)

### Attributes

| name | type | default | |
|---|---|---|---|
| `trackChanges` | array |  |  |
| `datapath` | datapath |  |  |

**`trackChanges`** — The values this node reports changes to: `trackChanges = [ "loaded", "kind" ]`. Each name
must be one of the node's own reactive values — an attribute it declares, a fact it carries
(`scrollY`, `loaded`, `hovered`), or an attribute bound to data. The checker refuses a stranger
in a written list, and the runtime refuses one in a computed list when the node arms. To
hear a record's field, declare an attribute over the path (`kind: string = { :kind }`) and
name that — there is one door. Nothing else is tracked, so a node that names nothing costs
nothing.

**`datapath`** — The data cursor: the place in a dataset this node and its descendants read and write
relative to. Written as a `:path` (extending the inherited cursor), a `{ }` expression
yielding a place (`datapath = { app.d.value.tasks[app.pick] }`), or null. The nearest
ancestor-or-self cursor wins, so a Node class with its own `datapath` stands on that
record, and views inside it read the same one. A `:path` ending in `[]` replicates — and
only a view replicates; on any other node that form is a compile error naming the
single-record spelling.

### Events

- `onInit()` — Fires once when the node has finished constructing and its subtree exists — the place for
setup that needs the built tree. Every node gets it, **faceless subclasses included** — the
init walk visits non-View children too. Answered by `onInit()`.
- `onChange(e: ChangeEvent)` — Fires at the **close of a settle** in which one or more tracked values ended different from
where they started: after every constraint has re-run and every reader already holds the new
value. One call per settle carries all of them, so a node whose two subjects move together
acts once. Answered by `onChange(e: ChangeEvent)`, where `e.changed` holds one `ValueChange`
per value — its `name`, its `previousValue` (what it held at the previous close), and its
`currentValue` (what the node holds now; reading the attribute directly gives the same
thing). Silent at boot: first values are not changes, and setup belongs in `onInit` or, for
the whole tree, the App's `onReady`. A handler's writes are the next settle, so a change may
cause a change; a handler may not assign a value it was told about, and a ring of handlers
ends on its own, because a value is delivered at most once per settle chain.

Not to be confused with an input's edits, which is the instinct the name carries in from
HTML and React: a field reports what the reader typed through `onInput`, and a control
reports its own value through `input()`. This event is about a value the *program* holds.

**Use it only for a genuine state change** — something happened and the program must act
once: record that the terms were read when the reader reaches their end, open a pane when the data
lands, start a fetch when a selection changes. It is not for following a value, which is a
constraint, nor for moving one, which is a Spring, and it is not meant for use in
conjunction with animation.

### Methods

- `$data(path: string | readonly unknown[]): unknown` — Reads the datum at a path **relative to the nearest cursor** — this node's own, or the
nearest ancestor's — the compiled form every
`:path` lowers to, callable by hand. `$data("")` is the whole record at the cursor, which
is what a replicated row calls to hand its own record to a method. Reach for the `:path`
spelling in ordinary code; reach for this when the path is computed, or when you need the
record itself rather than a field of it.

```declare-fragment
item() -> object { return this.datapath != null ? this.$data("") : this }
```
- `$cell(segs: readonly unknown[]): { value: unknown }` — The compiled form of a write to a record field: a handler's `:done = v` lowers to
`this.$cell(["done"]).value = v`, and `:n += 1` reads and writes through the same place.
The write lands through the dataset's `set`, relative to the nearest cursor, exactly where
the matching read resolves. Write `:field = v`; this is what the compiler emits, not a call
to make by hand.

# Slider

*Class — [Control](declare-docs:Control) → [View](declare-docs:View) → [Node](declare-docs:Node)*

A bounded number by drag. Same value contract as every control — `value` is the
attribute, **`input` owns the destination** (default: itself) — and the delivery
is continuous during a drag. Pressing the track jumps to that position (local
coordinates); the drag then follows the pointer by root-space delta
(`app.pointerX`), so it survives the pointer leaving the control. Arrow keys
nudge by `step`.

```declare
col: View [ x = 20, y = 20,
    layout: SimpleLayout [ axis = y, spacing = 10 ],
    vol: Slider [ value = 40 ],
    Text [ text = { `volume ${Math.round(vol.value)}` } ]
    ]
```

## Attributes

| name | type | default | |
|---|---|---|---|
| `value` | number | `0` |  |
| `min` | number | `0` |  |
| `max` | number | `100` |  |
| `step` | number | `1` |  |
| `frac` | number |  |  |
| `dragging` | boolean | `false` |  |
| `accessibilityRole` | none | button | toggle | checkbox | switch | radio | slider | progress | textField | link | image | heading | list | listItem | grid | row | cell | columnHeader | tabList | tab | tabPanel | menu | menuBar | menuItem | dialog | alertDialog | group | toolbar | region | status | listbox | option | tree | treeItem | radioGroup | combobox | separator | searchBox | spinButton | navigation | main | search | banner | complementary | `slider` |  |
| `accessibilityLabel` | string | `{ provided("fieldLabel", "") }` |  |
| `accessibilityValue` | number | `{ value }` |  |
| `accessibilityMin` | number | `{ min }` |  |
| `accessibilityMax` | number | `{ max }` |  |
| `accessibilityStep` | number | `{ step }` |  |
| `width` | Length | `220` |  |
| `height` | Length | `28` |  |
| `opacity` | number | `{ disabled ? (provided("theme").disabledOpacity) : 1 }` |  |

**`value`** — Where the handle sits, in your own units. Standalone the slider owns it; constrained
(`value = { app.volume }`) it needs an `input` override with it, or the drag's own
delivery is refused against the constraint.

**`min`** — The value at the left end.

**`max`** — The value at the right end.

**`step`** — The quantum every delivered value snaps to, and the distance one arrow key moves.
`step = 0.01` for a fine continuous control; **it is never zero** — the quantizer
divides by it.

**`frac`** — The handle's position as 0…1, derived from the value and the range. What the track,
fill, and thumb all position from; read it to hang your own decoration off the handle.

**`dragging`** — True from pointer-down until the captured release. **The `pressed` intrinsic
deliberately will not do here** — it is hit-chain-based, so it goes false the moment the
pointer leaves the thumb, while a drag must survive exactly that.

**`accessibilityLabel`** — The caption of a `Field` around it, unless the use site names the slider: its name to a screen
reader.

**`accessibilityValue`** — Follows `value`, in the slider's own units.

**`accessibilityMin`** — Follows `min`.

**`accessibilityMax`** — Follows `max`.

**`accessibilityStep`** — Follows `step` — what one increment moves. A slider shows no name, so its use site sets `accessibilityLabel`.

**`opacity`** — Disabled dims the whole control — every part alike, never a recolour — to the theme's `disabledOpacity`, or 0.45 when the theme states none: the one place the number lives.

## Events

- `onPointerDown(e)` — Jumps the value to the pressed position, claims focus, and latches the drag.
- `onPointerUp()` — Ends the drag.
- `onPointerMove()` — Tracks the drag by **root-space** pointer delta, so the handle keeps up with a pointer
that has left the control.
- `onKeyDown(e)` — Home and End go to `min` and `max`; Page Up and Page Down move a tenth of the range, never
less than a `step`. The arrows step, as `Control` gives every slider.

## Methods

- `focusShape()` — Rings the circular grabber — the part the arrow keys move — rather than the whole track.
- `input(v)` — **Where the value goes**, and it fires **continuously through a drag**, not once at
release: the owner decides what to do with the stream, and the data layer owns any
coalescing. Override it to redirect the value (`input(v: number) { app.volume = v }`);
the default writes `value`.
- `quant(v)` — Snaps a raw value to `step` and clamps it into `min`…`max`. Every delivery routes
through it, so an override changes what the slider can produce — logarithmic scales,
detents, a magnetic centre.
- `accessibilityIncrement()` — One `step` up, through `quant` and `input` like any other change — what the Right and Up
arrows run (Control's keys), and what a screen reader's increment calls.
- `accessibilityDecrement()` — One `step` down — what Left and Down run.
- `barStyle()` — True when the theme asks for the Material-3 rendition: a vertical bar handle with the
track shortened either side of it rather than drawn through. One theme token
(`provided("theme").sliderHandleStyle`) selects a rendition — **data, not a fork**.
- `dotStyle()` — True for the Fluent rendition: a round grabber with an accent dot inside that grows
under hover and press. The other value of the same token.

## Inherited from [Control](declare-docs:Control)

### Attributes

| name | type | default | |
|---|---|---|---|
| `disabled` | boolean | `false` |  |
| `focusVisible` | boolean | `false` |  |
| `iconLeft` | string | `""` |  |
| `iconRight` | string | `""` |  |
| `menu` | View? | `null` |  |
| `menuOpen` | boolean |  |  |
| `rightIcon` | string |  |  |
| `flash` | boolean | `false` |  |
| `flashMs` | number | `220` |  |
| `focusable` | boolean | `{ !disabled }` |  |
| `accessibilityRole` | none | button | toggle | checkbox | switch | radio | slider | progress | textField | link | image | heading | list | listItem | grid | row | cell | columnHeader | tabList | tab | tabPanel | menu | menuBar | menuItem | dialog | alertDialog | group | toolbar | region | status | listbox | option | tree | treeItem | radioGroup | combobox | separator | searchBox | spinButton | navigation | main | search | banner | complementary | `button` |  |
| `accessibilityExpanded` | boolean | `{ this.menu != null ? this.menuOpen : null }` |  |

**`disabled`** — Inert: not focusable, no activation, and `hovered`/`pressed` read false, so a
disabled control never lights up. **Constrain it rather than assigning it**
(`disabled = { app.muted }`) — it is ordinary derived state. Concrete controls also
dim themselves against `provided("theme").disabledOpacity`.

**`focusVisible`** — Focused **and** the focus arrived by keyboard — the web's `:focus-visible` channel.
Cleared by blur and by a pointer press on this control, so a clicked control shows no
keyboard edge while a tabbed one does. What a `Pane` header's focus edge reads.

**`iconLeft`** — A decorative icon for the leading slot, **named by class** (`iconLeft = "TrashIcon"`),
not nested as a child — a control is a leaf, and a name is the one form where authored
and data-bound are the same mechanism (`iconLeft = { "" + :icon }` in a replicated
toolbar). Control only declares the attribute; the concrete control lays it out. A
**computed** name needs `use [ Name ]` to survive the build, since no static reference
reaches it. The name is read once, when the control is built: a name read from data gives
each row its own icon, but changing the name later does not swap the icon (see `IconHost`).
Any icon class may be named, your own included — a library icon set another way is a
subclass: `class BackChevron extends ChevronIcon [ dir = "left" ]`, then
`iconLeft = "BackChevron"`.

**`iconRight`** — The trailing icon slot, same vocabulary as `iconLeft`. Setting it **wins over the
chevron a `menu` would imply** — see `rightIcon`.

**`menu`** — The menu this control drops — an instance, not a name (`menu = { app.optionsMenu }`).
Setting it is a *role*, not decoration: the disclosure mark, the anchored open below
the control, the held-open fill, and ArrowDown-to-open all follow together. **Declare
one menu and point many controls at it** rather than one per opener; the menu reads
`opener` to vary its items.

**`menuOpen`** — True while `menu` is showing *and* this control is what opened it. **Derived, never
written** — a flag set on open goes stale the moment the menu closes some other way
(Escape, a pick, a press on the backdrop) and strands the control in its held-open
look forever.

**`rightIcon`** — What actually renders on the right: `iconRight` when set, else the disclosure chevron
implied by `menu`, else nothing. One place decides, so every menu-dropping control
wears the same mark.

**`flash`** — The keyboard-activation pulse — the control's own state, which `pressed` reads as a
press, so Space/Enter shows the same look a pointer press does and styling reads only
`hovered` and `pressed`.

**`flashMs`** — How long `flashPress()` holds the pressed look.

**`focusable`** — A control takes focus unless it is disabled — one rule, so a disabled control drops out of the Tab order without saying so twice.

**`accessibilityRole`** — `button`: a control is something a person presses, and a screen reader says so with no word
from the program. A control that is something else — a checkbox, a slider, a tab — names its
own role.

**`accessibilityExpanded`** — Whether the control's `menu` is open — follows `menuOpen`, so a screen reader hears a
menu button as collapsed or expanded. Unset (null) on a control with no menu.

### Events

- `onFocus()` — Captures the keyboard modality into `focusVisible`. An override must keep it or the
focus channel goes dark. (`focused` itself is every view's fact, kept by the focus service.)
- `onBlur()` — Clears `focusVisible`.
- `onPointerDown()` — Claims focus, clears the `:focus-visible` channel, and opens `menu` if there is one —
menus open on **press**, not release, as the platform does. **An override must keep the
`Focus.focus(this)` call**, or clicking the control strands the keyboard elsewhere.
- `onKeyDown(e)` — Space and Enter run `press()`; ArrowDown opens `menu`. On a `slider`, the arrow keys
run `accessibilityIncrement()` and `accessibilityDecrement()` — the methods a screen
reader's adjust gesture calls, which the `slider` role requires a control to have — so
the keyboard and assistive technology move the value by one path; on a `spinButton`, Up and
Down do the same. Ignores auto-repeat for activation, not for the arrows.
- `onClick()` — A click runs `press()` unless the control is disabled — so a control that overrides
`press()` is activated by pointer and keyboard alike without writing a handler. Override
`onClick` only when a click means something other than activation; `Button` does, making
it the use site's action.

### Methods

- `openMenu()` — Opens `menu` anchored to this control, unless there is none or the control is disabled.
The seam a concrete control calls from its own `press()`.
- `press()` — **The activation seam — override this, not the handlers.** Pointer and keyboard both
land here — a click through `onClick`, Space and Enter through the keyboard — so one
override serves all three. The base opens `menu` when
there is one. A value control delivers through `input` from here and **never writes its
own value directly**, which is what lets a constrained control avoid fighting its
constraint.
- `focusShape()` — The focus silhouette the ring hugs, `{ x, y, w, h, rad }` in this control's own
coordinates. `null` (the default) rings the whole bounds at its `cornerRadius`. Override
to ring the part that means something — a `Radio` rings its dot, a `Slider` its thumb.
- `flashPress()` — Flashes the pressed look to acknowledge keyboard activation — the platform convention
for buttons and menu items. **Value controls whose state change is itself the feedback
(Checkbox, Switch, Radio) deliberately do not call it.**
