# Menu

*Class — [Floating](declare-docs:Floating) → [View](declare-docs:View) → [Node](declare-docs:Node)*

The record-driven menu: **items are data** — the class arranges; the
author never composes rows. The standard record covers real OS menus:

    { id, label, key?, icon?, enabled?, checked?, divider?, submenu?, kind?, props?, minWidth? }

- `key` renders right-aligned — display only; the menu registers no shortcut.
- `icon: "ClassName"` names an icon class for the leading column, and the label
  shifts right to make room — the same vocabulary `Segmented`'s choices use.
  One field covers every mark, including the ones no font gives you; a computed
  name needs its class kept with `use [ Name ]`, since no static reference
  reaches it.
- `enabled: false` dims the row (provided("theme").disabledOpacity) and refuses pick.
- `{ divider: true }` is a separator line.
- `submenu: [ …records… ]` marks a cascade (the ▸ arrow).
- `kind: "ClassName"` renders the row's content with a named author class
  (app.createView — keep data-only classes with `use [ Name ]`), passed
  `props` as its datapath context. Behavior stays the row's: highlight,
  pick, keyboard are the menu's, always.
- `minWidth` is the room a row needs when it has no label to measure — a
  `kind:` row's own content. The panel is at least this wide; a longer label
  elsewhere still wins. Only a custom row needs it.

Declared once, opened by many: rows carry
`onContextMenu(e) { app.rowMenu.openAt(this, e) }`; the menu's `items`
constraint derives from `opener` — per-row variation with zero per-row
instances, live while open. `openAt` point-positions (the context-menu
rule); `openFor` drops below a control (the attached-menu rule); both
place it in the overlay layer of its context — above everything opened before it — and clamp
it inside the app. A menu is a `Floating` (floating.declare).

Dismissal: a press outside closes the whole chain **and** is swallowed, the Mac rule (a
submenu lets a press on its parent menu through); Escape closes the chain; pick closes
after delivery.

```declare
App [ width = 320, height = 130,
    chose: string = "",
    edit: Menu [ items = { [ ({ id: "cut", label: "Cut", key: "⌘X" }),
                            ({ id: "copy", label: "Copy", key: "⌘C", checked: true }),
                            ({ divider: true }),
                            ({ id: "paste", label: "Paste", enabled: false }) ] },
        picked(id: string) { app.chose = id }
        ],
    Button [ x = 20, y = 20, label = "Edit", menu = { app.edit } ],
    Text [ x = 20, y = 74, text = { app.chose == "" ? "nothing picked" : "picked: " + app.chose } ]
    ]
```

**`asList`** — A list of choices rather than commands: each row is an `option`, not a `menuItem`, selected
when its record says `selected: true`. A `Combobox` makes its list this way, with the `listbox`
role given at creation (`createView("Menu", { accessibilityRole: "listbox", asList: true })`).

**`widestLabel`** — The widest row label, measured — the content the panel's width is built from.

**`widestKey`** — The widest key equivalent, measured; zero when no row carries one, which is what
decides whether the key column exists.

**`hasSubs`** — Whether any row opens a submenu — a cascade arrow needs its own trailing room.

**`widestCustom`** — The widest `minWidth` any row asks for. A `kind:` row renders its own content and has no
label to measure, so it states the room it needs in its record and the panel is at least
that wide; a longer label elsewhere still wins.

**`minWidth`** — The narrowest a menu gets, whatever its rows measure — a two-item menu of short words
still reads as a menu.

**`items`** — The rows, as **records — never children**. A menu arranges its own rows, so handing it
views is not merely discouraged, there is nowhere to put them. The record is
`{ id, label, key?, icon?, enabled?, checked?, selected?, divider?, submenu?, kind?, props?, minWidth? }`
(`selected` is read only in a list of choices: see `asList`);
a plain array is fine (no `Dataset` required). Because it is an ordinary attribute it
can be a constraint — **derive it from `opener` and one menu serves every row of a
table**, live while it is open.

**`hasIcons`** — Whether any row carries an `icon` — which is what decides the icon gutter exists at
all. **A menu with no icons has no gutter**, and the text edge moves accordingly.

**`hasChecks`** — Whether any row *can* be checked — a record carrying `checked`, true or false — which
is what decides the check column exists, exactly as AppKit reserves its state column
for any item with a state image to draw. A menu of plain
commands leads its text 17 in; one with a checkable row, 24.

**`checkW`** — What the check column adds to the leading air when it exists (7 — the Mac's 25.5 vs
17.5, measured), else 0: the amount every column to its right shifts by.

**`textEdge`** — The x every row's label starts at — one line for the whole menu, icons or not, and what
a `kind` row must align its own content to.

**`isRoot`** — False on a cascade child. The root owns the backdrop, the deferred delivery, and the
Escape-closes-everything behaviour; a submenu delegates all three upward.

**`rootMenu`** — The root of this menu's cascade chain — null on the root itself.

**`child`** — The one lazily-created submenu instance, reused across every row that cascades. **A
`Menu` cannot declare a `Menu` child** (it would recurse), so the cascade is built by
name at first use.

**`activeRow`** — The row the keyboard rover currently highlights, or null when the pointer is driving.
Read-only in practice.

**`typeahead`** — Whether typing a letter moves the keyboard highlight to a row — `true` by default, as in
every desktop menu: type "ex" to land on Export. The highlight only moves; Return picks.
A `Combobox` turns it off on its list, whose letters belong to its text field.

**`takesFocus`** — True: an open menu holds the focus, so a screen reader follows it, and hands it back to
what had it when the menu closes. A `Combobox` turns it off for its list, whose field keeps
the focus.

**`accessibilityActiveItem`** — The highlighted row's item: a screen reader hears each row as the arrows reach it.

**`accessibilityLabel`** — The opener's name, so a menu opened from "Styling" is the "Styling" menu.

**`pressPolicy`** — `dismiss` for the root — an outside press closes the chain and goes no further; `dismissAndDeliver` for a submenu, so a press on its parent menu goes on to it.

**`visible`** — Derived from `shown`, the menu's own open fact. Visibility is never set from outside — `openAt` and `openFor` set the fact, and dismissal clears it.

**`height`** — As tall as its panel, which is as tall as its rows — capped just inside the app's
height, past which the panel scrolls its rows and the rover keeps the landing row in
view.

**`width`** — Follows the rows: the text edge, the widest label, then the key column or the trailing
air — the metrics of a real macOS menu, measured (the longest label trails the edge by
18; a key column sits 26 clear of the longest label and ends 16 from the edge; menu bar
menus and popups measure the same). A use site's own `width` overrides; `minWidth`
floors it.

## Events

- `onKeyDown(e)` — Takes nothing itself: a menu's keys are its rover's, which hears them however the focus
lies. Declared so that a menu holding the focus inside a group (a menu bar's) is not
walked by the group's arrows.
- `onOutsidePress()` — A press outside closed it: the root closes the whole chain; a submenu closes itself and
lets the press go on to its parent menu.

## Methods

- `focusFirst()` — Holds the focus on the menu itself, never on a view inside it: the menu names the row
the keys are on.
- `picked(id)` — **The delivery seam — override it at the use site.** Receives the picked row's `id`,
and the id is the whole message. Called *after* the menu has left the screen, so a slow
action can never freeze an open menu.
- `expectedHeight()` — The panel's height *before it has been laid out*, measured when it exists and estimated
from the record count when it does not. The flip-above decision cannot wait for a
settle, which is why this exists.
- `openAt(v, e)` — Opens the menu **at the pointer**, given the serving view and the pointer event — the
context-menu rule. Clamped inside the app like any placement. `ContextMenu` wraps this
as `open`.
- `openFor(v)` — Opens the menu **anchored below a control**, flipping above it when there is not room
below and more room above — the native select discipline. The attached-menu rule; what
`Control.menu` uses.
- `place(x, y)` — Positions the panel at a point in the frame of the layer it paints in, moved as little as
it must be to stay on the App — a menu opened in a window may hang past the window's edge,
not off the App. The place is taken at open: menu chrome does not move while a menu is up.
- `close()` — Takes the menu down, closes any cascade under it, and releases the keyboard claim.
- `escape()` — Esc closes the whole chain.
- `pick(id)` — Delivers a row: **dismisses first, then delivers**, one painted frame later — the
native menu contract, and the reason a long-running action cannot leave a menu stranded
on screen. A submenu routes to the root so the whole chain closes as one.
- `openSub(row, subItems)` — Opens a row's `submenu`, creating the shared child menu on first use and placing it
alongside the row.
- `closeSub()` — Closes the cascade under this menu, if any.
- `rootClose()` — Closes the entire chain from wherever it is called — what Escape and an outside press
both do.
- `step(d)` — Moves the keyboard rover by ±1 over the pickable rows, skipping dividers, disabled rows
and custom-content rows, and scrolls the landing row into view.
- `typeTo(ch)` — Moves the highlight to the first enabled row whose label starts with what has been typed:
the prefix grows while typing continues and starts over after a pause, and the same
letter again goes on to the next row that starts with it.
- `pickActive()` — Picks the roved row — Enter's action. On a row with a `submenu` it enters the cascade
instead.
- `enterSub()` — Enters the roved row's submenu and puts the rover on its first row — ArrowRight's action.
- `sideways(d)` — **Where Right and Left go past the menu's own levels**: Right on a row with no submenu, Left
in the top menu. Nothing by default; a `MenuBar` answers it by opening the menu beside
this one, as every desktop menu bar does.

class-level fact.

opens and closes as the state does (SwiftUI's `isPresented`).

fresh for each opening reads it, so it stays through the closing motion instead of
emptying the panel as it goes: `entry: Form [ exists = { app.formSheet.present } ]`.

**`opener`** — The view it was opened for, when it was opened for one.

**`scrollPolicy`** — What a scroll outside it does while it is open — `scrollBelow`'s value then.

**`paintsIn`** — Follows `host`: it paints in the layer it opened into.

**`scale`** — Its program's scale where it opens in a host's layer (`_baseScale`) — a subclass multiplies

**`rotation`** — Its program's turn where it opens in a host's layer (`_baseRotation`), in degrees.

**`scrollBelow`** — `scrollPolicy` while it is open, `none` once it closes.

- `onInit()`

**`x`** — The horizontal offset within the parent's content box, in pixels — `center` and `end`
place the view centered or flush against the far edge. **What a parent's `layout` places,
the child does not declare**: under a row (which places `x`), setting `x` in any spelling is
a compile error naming what to use instead, and a handler writing it while the layout
arranges the child is refused. Use `x` for free-form placement, a `layout` for arrangement,
and `ignoreLayout = true` for a child that must stand apart from its parent's layout.

**`y`** — The vertical offset within the parent's content box — the twin of `x`, with the same
ownership rule: a layout that places `y` (a stack, or a row with `align`) owns it.

**`width`** — The box's width, in **pixels** (`Length`). Left unset, a view is as wide as its content —
the run a `Text` lays out, the bitmap an `Image` shows, and the boxes of its visible
children (padding included); a view with nothing in it is `0`. Otherwise set a constant,
`100%` (the parent's content box), or a `{ }` constraint. Set it live and children
constrained to it reflow in the same frame; there is no re-layout call. To size to content
with a limit, constrain it: `width = { Math.min(contentWidth, 480) }`.

**`height`** — The box's height in pixels (`Length`), mirroring `width`: left unset, a view is as tall as
its content. A `Text` left unsized takes its natural measured height, so you usually set
`height` only to fix a size, to clip, or to limit growth.

**`fill`** — What paints the box: a solid `Color` or a `gradient(…)` — the one attribute, subsuming a
plain background color. `null` (the default) paints **nothing** — an unfilled box is
invisible but still lays out and still catches clicks. In a `[ ]` literal a color is
`#RRGGBB`; inside a `{ }` body it is `0xRRGGBB` (the one place the spelling differs).

```declare
App [
    View [ x = 20, y = 20, width = 260, height = 80, cornerRadius = 8, fill = { gradient("90deg", 0x1E2A36, 0x0B141B) } ]
    ]
```

**`padding`** — **The view's content box** — the inset between this box and the room its children live in.
One number insets all four sides; four are `[top, right, bottom, left]`, clockwise from the
top, the one-or-four house pattern `cornerRadius` and `stroke` share. A negative number is
clamped to 0. This is the attribute a fixed inset wants — not a wrapper view, and not the
layout.

**A padded view has an *inside*, and `x = 0` / `y = 0` mean that inside's origin — for
every child.** One a layout arranged, one that placed itself at `x = center`, one with
`ignoreLayout = true`: they all start at the content origin, because a position in this
view is *by definition* measured from the content box. There is no CSS-style split where
an absolutely-positioned child escapes the inset. A layout is not involved — it simply
arranges within the room it is given (`Layout.contentExtent`), so a view with no `layout:`
at all is padded just the same, a `place()` you write yourself honors the inset without
naming it, and **replacing a `layout:` member does not replace the padding** (`padding = 0`
is what takes it away).

**`100%` means the content box; `{ parent.width }` still means the parent's box.** A
percent — and `x = center` and `x = end` with it — resolves against the room you are given,
so `width = 100%` in a `padding = 16` card is the card's width less 32, and a centered child
is centered between the insets. `{ parent.width }` is the deliberate escape hatch — the
parent's literal width, padding and all — and an edge-to-edge child inside a padded box is
that paired with a negative `x`: `x = -16, width = { parent.width }`, the divider that runs
wall to wall across a card. The asymmetry is the point: "the space I am given" and "the
parent's own width" are different questions, and the spelling says which one you asked.

**Paint does not move.** `fill`, `stroke`, `cornerRadius` and `draw()` are all this view's
own box, so a card's background still covers its padding and a border still runs around the
outside of it — nothing about the inset changes what the view looks like, only where its
children begin. The inset lives in this view's own coordinate space, so it scales and
rotates with the box like any other geometry. Hit-testing walks the same content box a
layout places into, so a press finds a child exactly where it is drawn.

**Both insets count toward size.** A view with an unset width or height grows by the pair on
that axis, so a padded panel sizing to `contentHeight` reserves the room under its last
child as well as above its first. A *scrolling* view's extent includes them on all four
sides too: a padded scroller stops a full inset past its last child rather than flush
against it.

```declare
App [ fill = white, textColor = black,
    card: View [ x = 20, y = 20, width = 260, fill = whitesmoke, cornerRadius = 10,
        padding = 16,
        layout: SimpleLayout [ axis = y, spacing = 8 ],
        Text [ fontWeight = semibold, text = "Storage" ],
        Text [ textColor = slategray, text = "39.2 GB of 128 GB used" ]
        ]
    ]
```

**`cornerRadius`** — Rounds the **painted** box (default `0`, square). One number rounds all four corners;
four — `[topLeft, topRight, bottomRight, bottomLeft]`, clockwise from the top-left as
CSS orders them — round each on its own, and a corner given `0` stays square:
`cornerRadius = [0, 8, 0, 8]` rounds only the top-right and bottom-left, `[8, 8, 0, 0]`
is a tab that joins the pane below it. **One value, or four clockwise, is the house
pattern** for anything said per corner or per side: `stroke` and `padding`
read exactly the same way, each list starting at its own first edge — the top for those
two, the top-left corner for this one, because corners are what it names. A list of any
other length is a mistake, never a shorthand. Radii that would overlap along an edge shrink
together, so a radius past half the box is a pill, never a fold. It shapes fill, border,
and shadow — but not hit-testing or clipping: the box stays a rectangle for layout and
clicks. To clip children to the rounded shape, set `clip = true` as well. A `Spring` on
this attribute animates the number form.
